thrones.title: Sultan of Sokoto
thrones.grade: First class (pre-eminent; heads the Sokoto Sultanate Council)
thrones.established: 1804 (caliphate); title Sultan from 1817
thrones.about: The Sultan of Sokoto heads the dynasty founded by Usman dan Fodio, whose 1804 jihad created the Sokoto Caliphate, the largest state in nineteenth-century West Africa. Since the British conquest of 1903 the office has been a traditional throne without sovereign power, but it remains the most senior Islamic office in Nigeria. The current Sultan is Muhammadu Sa'adu Abubakar III, in office since 2006.

authority.text: This is a fused office: the Sultan is both a traditional ruler and Nigeria's foremost Muslim religious leader. He carries the titles Sarkin Musulmi ('King of the Muslims') and Amir al-Mu'minin ('Commander of the Faithful'), is President-General of the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs (NSCIA) and heads Jama'atu Nasril Islam (JNI). He is regarded as leader of the Qadiriyya Sufi order in Nigeria and formally announces the new moon that marks the start and end of Ramadan nationwide. As a traditional ruler he chairs the Sokoto Sultanate Council and the Sokoto State Council of Chiefs.

sections.history:
The office grew out of the reform movement of Usman dan Fodio, a Fulani scholar of the Torodbe clerical lineage who preached in the Hausa kingdom of Gobir. Conflict with the Gobir court led to his withdrawal (hijra) and the jihad of 1804, after which his followers acknowledged him as Amir al-Mu'minin. Commanders he commissioned with flags founded emirates from Kano and Zaria to Adamawa and Ilorin, all owing allegiance to the caliph.

Around 1812 dan Fodio divided the administration: his son Muhammad Bello governed the eastern emirates from Sokoto, while his brother Abdullahi governed the western emirates from Gwandu. On dan Fodio's death in 1817 Bello became the first ruler styled Sultan. Through the nineteenth century the throne passed among dan Fodio's descendants, chiefly the Houses of Bello and Atiku, with smaller lines such as Rufai and Buhari; emirs travelled or sent tribute to Sokoto and were confirmed by the Sultan.

British forces under Lord Lugard took Sokoto in March 1903. Sultan Muhammadu Attahiru I left the city with a large following and was killed later that year at Burmi; the British installed Muhammadu Attahiru II and turned the caliphate into a protectorate governed through indirect rule, with the Sultan as the senior Native Authority. The office kept great prestige, and Sultans such as Siddiq Abubakar III (1938–1988) played major roles in Northern Nigerian politics around independence.

Since independence the throne has been shaped by federal and state governments. The 1988 selection of Ibrahim Dasuki, favoured by the Babangida government over Muhammadu Maccido, set off deadly riots; in 1996 the Abacha regime deposed Dasuki and installed Maccido. After Maccido died in a 2006 plane crash, his brother Sa'adu Abubakar became the twentieth holder of the leadership (counting dan Fodio).
sections.selection: Sultans are chosen from male descendants of Usman dan Fodio. Candidates have historically come from several branches of the family, above all the Houses of Bello and Atiku, with the Rufai and Buhari lines also producing Sultans; there is no fixed rotation. A body of senior kingmakers of the Sultanate, traditionally led by the Waziri of Sokoto, assesses candidates and recommends one, and the state government formally approves and installs the choice. The 1988 and 1996 successions showed that the government's approval can be decisive: the military authorities installed Dasuki in 1988 over the candidate many electors preferred, then deposed him in 1996.
sections.council: The Sultan presides over the Sokoto Sultanate Council, which brings together the senior titled officials of the Sultanate (such as the Waziri, the Sultan's chief minister and head of the kingmakers), district heads and other emirs and chiefs of Sokoto State. Historically district and village heads were appointed by the Sultan, but a 2024 amendment to the Sokoto State Local Government and Chieftaincy Law moved that power to the governor, leaving the Sultanate Council a recommending role.
sections.palace: The Sultan's palace stands in the old city of Sokoto near the Sultan Bello Mosque, where Sultans are turbaned. Previous Sultans are buried at the Hubbare, the family tomb near dan Fodio's grave. The throne's insignia include the turban of office and the staff of office presented by the state, and the Sultan appears at durbars and Sallah (Eid) celebrations with mounted horsemen. Because he heads the moon-sighting committee, his announcements of Ramadan and the Eids are national events.
sections.today: Under Nigerian law the Sultan has no constitutional powers; his authority is moral, religious and customary, exercised through the Sokoto State Council of Chiefs, the NSCIA and the JNI. He is widely consulted on national security, interfaith relations and public-health campaigns. In June–July 2024 the Sokoto State House of Assembly amended the state chieftaincy law, and Governor Ahmed Aliyu signed it on 11 July 2024; it transferred the appointment of district and village heads from the Sultan to the governor. The move drew objections from Muslim groups who feared it was a step towards deposing the Sultan; the government denied any such plan, and as of the latest reports Sa'adu Abubakar III remains on the throne.

rulers.name: Usman dan Fodio
rulers.note: Scholar-reformer who led the jihad from 1804 and was acknowledged as Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful); he never used the title Sultan and later delegated the eastern and western halves of the caliphate to his son Muhammad Bello and his brother Abdullahi.
rulers.bio: A Fulani scholar of the Torodbe clerical lineage, Usman dan Fodio spent decades preaching reform in Gobir before open conflict with the Gobir court led to the hijra and jihad of 1804. His followers acknowledged him as Amir al-Mu'minin, and flag-bearers he commissioned went on to found emirates across what is now northern Nigeria and northern Cameroon. Around 1812 he divided administration between his son Muhammad Bello (east, from Sokoto) and his brother Abdullahi (west, from Gwandu), withdrawing himself to scholarship. He died in 1817. Every later Sultan of Sokoto descends from him, and his writings remain central to the identity of the office.

image.caption: The tomb of Usman dan Fodio in Sokoto

rulers.name: Muhammad Bello
rulers.note: First ruler to take the style of Sultan; consolidated the caliphate, founded Sokoto as its capital and wrote widely on government. Reigned 21 April 1817 – 25 October 1837.
rulers.bio: Muhammad Bello was Usman dan Fodio's son and one of the jihad's principal commanders. On his father's death in 1817 he became head of the caliphate and the first to be styled Sultan, governing the eastern emirates from Sokoto while his uncle Abdullahi governed the west from Gwandu. He spent much of his reign suppressing revolts and securing frontiers, founding fortified settlements (ribats) and building up Sokoto. A prolific author, he wrote histories and treatises on Islamic governance, including advice addressed to emirs such as Katsina's. He died at Wurno in 1837 and founded the House of Bello, one of the main lines from which later Sultans came.

image.caption: Official seal of Muhammad Bello, inscribed Amir al-mu'minin

rulers.name: Abubakar I Atiku
rulers.note: Founder of the House of Atiku; reigned 26 October 1837 – 23 November 1842.

rulers.name: Aliyu Babba
rulers.note: Reigned 30 November 1842 – 21 October 1859 (House of Bello).

rulers.name: Ahmadu Atiku
rulers.note: Reigned 24 October 1859 – 2 November 1866 (House of Atiku).

rulers.name: Aliyu Karami
rulers.note: Brief reign, 6 November 1866 – 18 October 1867.

rulers.name: Ahmadu Rufai
rulers.note: Reigned 21 October 1867 – 12 March 1873; founder of the House of Rufai.
rulers.dispute: The Wikipedia list gives his death as 1867 although his reign is dated to 1873; the reign dates are followed here.

rulers.name: Abubakar II Atiku na Raba
rulers.note: Reigned 16 March 1873 – 28 March 1877.

rulers.name: Mu'azu
rulers.note: Reigned 6 April 1877 – 26 September 1881; ancestor of Sultans Hasan, Siddiq Abubakar III, Maccido and Sa'adu Abubakar.

rulers.name: Umaru bin Aliyu
rulers.note: Reigned 3 October 1881 – 25 March 1891; died at Kaura Namoda.

rulers.name: Abdurrahman Atiku
rulers.note: Reigned 25 March 1891 – 10 October 1902, as British forces closed in on the caliphate.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Attahiru I
rulers.note: Shortest reign (13 October 1902 – 15 March 1903). Fled when the British took Sokoto in March 1903 and was killed later that year at Burmi (listed as Mbormi), resisting British forces.
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Attahiru I was a son of Sultan Ahmadu Atiku and took office in October 1902, as Lord Lugard's forces were advancing through the northern emirates. When British troops captured Sokoto in March 1903 he left the city rather than submit, and a large body of followers joined him on a migration eastward. The British treated him as deposed and installed a successor. He was killed in 1903 at Burmi, in present-day Gombe State, where his followers made a final stand. His reign of about five months is the shortest in the dynasty's history and marks the end of the independent caliphate.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Attahiru II
rulers.note: Installed on 21 March 1903 after the British conquest; first Sultan under colonial indirect rule.

image.caption: Sultan Muhammadu Attahiru II with his scribe

rulers.name: Muhammadu dan Ahmadu (Maiturare)
rulers.note: Reigned 1915–1924.

rulers.name: Muhammadu dan Muhammadu (Tambari)
rulers.note: Reigned 1924–1931 (House of Atiku).

rulers.name: Hasan dan Mu'azu
rulers.note: Reigned 1931–1938 (House of Bello).

image.caption: Sultan Hasan dan Mu'azu (with the Emirs of Gwandu and Kano) in London

rulers.name: Siddiq Abubakar III
rulers.note: Longest-reigning Sultan (crowned 17 June 1938; died 1 November 1988); bridged colonial rule, independence and military government.
rulers.bio: Born on 15 March 1903 at Dange, Abubakar received an Islamic education and served as a district scribe and then as a Native Authority councillor for Talata Mafara before the kingmakers chose him in 1938. He was crowned on 17 June 1938 and reigned for about fifty years, the longest in the dynasty. In 1951 he became a minister without portfolio in the Northern Regional Government, backing Premier Ahmadu Bello and the push for self-government. After Bello's assassination in January 1966 he worked to calm regional tensions. He was knighted (KBE) in 1944 and received the GCON in 1964. He died in Sokoto on 1 November 1988, and two of his sons, Maccido and Sa'adu Abubakar, later became Sultan.

image.caption: Sultan Siddiq Abubakar III, Sarkin Musulmi

rulers.name: Ibrahim Dasuki
rulers.parent: great-great-grandson of Usman dan Fodio (House of Buhari)
rulers.note: Chosen in December 1988 amid riots, as the military government's preferred candidate; deposed by the Abacha regime on 20 April 1996 and exiled to Jalingo.
rulers.bio: Ibrahim Dasuki was born on 31 December 1923 at Dogon Daji, the son of the district head Haliru ibn Barau, and was educated at Barewa College. He worked in publishing and the Northern civil service, became private secretary to Premier Ahmadu Bello, and later had a long business career, including chairing the Northern Nigeria Produce Marketing Board and the Nigerian Railway Corporation. He was the first Sultan from the Buhari branch of the dan Fodio family; his selection over Muhammadu Maccido in 1988 was seen as favoured by the Babangida government, and the announcement set off several days of rioting in Sokoto in which about ten people died. As Sultan he promoted Qur'anic schooling and adult literacy and worked to reorganise Jama'atu Nasril Islam and the NSCIA. On 20 April 1996 the Abacha military government deposed him and sent him into internal exile at Jalingo. He died in Abuja on 14 November 2016.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Maccido
rulers.note: Appointed after Dasuki's removal (crowned 21 April 1996); led the 2004 bicentenary of the jihad; killed in the ADC Airlines crash near Abuja on 29 October 2006.
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Maccido was born on 20 April 1928 near Sokoto, a son of Sultan Siddiq Abubakar III, and studied in Zaria and at South Devon College in Britain. He sat in the Northern House of Assembly, held posts in the Sokoto Native Authority, served as a North-Western State commissioner for agriculture and then health, and was a presidential liaison officer under Shehu Shagari. The electors favoured him in 1988, but the military government installed Ibrahim Dasuki instead. After Dasuki was deposed in 1996 he became Sultan and was crowned in the Sultan Bello Mosque on 21 April 1996. His decade on the throne emphasised reconciliation among Muslim groups and between faiths, and he presided over the 2004 bicentenary of dan Fodio's jihad. He died on 29 October 2006 when ADC Airlines Flight 53 crashed shortly after take-off from Abuja; his son, Senator Badamasi Maccido, also died.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Sa'adu Abubakar III
rulers.note: Retired brigadier-general; installed 2 November 2006 after his brother Maccido's death. Reigning; also President-General of the NSCIA and head of Jama'atu Nasril Islam.
rulers.bio: Sa'adu Abubakar was born in Sokoto on 24 August 1956, the youngest son of Sultan Siddiq Abubakar III. He attended Barewa College and the Nigerian Defence Academy and was commissioned into the Armoured Corps in 1977. His army career included command of a peacekeeping battalion in Chad, a battalion command in Kaduna, ECOWAS liaison duties, ECOMOG service in Sierra Leone, and a posting as defence attaché in Pakistan (also covering Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Afghanistan) from 2003 to 2006; he retired as a brigadier-general. He became Sultan on 2 November 2006, days after his brother Maccido died in a plane crash. As Sultan he heads the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs and Jama'atu Nasril Islam and announces the sighting of the new moon that begins and ends Ramadan. In 2024 the Sokoto State government enacted a law transferring the power to appoint district and village heads from the Sultan to the governor, a move widely seen as a curb on the throne.

thrones.title: Emir of Gwandu
thrones.established: c. 1808–1812 (Abdullahi dan Fodio's western capital)
thrones.about: Gwandu was the western twin capital of the Sokoto Caliphate, governed by Usman dan Fodio's brother Abdullahi and his descendants, with suzerainty over emirates such as Ilorin, Nupe and Kontagora. The emir has resided at Birnin Kebbi since the colonial period. The current holder, Muhammadu Iliyasu Bashar, has reigned since 2005.

authority.text: A fused office: the Emir of Gwandu is a traditional ruler and also the Islamic leader of his emirate. Historically he ranked as the second figure of the caliphate, the leader of the faithful in the western emirates, and the Sultan's counterpart; today he leads Eid prayers and religious observances in the emirate and sits with the Sultan in national Muslim bodies, while carrying out customary functions (titles, dispute mediation, district administration) under Kebbi State law.

sections.history:
Jihadist forces took Birnin Kebbi, capital of the Hausa kingdom of Kebbi, in 1805, and made the small town of Gwandu a base. Around 1812 Usman dan Fodio gave his brother Abdullahi responsibility for the western and southern parts of the caliphate. Abdullahi governed first from Bodinga and then Gwandu, and the emirates in his sphere, including Ilorin, Nupe (Bida), Kontagora, Agaie, Lapai and Yauri, looked to Gwandu rather than Sokoto.

Much of the nineteenth century was taken up by the Kebbi wars against the Kebbawa, who regrouped at Argungu. The Sarkin Kebbi Karari was killed in 1831 and Yakubu Nabame led resistance from 1849; an 1868 truce (Lafiyar Toga) broke down in 1873, and fighting continued until the British arrived.

Gwandu capitulated to the British on 12 March 1903 without fighting, under the elderly Emir Bayero Aliyu. It was placed in Sokoto Province under indirect rule. The British deposed Emir Muhammadu Aliyu in 1906 and installed Haliru of Kalgo, whose appointment met strong local opposition; the seat of the emirate then moved from Gwandu to Birnin Kebbi.

Kebbi State was created in 1991 with Birnin Kebbi as its capital. In 2005 Emir Mustapha Jokolo was deposed after a public clash with President Obasanjo, and his cousin, Major-General Muhammadu Iliyasu Bashar, was appointed; litigation over the throne lasted twenty years until the Supreme Court upheld Bashar in 2025.
sections.selection: Emirs are drawn from the descendants of Abdullahi dan Fodio. Historically the electors were senior officials, most often named as the Magajin Gari, Sarkin Dendi, Zogirma, Sarkin Aliero, the chief judge (Qadi) and the Sarkin Kebbi of Jega, and the Dan Galadima, as heir presumptive, normally succeeded. Today the kingmakers recommend a candidate and the Kebbi State governor approves the appointment under the Kebbi State Chiefs (Appointment and Deposition) Law, which also governs deposition and requires grievances to go first to the governor.
sections.council: The Gwandu Emirate Council brings together the emir, his senior title-holders (including the kingmakers) and the district heads of the emirate's districts across central and southern Kebbi State. District heads, often princes or senior titled officials, are the emir's representatives in local government areas.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in Birnin Kebbi; the old town of Gwandu, about 30 km away, keeps the tomb of Abdullahi dan Fodio and remains a place of historic and religious significance. The emir is turbaned and receives a staff of office from the state, and the emirate stages Sallah durbars with mounted horsemen during the Eid festivals.
sections.today: The Emir of Gwandu is a first-class ruler and a senior member of the Kebbi State Council of Chiefs, alongside the Emirs of Argungu, Yauri and Zuru. In 2025 the Supreme Court ended the twenty-year dispute with the deposed Emir Mustapha Jokolo, ruling 3–2 that Jokolo's suit had been filed prematurely and that the trial court lacked jurisdiction, which left Muhammadu Iliyasu Bashar's appointment intact.

rulers.name: Abdullahi dan Fodio
rulers.note: Brother of Usman dan Fodio and leading jihad scholar; governed the western half of the caliphate from Gwandu.
rulers.bio: Abdullahi was Usman dan Fodio's younger brother, his student and one of the foremost scholars and poets of the jihad. When dan Fodio divided the caliphate's administration, Abdullahi received the western and southern territories, which he governed first from Bodinga and then from Gwandu. He was critical of what he saw as worldliness creeping into the movement, and after 1817 he was estranged from his nephew Sultan Muhammad Bello until a reconciliation around 1821. He wrote extensively on law, theology and governance. He died in 1829, and his descendants have held the Gwandu throne ever since.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen dates his rule from 1808; Wikipedia's Gwandu table gives 1812, the date usually given for dan Fodio's formal division of the caliphate.

rulers.name: Ibrahim Khalilu

rulers.name: Al-Mustafa

rulers.name: Maliki

rulers.name: Umaru Bakatara
rulers.note: Reigned 1888–1897.

rulers.name: Abdullahi Bayero

rulers.name: Bayero Aliyu
rulers.note: Old and ill when Gwandu capitulated to the British on 12 March 1903; offered no resistance.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Aliyu
rulers.note: Installed May 1903; deposed by the British in March 1906 after relations soured.

rulers.name: Haliru II (Haliru of Kalgo)
rulers.note: British appointee (March 1906 – 21 March 1915); the seat moved from Gwandu to Birnin Kebbi after local opposition to his appointment.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Basharu
rulers.note: Reigned March 1915 – 22 January 1918.

rulers.name: Usman
rulers.note: Appointed January 1918 despite opposition from some kingmakers; reigned to 1938.

rulers.name: Yahaya
rulers.note: Reigned 1938 – 12 January 1954.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Haruna (Haruna Rasheed)
rulers.note: Reigned from 13 January 1954 to 1995, spanning the end of colonial rule and the creation of Kebbi State (1991).

rulers.name: Al-Mustapha Haruna Jokolo
rulers.note: Former army officer; deposed in June 2005 after publicly criticising President Obasanjo. His long court fight for reinstatement ended in a Supreme Court loss in 2025.
rulers.bio: Mustapha Jokolo, born in 1952, was a son of Emir Muhammadu Haruna and an army officer before succeeding his father in July 1995 (he was formally installed in 1997). In June 2005 he publicly accused President Olusegun Obasanjo of marginalising Muslims; the presidency reportedly pressed the Kebbi State governor, Adamu Aliero, to act, and Jokolo was removed in early June 2005. He challenged his deposition in the Kebbi State High Court and won at lower levels, but in 2025 the Supreme Court, by a 3–2 majority, held that his suit was premature because he had not first petitioned the governor as the Kebbi State chieftaincy law requires, and it voided the lower-court judgments.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Iliyasu Bashar
rulers.note: Retired major-general and twice military governor of Gongola State; named emir on 5 June 2005. His title was affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2025.
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Iliyasu Bashar, also known as Mohammed Jega or Muhammadu Dan-Ma'aji, was born on 23 April 1942 at Jega. He trained at the Nigerian Military Training College and the Pakistan Military Academy, later attending the US Army Command and General Staff College and the National Institute at Kuru. He fought in the Nigerian Civil War, commanded the 2nd Mechanised Division, and rose to major-general. He was military governor of Gongola State twice, in 1976–1978 under Obasanjo and in 1984–1985 under Buhari. Named Emir of Gwandu on 5 June 2005 after the removal of his cousin Mustapha Jokolo, he reigned for twenty years under a legal cloud until the Supreme Court confirmed his title in 2025.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives his birth year as 1941; his Wikipedia biography gives 23 April 1942.

thrones.title: Emir of Kano
thrones.established: Hausa kingdom c. 999 (Bagauda); Fulani emirate 1807
thrones.about: Kano was one of the oldest Hausa kingdoms, ruled by Sarakuna said to descend from Bagauda (c. 999), before Fulani jihadists took it in 1807 and made it the richest emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate. Its throne has been at the centre of Nigeria's best-known chieftaincy dispute since 2019. Kano State recognises Muhammadu Sanusi II, reinstated in May 2024; the rival claimant Aminu Ado Bayero's final appeal is pending at the Supreme Court.

authority.text: A fused office: the Emir of Kano is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the Kano Emirate, which is one of the largest Muslim communities in West Africa. He leads the Eid prayers and festivities, appoints Islamic office-holders such as imams of the central mosque within custom, and is formally under the Sultan of Sokoto as Sarkin Musulmi. Sanusi II also holds the separate religious title of Khalifa of the Tijjaniyya Sufi order in Nigeria (since 2021), which is personal rather than attached to the throne.

sections.history:
According to the Kano Chronicle, Kano's kings descend from Bagauda, who is said to have reigned from about 999. Kano was one of the Hausa Bakwai, the seven 'true' Hausa states, and its rulers bore the title Sarki. Islam became the court religion over the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and the most celebrated of the Hausa kings, Muhammad Rumfa (1463–1499), built the Gidan Rumfa palace, expanded the city walls and reorganised the state. The Hausa dynasty ended with Muhammad Alwali II (1781–1807).

In 1807 Fulani supporters of Usman dan Fodio's jihad overthrew Alwali II, and Suleimanu dan Aba Hama became the first emir, owing allegiance to Sokoto. In 1819 Sultan Muhammad Bello appointed Ibrahim Dabo, founder of the Dabo dynasty that has supplied every emir since. Kano grew into the commercial heart of the caliphate, famous for textiles, dyeing and trans-Saharan trade. A disputed succession in 1893 led to the Basasa civil war, from which Aliyu Babba emerged as emir.

British forces captured Kano in February 1903 while Aliyu Babba was away in Sokoto; he was later captured and exiled to Lokoja, and the British installed his brother Muhammad Abbas. Under indirect rule the emir headed the Kano Native Authority. After independence, Premier Ahmadu Bello's regional government deposed Muhammadu Sanusi I in 1963, and Ado Bayero began a reign of more than fifty years.

In 2014 Governor Rabiu Kwankwaso chose the former Central Bank governor Sanusi Lamido Sanusi (Muhammadu Sanusi II) to succeed Ado Bayero. Under Governor Abdullahi Ganduje the Kano Emirate Council Law of May 2019 split the emirate into five first-class emirates: Kano, Bichi, Rano, Karaye and Gaya. On 9 March 2020 Ganduje deposed Sanusi II and installed Aminu Ado Bayero. In May 2024 the state assembly under Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf repealed the 2019 law, dissolved the four new emirates and reinstated Sanusi II, beginning the current dual-claimant standoff.
sections.selection: Since 1819 emirs have been chosen from descendants of Ibrahim Dabo, whose principal branches are the Bayero/Abbas line and the Sanusi line. A council of kingmakers, senior title-holders of the emirate, assesses eligible princes and forwards recommendations, and the Kano State governor makes the appointment and presents the staff of office. Successive governors have used this power decisively: Kwankwaso chose Sanusi II over Ado Bayero's sons in 2014; Ganduje deposed him in 2020; and Yusuf reinstated him in 2024.
sections.council: The Kano Emirate Council comprises the emir, his principal title-holders (including the kingmakers and senior princes) and the district heads (hakimai) who represent the emir across the emirate's local government areas. District heads, ward heads and village heads form the lower tiers of the traditional administration and play a role in local dispute resolution, tax mobilisation and public campaigns.
sections.palace: The emir's seat is the Gidan Rumfa, built in the fifteenth century by Muhammad Rumfa and one of the largest traditional palaces in Nigeria, inside the old walled city. The Kano Durbar, held during Eid el-Fitr and Eid el-Kabir, is the most famous in Nigeria: cavalry from the districts parade before the emir in elaborate costume, and the Hawan Daushe and other processions follow. Regalia include the turban of office, swords, ceremonial trumpets (kakaki) and the state staff of office. Since 2024 durbars have repeatedly been suspended or banned by police because of the rival claims to the throne.
sections.today: As of the latest reports (mid-2026), Kano has two men claiming to be emir. The Kano State government recognises Muhammadu Sanusi II, reinstated on 23 May 2024, who occupies Gidan Rumfa. Aminu Ado Bayero, removed by the 2024 repeal law, holds court at the Nasarawa mini-palace. The litigation is tangled: in May 2024 a Federal High Court suspended the repeal law and in June 2024 nullified the state's actions, while a Kano State High Court ordered Bayero's eviction and restrained the deposed emirs from parading themselves as emirs. On 10 January 2025 the Court of Appeal held that the Federal High Court had no jurisdiction over a chieftaincy matter and struck out its proceedings, which leaves Sanusi's reinstatement standing in law. Bayero's camp appealed to the Supreme Court, which heard preliminary arguments on 20 April 2026 and adjourned further hearing to 19 April 2027. In July 2024 the state re-created Rano, Karaye and Gaya as second-class emirates under Kano; Bichi was not restored.

rulers.name: Suleimanu dan Aba Hama
rulers.note: Fulani scholar who led the jihad in Kano, ended the Hausa (Bagauda) dynasty of Sarki Muhammad Alwali II and became the first emir under Sokoto.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia's Kano infobox gives 1805 for the start of Fulani rule; its ruler list and the date of Alwali II's fall give 1807.

rulers.name: Ibrahim Dabo
rulers.note: Appointed by Sultan Muhammad Bello; scholar and mystic who founded the Dabo dynasty, from which every later Emir of Kano descends.
rulers.bio: Ibrahim Dabo was a Fulani scholar of the Sullubawa clan and a lieutenant of Emir Suleimanu. Sultan Muhammad Bello of Sokoto appointed him emir in 1819, passing over other jihad leaders. His reign of nearly three decades was spent putting down revolts and building the emirate's administration on the model of the old Hausa state, including taking over the Gidan Rumfa palace. He is regarded as the founder of the Dabo dynasty, and all subsequent emirs, including both of the rivals in the present dispute, are his descendants. He died in 1846.

rulers.name: Usman I Maje Ringim
rulers.note: Reigned 1846–1855.

rulers.name: Abdullahi Maje Karofi
rulers.note: Reigned 1855–1883; father of Emirs Aliyu Babba, Muhammad Abbas and Usman II.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Bello
rulers.note: Reigned 1883–1893; his death led to the succession crisis of the Basasa.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Tukur
rulers.note: Appointed by Sokoto but opposed by the sons of Abdullahi; overthrown in the Basasa civil war (1893–1894).

rulers.name: Aliyu Babba
rulers.note: Won the Basasa civil war; last independent emir. Was in Sokoto when the British took Kano in 1903; later captured and exiled to Lokoja, where he died in 1926.

image.caption: An audience with Emir Aliyu Babba, 1900 (illustration)

rulers.name: Muhammad Abbas
rulers.note: Installed by the British after the capture of Kano in 1903; first emir under colonial rule.

rulers.name: Usman II
rulers.note: Reigned 1919–1926.

rulers.name: Abdullahi Bayero
rulers.note: Scholarly emir who promoted Islamic education and trade; Bayero University Kano is named after him.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Sanusi I
rulers.note: Removed in 1963 by the Northern Regional Government of Premier Ahmadu Bello and banished to Azare; the first Emir of Kano to be deposed by a government. Grandfather of Sanusi II.

image.caption: Framed portrait of Emir Muhammadu Sanusi I, Gidan Makama Museum

rulers.name: Muhammadu Inuwa
rulers.note: Former Galadima; reigned only from April to October 1963.

rulers.name: Ado Bayero
rulers.note: Reigned for more than fifty years, the longest in Kano's history; survived a 2013 assassination attempt.
rulers.bio: Ado Bayero was born on 25 July 1930, a son of Emir Abdullahi Bayero, and educated in Islamic studies and at Kano Middle School and Zaria Clerical College. He worked as a bank clerk, joined the Kano Native Authority in 1949, briefly sat in the Northern House of Assembly, headed the Native Authority police and was Nigeria's ambassador to Senegal from 1962. He became emir in October 1963 and reigned for over fifty years, the longest reign in Kano's recorded history, through civil war, military rule and the creation of Kano State. He clashed with Governor Abubakar Rimi in 1981 over reductions in his powers and survived an attack blamed on Boko Haram in January 2013 that killed his driver and a bodyguard. He died at Gidan Rumfa on 6 June 2014; his sons include the rival claimant Aminu Ado Bayero.
rulers.dispute: Sources give 22 October 1963 for his turbaning and 27 February 1964 for his formal coronation.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Sanusi II (first reign)
rulers.note: Former Central Bank governor; chosen by Governor Rabiu Kwankwaso in June 2014; deposed by Governor Abdullahi Ganduje on 9 March 2020 and banished to Nasarawa State.
rulers.bio: Sanusi Lamido Sanusi was born in Kano on 31 July 1961, a grandson of the deposed Emir Muhammadu Sanusi I. He studied economics at Ahmadu Bello University and Islamic studies in Khartoum, and later took a PhD in Islamic law at SOAS. A banker at United Bank for Africa and First Bank (chief executive from 2009), he became Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria in June 2009, leading sweeping bank reforms, until his suspension in February 2014 after he alleged that billions of dollars of oil revenue had not been remitted. On 8 June 2014 he was chosen as Emir of Kano, taking the regnal name Muhammadu Sanusi II, in a contested succession to his great-uncle Ado Bayero. As emir he pushed for reform of Muslim family law, girls' education and heritage tourism, and often criticised governments, which led to a long feud with Governor Ganduje. In 2019 the state split his emirate into five, and on 9 March 2020 he was deposed and sent into exile at Loko and then Awe in Nasarawa State; a Federal High Court ordered his release days later.

image.caption: Muhammadu Sanusi II in 2011, before his accession

rulers.name: Aminu Ado Bayero
rulers.note: Installed by Governor Ganduje on 9 March 2020; removed when the 2024 repeal law dissolved the 2019 emirates. He rejects his removal and remains in the Nasarawa mini-palace pending the Supreme Court.
rulers.bio: Aminu Ado Bayero was born on 21 August 1961, a son of Emir Ado Bayero. He studied mass communication at Bayero University Kano and trained at a flying college in California, and held a succession of princely titles, including Turakin Kano and Wamban Kano. Governor Abdullahi Ganduje appointed him Emir of Kano on 9 March 2020, after Sanusi II's deposition, under the 2019 law that had split the emirate into five; he received the staff of office in July 2021. In May 2024 the new government of Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf repealed that law and reinstated Sanusi II. Aminu Ado Bayero did not accept his removal, returned to Kano and has since held court at the Nasarawa mini-palace while his appeal makes its way through the courts.
rulers.dispute: Whether his reign ended in May 2024 is the subject of litigation pending at the Supreme Court (see the throne's 'today' section). Kano State recognises Sanusi II; Bayero's supporters regard him as the lawful emir.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Sanusi II (second reign)
rulers.note: Reinstated by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf on 23 May 2024 under the Kano Emirates Council (Repeal) Law 2024; recognised by the Kano State government, but the matter is pending before the Supreme Court.
rulers.bio: After the Kano State House of Assembly repealed the 2019 emirates law, Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf restored Sanusi II as Emir of Kano on 23 May 2024, and he returned to the Gidan Rumfa palace. Since May 2021 he has also been the Khalifa (leader) of the Tijjaniyya Sufi order in Nigeria, a position his grandfather Sanusi I held. His second reign has been overshadowed by the standoff with Aminu Ado Bayero, conflicting court orders and police restrictions on durbars. The Kano State government recognises him, the Court of Appeal in January 2025 struck out the Federal High Court proceedings that had favoured Bayero, and the final appeal is pending at the Supreme Court, which in April 2026 adjourned further hearing to April 2027.

image.caption: Muhammadu Sanusi II in 2011, before his accession

rulers.dispute: Numbered 14th (first reign) and 16th (second reign) in Wikipedia's list; some sources number him only as 14th. The legal position remains contested until the Supreme Court rules.

thrones.title: Emir of Katsina
thrones.established: Hausa kingdom c. 11th century; Fulani emirate 1806–1807
thrones.about: Katsina was one of the great Hausa city-states, a centre of learning and trans-Saharan trade, before jihadists under Ummarun Dallaje took it in 1806. The Fulani Dallazawa dynasty ruled until 1906, when the British installed Muhammadu Dikko, founder of the Sullubawa dynasty that still reigns. The current emir is Abdulmumini Kabir Usman (since 2008).

authority.text: A fused office: the Emir of Katsina is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the emirate, leading Eid prayers and festivities and overseeing the emirate's religious hierarchy, while owing spiritual allegiance to the Sultan of Sokoto as Sarkin Musulmi. Alongside this he exercises customary authority over titles, district heads and local dispute resolution under Katsina State law.

sections.history:
Katsina traditions trace its first dynasty to Kumayo, a grandson of the legendary Bayajidda, dated in the regnal lists to about 1015 and based at Durbi ta Kusheyi. In the fifteenth century Muhammadu Korau killed Sanau, the last of Kumayo's line, and founded a new dynasty; he is remembered as Katsina's first Muslim ruler and the founder of the walled city, and the Gobarau mosque, which also served as a centre of learning, is linked to his era. Katsina later paid tribute to Songhai and Bornu but grew into a leading centre of scholarship and commerce.

During Usman dan Fodio's jihad, Ummarun Dallaje led the Fulani forces that captured Katsina in 1806. The Hausa ruler Mare Mawa Mahmudu was killed and his successor Magajin Halidu died soon after, ending the Korau dynasty; Hausa loyalists withdrew north and founded a rival state at Maradi in present-day Niger. Dallaje was appointed emir by Sokoto in about 1807, and his Dallazawa descendants ruled for a century.

The British occupied Katsina in 1903. They deposed Emir Abubakar in 1904 and his successor Yero in 1906, and installed Muhammadu Dikko of the Sullubawa clan, whose descendants have held the throne since. Dikko was a modernising emir who founded Katsina College in 1922 and made the hajj in 1921.

After independence, Katsina Emirate was part of the North-Central State and then Kaduna State, where in 1981 Governor Balarabe Musa's refusal to approve Muhammadu Kabir Usman as emir caused a months-long deadlock. Katsina State was created in 1987 from the Katsina and Daura emirates.
sections.selection: Since 1906 emirs have been drawn from the Sullubawa dynasty founded by Muhammadu Dikko; recent successions have passed from father to son. The emirate's kingmakers consider eligible princes and recommend a candidate, and the state governor gives final approval and presents the staff of office. The 1981 succession showed that the governor's approval is necessary: the kingmakers' choice could not be installed until a new governor approved it.
sections.council: The Katsina Emirate Council brings together the emir, senior title-holders and the district heads who represent the emir across the emirate's local government areas. Titles such as Magajin Gari (head of Katsina town), Durbi, Kauran Katsina and Galadima are held by princes and senior officials. The Katsina State House of Assembly has created new districts under the Katsina and Daura emirates, and the emir turbaned new district heads in 2026.
sections.palace: The emir's palace, known as Gidan Korau, stands in the old walled city. Katsina is famous for its Sallah durbars at Eid, with mounted horsemen in quilted armour, and for polo, which several emirs played. The Gajere sword, an heirloom of the throne, was carried outside Katsina for the first time at a 1959 royal durbar. The Gobarau minaret, one of the oldest structures in the city, is a symbol of Katsina's scholarly past.
sections.today: The Emir of Katsina is one of two first-class emirs in Katsina State (with Daura) and a senior member of the state council of traditional rulers. He has no constitutional powers but is influential in public campaigns, peace and security initiatives and the appointment of district heads. Unlike Kano, Sokoto, Adamawa and Bauchi, Katsina's emirate has not been broken up, though the state has created new districts within it.

rulers.name: Ummarun Dallaje
rulers.note: Jihad commander who took Katsina in 1806, was appointed emir by Sokoto in about 1807 and founded the Dallazawa dynasty.
rulers.bio: Ummarun Dallaje was born in 1781 at Dallaje village, the son of Malam Abdulmumin, in a family said to trace its origins to Kanem-Bornu. He studied under several scholars including Usman dan Fodio and became one of the jihad's commanders in the Katsina area. He conquered Katsina in 1806, displacing the last Hausa ruler, Magajin Halidu, and was formally appointed emir towards the end of 1807. Sultan Muhammad Bello addressed a treatise on government to him. He built a mosque in the city and ruled until his death in 1835, founding the Dallazawa dynasty that held the throne for a century.

rulers.name: Siddiku
rulers.note: Reigned 1835–1844.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Bello
rulers.note: Reigned 1844–1869 (Dallazawa).

rulers.name: Ahmadu Rufa'i
rulers.note: Brief reign in 1869–1870 (Dallazawa).

rulers.name: Ibrahim
rulers.note: Reigned 1870–1882 (Dallazawa).

rulers.name: Musa
rulers.note: Dallazawa emir between Ibrahim and Abubakar.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia's Katsina table prints Musa's reign as 1890–1901, which overlaps Abubakar's documented reign (1887–1904); the dates here are inferred from the gap between Ibrahim (to 1882) and Abubakar (from 1887) and are approximate.

rulers.name: Abubakar
rulers.note: Last sovereign Dallazawa emir; deposed by the British colonial administration in 1904.

rulers.name: Yero
rulers.note: Last Dallazawa emir; removed by the British in 1906, ending the dynasty.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Dikko
rulers.note: First emir of the Sullubawa dynasty; modernising ruler who founded Katsina College (1922) and was the first reigning emir to perform the hajj (1921).
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Dikko was born in 1865, the son of Muhammadu Gidado, who held the title of Durbi, and himself served as Karshi and then as Durbi and district head of Mani. When the British removed Emir Yero in 1906 they made Dikko acting emir, confirming him in January 1907 as the first ruler of the Sullubawa dynasty. He embraced Western education, founding Katsina College in 1922, the first secondary school in Northern Nigeria, and building a hospital. In 1921 he became the first reigning emir to make the hajj, travelling to Mecca by car, and he was the first emir to visit England, where he met King George V. He rebuilt the city's old mosque in 1935 and laid out a polo ground still in use. He died in May 1944 and was succeeded by his son Usman Nagogo.

rulers.name: Usman Nagogo
rulers.note: Reigned 1944 until his death on 18 March 1981; a renowned polo player who carried the Gajere sword at the 1959 royal durbar.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Kabir Usman
rulers.note: Former police chief and Magajin Gari; his accession was delayed by Governor Balarabe Musa's refusal to approve it. Reigned 1981–2008.
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Kabir Usman was born in January 1928, a son of Emir Usman Nagogo, and educated in a palace school and at Katsina Middle School. He joined the Katsina Native Authority police in 1947, trained in Kaduna, Lagos and London, and became its head (Wakilin Doka) in 1951. He later served as a Native Authority councillor, became Magajin Gari and district head of Katsina town, sat in the Northern House of Assembly and was parliamentary secretary in Premier Ahmadu Bello's office. Selected emir on his father's death in March 1981, he was not approved until Kaduna State Governor Balarabe Musa was impeached later that year, and he was formally installed in February 1982. He replaced the old Dikko-era mosque with the present Katsina central mosque, was chancellor of Obafemi Awolowo University and life president of the Nigerian Polo Association. He died on 8 March 2008.

rulers.name: Abdulmumini Kabir Usman
rulers.note: Eldest son of his predecessor; crowned 13 March 2008. Reigning; chancellor of the University of Ilorin.
rulers.bio: Abdulmumini Kabir Usman was born on 9 January 1949, the eldest son of Emir Muhammadu Kabir Usman. He succeeded his father in March 2008, being crowned on 13 March, and is counted as the 50th Emir of Katsina and the fourth of the Sullubawa dynasty. He has served as chancellor of Obafemi Awolowo University and later of the University of Ilorin. His reign has coincided with severe rural banditry in Katsina State, in response to which the emirate has backed peace and security initiatives with the state government. In 2026 he turbaned new district heads under districts created by the state assembly.

thrones.title: Emir of Zazzau
thrones.established: Hausa kingdom (Zazzau) c. 11th–16th century; Fulani emirate 1804
thrones.about: Zazzau, with its capital at Zaria, was one of the seven Hausa Bakwai states and is famous for the warrior queen Amina. Fulani jihadists took it in 1804, and the throne has since rotated among four ruling houses descended from the early Fulani emirs. The current emir is Ahmed Nuhu Bamalli (since 2020), the 19th Fulani emir.

authority.text: A fused office: the Emir of Zazzau is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the emirate. He presides over religious festivals, leads Sallah (Eid) observances and the associated durbar, and has a say in senior Islamic appointments in the emirate, while acknowledging the Sultan of Sokoto as Sarkin Musulmi. His customary functions include conferring titles and overseeing district heads under Kaduna State law.

sections.history:
Zazzau is counted among the Hausa Bakwai, the seven Hausa states of the Bayajidda legend. Its later capital, Zaria, takes its name from a sister of Queen Amina, whose sixteenth-century campaigns are remembered as the peak of Zazzau's power and whose earthen walls (ganuwar Amina) are linked to her name. Zazzau later came under Songhai and Jukun influence and traded slaves, salt and cloth across the region.

During Usman dan Fodio's jihad, Malam Musa led the Fulani forces that took Zaria in 1804, and he became the first emir under Sokoto. The Hausa ruler Muhammadu Makau withdrew south and founded a successor state at Zuba, later moved to Abuja (now Suleja).

The throne came to rotate among the descendants of four early emirs: Malam Musa (Mallawa), Yamusa (Bare-Bari or Bornawa), Abdulkarim (Katsinawa) and Abdussalam (Sullubawa). British forces under Lugard occupied Zaria from 1901–1902; Emir Kwassau was removed in 1902, and the British installed Aliyu Dan Sidi in 1903, who was himself dethroned in 1920.

Shehu Idris (1975–2020) reigned for 45 years, the longest in the emirate's history. On his death, Governor Nasir El-Rufai set aside the kingmakers' list and appointed Ahmed Nuhu Bamalli, returning the throne to the Mallawa house for the first time in a century.
sections.selection: Candidates come from four ruling houses: Mallawa, Bare-Bari (Bornawa), Katsinawa and Sullubawa. When the throne falls vacant, the emirate's kingmakers screen princes from the houses and send a shortlist to the Kaduna State governor, who makes the final choice. In 2020 the kingmakers' list included two Katsinawa and one Bare-Bari candidate; Governor El-Rufai rejected it on procedural grounds and appointed Bamalli of the Mallawa house, a decision widely read as redressing that house's century-long exclusion.
sections.council: The Zazzau Emirate Council includes the emir, the kingmakers, other senior title-holders such as the Wazirin Zazzau and Magajin Garin Zazzau (a senior princely title), and district heads across the emirate's local government areas, including Zaria, Sabon Gari, Giwa, Soba, Ikara, Kudan, Makarfi and Kubau. Since the late 1990s and 2000s many chiefdoms in southern Kaduna, once under Zazzau, have been given their own rulers.
sections.palace: The emir's palace (Gidan Sarki) stands in the old walled city of Zaria (Birnin Zazzau), with façades decorated in traditional Hausa relief patterns. The Zazzau durbar at Sallah, with mounted cavalry from the districts, is one of the main events of the year, and new emirs are turbaned and receive the state staff of office in public ceremonies.
sections.today: The Emir of Zazzau is a first-class ruler and one of the most senior members of the Kaduna State Council of Chiefs and Emirs. He has no constitutional powers but is influential in public campaigns and local security matters. The 2020 succession, in which the governor overrode the kingmakers' shortlist, sparked legal challenges by unsuccessful candidates and debate over the extent of gubernatorial power in emir selection.

rulers.name: Malam Musa
rulers.note: Jihad leader and first Fulani emir; founder of the Mallawa ruling house. Died 17 May 1821.

rulers.name: Yamusa
rulers.note: Founder of the Bare-Bari (Bornawa) ruling house.

rulers.name: Abdulkarim
rulers.note: Founder of the Katsinawa ruling house.
rulers.dispute: The list gives his reign ending 18 December 1846 but his successor's starting 6 January 1846; the end year was probably 1845.

rulers.name: Hammada
rulers.note: Reigned only about seven weeks (January–February 1846).

rulers.name: Muhammad Sani
rulers.note: Reigned April 1846 – April 1853.

rulers.name: Sidi Abdulkadir
rulers.note: Second Mallawa emir; reigned April–December 1853.

rulers.name: Abdussalam
rulers.note: Founder of the Sullubawa ruling house; reigned January 1854 – August 1857.

rulers.name: Abdullahi
rulers.note: First reign, September 1857 – late 1871; he returned for a second reign in 1874.

rulers.name: Abubakar
rulers.note: Third Mallawa emir; reigned November 1871 – mid-1874.
rulers.dispute: Daily Trust gives Abubakar's reign as 1879–1888, which conflicts with the list followed here.

rulers.name: Abdullahi (second reign)
rulers.note: Restored c. 1874 and reigned until late 1879.

rulers.name: Muhammad Sambo
rulers.note: Katsinawa emir; reigned December 1879 – January 1888.

rulers.name: Uthman Yero
rulers.note: Reigned 1888 – 13 February 1897.

rulers.name: Muhammad Lawal Kwassau
rulers.note: Last emir before British rule; removed by the British in 1902, after which a regent governed until April 1903.

rulers.name: Aliyu Dan Sidi
rulers.note: Mallawa emir installed 8 April 1903; dethroned on 9 November 1920; grandfather of the present emir.

rulers.name: Dallatu
rulers.note: Reigned 1920–1924.

rulers.name: Ibrahim
rulers.note: Reigned 1924–1936.

rulers.name: Malam Jafaru
rulers.note: Reigned 1937 – August 1959.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Aminu
rulers.note: Reigned September 1959 – 4 February 1975.

rulers.name: Shehu Idris
rulers.note: Katsinawa emir and former teacher and Native Authority secretary; reigned 45 years, the longest in Zazzau's history.
rulers.bio: Shehu Idris was born in Zaria on 20 February 1936 into the Katsinawa ruling house; his grandfather and great-grandfather had been emirs. He trained as a teacher at Katsina Training College and taught in Zaria, then became private secretary to Emir Muhammadu Aminu and, in 1965, secretary of the Zaria Native Authority council. In 1973 he was given the title Dan Madamin Zazzau and made district head of Zaria. He became emir on 8 February 1975 and reigned for some 45 years, the longest reign in the emirate's history, also chairing the Kaduna State Council of Chiefs. He died in Kaduna on 20 September 2020.

rulers.name: Ahmed Nuhu Bamalli
rulers.parent: grandson of Aliyu Dan Sidi; son of Nuhu Bamalli
rulers.note: Lawyer and diplomat appointed by Governor Nasir El-Rufai on 7 October 2020; first Mallawa emir in a century.
rulers.bio: Ahmed Nuhu Bamalli was born on 8 June 1966 in Zaria, a son of the former foreign minister Nuhu Bamalli and grandson of Emir Aliyu Dan Sidi. He studied law at Ahmadu Bello University and later took a master's in international affairs there, with further courses at York, Harvard and Oxford. He worked in banking and was executive director and later acting managing director of the Nigerian Security Printing and Minting Company, served on the Kaduna State electoral commission and, from 2017, was Nigeria's ambassador to Thailand and Myanmar. He held the title Magajin Garin Zazzau. After Shehu Idris died in 2020, Governor Nasir El-Rufai rejected the kingmakers' shortlist, which did not include Bamalli, and appointed him on 7 October 2020; he was turbaned on 9 November 2020. He is the first emir from the Mallawa house since his grandfather was dethroned in 1920.

thrones.title: Emir of Daura
thrones.established: Ancient Hausa kingdom (traditionally the oldest); Fulani emirate 1805–1806; reunited emirate 1903–1906
thrones.about: Daura is regarded in Hausa tradition as the cradle of the Hausa states: here, according to legend, Bayajidda killed the serpent in the Kusugu well and married Queen Daurama. After a century of Fulani rule following the 1805 jihad, the British restored the Hausa dynasty from the rival kingdom of Zango. The current emir is Umar Faruk Umar (since 2007).

authority.text: A fused office: the Emir of Daura is a traditional ruler who is also the Islamic leader of his emirate, leading Eid prayers and the Sallah durbar and overseeing religious affairs in the emirate under the Sultan of Sokoto as Sarkin Musulmi. He is also the custodian of the Bayajidda legend and of the Kusugu well, a heritage role in which pre-Islamic traditions of the founding are told as history and culture rather than practised as religion.

sections.history:
Daura's traditions describe an ancient town ruled by a line of queens. In the Bayajidda legend, a prince from the east (often said to be from Baghdad) arrived at Daura, killed a serpent called Sarki that guarded the Kusugu well and stopped people drawing water, and married the reigning queen, Daurama. Their son Bawo is said to have fathered the founders of the seven Hausa Bakwai states (Daura, Kano, Katsina, Zazzau, Gobir, Rano and Biram), while Bayajidda's son by another wife founded the 'illegitimate' Banza Bakwai states. The legend makes Daura the spiritual home of the Hausa.

In 1805, during the jihad, the Fulani leader Malam Ishaqu besieged and took Daura and founded an emirate under Sokoto. The Hausa dynasty withdrew and founded successor kingdoms nearby, of which Zango (founded about 1825) and Baure were the most important, so that for a century rival Fulani and Hausa rulers each claimed the name Daura.

When Britain and France partitioned the region in 1903–04, the British installed the king of Zango, Malam Musa, as Emir of Daura, returning the throne to the Hausa line and reuniting the Nigerian part of the old kingdom; part of the historic Daura lands fell under French rule in Niger. Musa's son Abdurrahman reigned for 55 years.

After independence Daura was part of the North-Central State and then Kaduna State; since 1987 it has been one of the two emirates of Katsina State. Daura gained national prominence as the hometown of President Muhammadu Buhari (2015–2023).
sections.selection: Emirs are chosen from the restored Hausa royal house descended from Malam Musa of Zango. The emirate's kingmakers select a candidate from eligible princes and the Katsina State governor approves the appointment and presents the staff of office. In recent generations the throne has passed among Musa's descendants rather than strictly from father to son.
sections.council: The Daura Emirate Council comprises the emir, senior title-holders and the district heads who represent him across the emirate's local government areas in north-eastern Katsina State. The emir confers honorary titles on prominent citizens, a practice that brought many national figures to Daura during the Buhari years. The state assembly has approved new districts under the Daura and Katsina emirates.
sections.palace: The emir's palace stands in the old town near the city gates. The Kusugu well, where Bayajidda is said to have killed the serpent, is protected by a shelter and is the town's best-known heritage site. Daura holds Sallah durbars at the Eid festivals, with horsemen paying homage to the emir.
sections.today: The Emir of Daura is a first-class ruler and one of the two senior emirs on the Katsina State council of traditional rulers. Umar Faruk Umar has reigned since 2007 and remains active in public life, conferring titles and backing peace and security initiatives in a state troubled by rural banditry.

rulers.name: Malam Ishaqu
rulers.note: Fulani jihad leader who took Daura after a siege and founded the Fulani emirate there.
rulers.dispute: Britannica and Wikipedia date the capture of Daura to 1805; WorldStatesmen dates Ishaqu's reign from 1806.

rulers.name: Yusufu
rulers.note: Fulani emir of Daura.

rulers.name: Muhamman Sani
rulers.note: Fulani emir of Daura.

rulers.name: Zubayru
rulers.note: Brief reign in 1837.

rulers.name: Muhamman Bello
rulers.note: Fulani emir of Daura for three decades.

rulers.name: Muhamman Altine
rulers.note: Fulani emir of Daura.

rulers.name: Muhamman Mai Gurdo

rulers.name: Malam Musa
rulers.note: King of the Hausa successor state of Zango, installed by the British as Emir of Daura, restoring the Hausa (Habe) line to Daura town and reuniting the divided kingdom.
rulers.dispute: Britannica dates his installation to 1903–04; WorldStatesmen dates the reunited emirate under him from 1906.

rulers.name: Abdurrahman
rulers.note: Reigned for 55 years, through the whole colonial period and into independence.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Bashar

rulers.name: Umar Faruk Umar
rulers.note: Installed 28 February 2007; reigning. Daura's emir is the custodian of the Bayajidda tradition and the Kusugu well.
rulers.bio: Umar Faruk Umar (also styled Faruk Umar Faruk) became Emir of Daura on 28 February 2007 after the death of Muhammadu Bashar, and is counted as the 60th ruler in Daura's long king list. He received the national honour of Commander of the Order of the Niger in December 2007. In February 2009 he intervened to calm deadly mob violence at the Kongolam border post, and in 2010 he pledged personal funds to rebuild three of Daura's city gates and the monument at the Kusugu well. As the traditional ruler of former President Muhammadu Buhari's hometown, he hosted many national figures during Buhari's presidency. He has continued to confer titles and appear in public functions into 2025.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia gives his birth year as 1928; WorldStatesmen gives 1931.

thrones.title: Emir of Bauchi
thrones.established: 1805 (jihad flag); capital founded c. 1809
thrones.about: Bauchi Emirate was founded by Yakubu dan Dadi, a Hausa scholar and pupil of Usman dan Fodio who received a jihad flag and built Bauchi city as his capital. It became one of the larger emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate's eastern frontier. The current emir, Rilwanu Suleimanu Adamu, has reigned since 2010.

authority.text: A fused office: the Emir of Bauchi is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of his emirate, leading Eid prayers and festivities and overseeing religious matters under the Sultan of Sokoto as Sarkin Musulmi. He also holds the honorary caliphate title Sarkin Yakin Daular Usmaniya. His customary role covers titles, district administration and dispute mediation under Bauchi State law.

sections.history:
Yakubu dan Dadi, a Hausa-speaking scholar who had studied under Usman dan Fodio, received a flag to spread the jihad in the region that became Bauchi. Between about 1809 and 1818 his forces conquered much of the surrounding country, and he founded Bauchi city as the capital. He is the only certainly non-Fulani founder among the caliphate's emirs, although the dynasty has since become Fulani in identity.

Yakubu's son Ibrahima reigned for 32 years but abdicated in 1877 in favour of his son Usman, setting off a civil war. The Sultan of Sokoto removed Usman in 1883 and appointed Umaru dan Salamanu, who struggled with rebellious district chiefs; his unpopular 1900 campaign against Gwaram weakened him further.

A British expedition occupied Bauchi without a fight in February 1902, deposed Umaru and exiled him to Lokoja and later Ilorin. Their first appointee died within months; his successor Hassan swore allegiance to the British Crown in 1904, and Bauchi became a province under indirect rule.

Since 1976 Bauchi has been capital of Bauchi State. Recent successions have passed from father to son: Suleiman Adamu (1982–2010) and his son Rilwanu Suleimanu Adamu (since 2010). In October 2025 the state government created 13 new emirates and chiefdoms, plus the Zaar chiefdom, in a reorganisation of traditional rule across the state.
sections.selection: Emirs are chosen from the descendants of Yakubu dan Dadi. The emirate's kingmakers recommend a candidate from eligible princes, and the Bauchi State governor approves and installs him under the state's chieftaincy law. Recent successions, in 1982 and 2010, passed from father to son.
sections.council: The Bauchi Emirate Council includes the emir, senior title-holders and district heads across the emirate's local government areas. The October 2025 laws created new emirates and chiefdoms elsewhere in Bauchi State (including Burra, Dambam, Darazo, Duguri, Gamawa, Giade, Toro, Warji, Ari, Jama'a, Lame, Bununu and Lere), each with its own ruler, which changes the balance of the state council of chiefs.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in central Bauchi city, near the central mosque, and the tombs of earlier emirs are nearby. The emirate holds Sallah durbars at the two Eid festivals, with horsemen from the districts paying homage to the emir.
sections.today: The Emir of Bauchi is a first-class ruler and a leading member of the Bauchi State Council of Chiefs. In October 2025 Governor Bala Mohammed signed laws creating 13 new emirates and chiefdoms plus the Zaar chiefdom. The move was opposed by some Fulani groups and stakeholders in Tafawa Balewa and Ningi, who pledged court challenges, and it reduced the dominance of the older emirates in the state's traditional structure.

rulers.name: Yakubu I dan Dadi
rulers.note: Hausa scholar and pupil of Usman dan Fodio; received a flag for the jihad and founded Bauchi, the only emirate founded by a non-Fulani flag-bearer.
rulers.bio: Yakubu dan Dadi was a Hausa-speaking Islamic scholar who studied under Usman dan Fodio before the jihad. He received a flag from dan Fodio and led the campaign in the Bauchi region, conquering the area between about 1809 and 1818; Bauchi city became his capital. He is described as the only certainly non-Fulani founding ruler among the emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate. He ruled for four decades and died in 1845, leaving the throne to his son Ibrahima.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen and the Bauchi ruler list date his rule from 1805; the emirate is often said to have been established in 1809, the date usually given for the founding of Bauchi city.

rulers.bio: Rilwanu Suleimanu Adamu, born in 1970, is a son of Emir Suleiman Adamu and a builder by profession. He succeeded his father on 29 July 2010 as the 11th Emir of Bauchi. He holds the honorary caliphate title Sarkin Yakin Daular Usmaniya ('war commander of the Sokoto Caliphate'). His reign has emphasised peace-building, including efforts against political thuggery, and in 2023 he chaired the state's fuel-subsidy palliative distribution committee and an education steering committee focused on out-of-school children. He has also called for a constitutional role for traditional rulers.

thrones.title: Lamido of Adamawa (Lamido Fombina)
thrones.about: The Lamido of Adamawa heads the emirate founded in 1809 by Modibbo Adama, who received a jihad flag from Usman dan Fodio and built a realm reaching deep into present-day Cameroon. Colonial partition split the emirate between British and German rule, leaving Yola on the Nigerian side. The current Lamido, Muhammadu Barkindo Aliyu Mustafa, has reigned since 2010.

authority.text: A fused office: the Lamido is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the emirate, leading Eid prayers and religious observances and acknowledging the Sultan of Sokoto as Sarkin Musulmi. 'Lamido' is a Fulfulde word for ruler, and the title Lamido Fombina ('ruler of the southlands') recalls the emirate's role as the caliphate's southern frontier. His customary role includes conferring titles and overseeing district heads under Adamawa State law.

sections.history:
Fulani communities in the upper Benue region sent a delegation to Sokoto in 1808, and in March 1809 Usman dan Fodio gave the scholar Modibbo Adama a flag and named him Lamido Fombina. Adama's campaigns created a large, loosely knit emirate made up of many sub-emirates (lamidates) such as Ngaoundéré, Garoua, Tibati and Maroua. The capital moved from Gurin to Ribadu and Njoboliyo before settling at Yola around 1841. The emirate paid tribute to Sokoto and was among its largest in area.

Adama's sons Muhammadu Lawal, Umaru Sanda and Zubayru ruled in turn through the rest of the century. Zubayru resisted European encroachment; when British forces took Yola on 2 September 1901 he fled and fought on until his death in 1903. The British installed his brother Bobbo Ahmadu.

Anglo-German agreements in 1893–94 and later boundary work split Adamawa: most of the emirate, including many sub-emirates, went to German Kamerun (later French Cameroun), while Yola and the western districts came under Britain. After the First World War part of the former German territory, the Northern Cameroons, was administered by Britain and joined Nigeria in 1961.

Lamido Aliyu Mustafa reigned for nearly 57 years (1953–2010) and presided over the emirate's bicentenary celebrations in 2009. His son Muhammadu Barkindo succeeded him in 2010.
sections.selection: Lamidos are chosen from the descendants of Modibbo Adama. The emirate's kingmakers consider eligible princes and recommend a candidate, historically subject to approval at Yola and today to approval by the Adamawa State governor. In 2010 the kingmakers chose Barkindo unanimously and he was turbaned five days after his father's death. A 2024 state law gave the governor express powers to appoint and depose traditional rulers and to create new emirates.
sections.council: The Lamido presides over the Fombina (Adamawa) Emirate Council, made up of senior title-holders (such as the Chiroma, a title the present Lamido held before his accession) and district heads. After the District Creation Law of December 2024, only three local government areas, Girei, Yola North (Jimeta) and Yola South, remain under the Lamido's direct authority.
sections.palace: The Lamido's palace, the Fombina Palace, stands in Yola town. The Lamido is turbaned there and holds Sallah durbars with horsemen during the Eid festivals. The emirate celebrated its bicentenary in 2009.
sections.today: Traditional rule in Adamawa State was reorganised in December 2024. A new law ended the Lamido's permanent chairmanship of the Adamawa State Council of Chiefs, making it rotate yearly among first-class rulers, and gave the governor power to create emirates and to appoint and depose rulers. The District Creation Law of 4 December 2024 cut the local government areas under the Lamido from eight to three. On 23 December 2024 Governor Ahmadu Fintiri announced seven new emirates and chiefdoms (Hoba, Madagali, Michika, Fufore, Gombi, Maiha and Yungur); the Fufore emirate has been challenged in court.

rulers.name: Modibbo Adama
rulers.note: Scholar-commander commissioned by Usman dan Fodio in 1809 as Lamido Fombina; conquered a vast realm stretching into present-day Cameroon.
rulers.bio: Modibbo Adama, a Fulani scholar and teacher (modibbo), was born around 1771, the son of Ardo Hasana. In 1808 Fulani leaders of the upper Benue region sent a delegation to Sokoto, and in March 1809 Usman dan Fodio gave Adama a flag and appointed him Lamido Fombina, 'ruler of the southlands'. He waged war against neighbouring peoples from capitals at Gurin, Ribadu and Njoboliyo before settling at Yola around 1841. By his death the emirate covered parts of present-day Nigeria and much of northern Cameroon, organised as many sub-emirates (lamidates). The emirate, and the region now known as Adamawa, take their name from him.

rulers.bio: Muhammadu Barkindo Aliyu Mustafa was born on 13 February 1944, a son of Lamido Aliyu Mustafa. He attended Barewa College and Ahmadu Bello University, where he took a diploma in law in 1969, and later studied in London. He worked with the Nigeria Customs Service, the Nigerian Ports Authority and the National Freight Company, was a Gongola State commissioner for works and later for animal health, and chaired Stirling Civil Engineering Nigeria and the Federal Radio Corporation of Nigeria. His father made him Chiroma Adamawa in 1980. After Aliyu Mustafa died on 13 March 2010, the kingmakers chose Barkindo unanimously and he was turbaned on 18 March 2010. He chaired the Adamawa State Council of Chiefs until a 2024 law made the chairmanship rotate, and in 2024 his emirate was sharply reduced when new districts, emirates and chiefdoms were created.

thrones.title: Emir of Ilorin
thrones.about: Ilorin began as a frontier town of the Oyo Empire, where the rebel general Afonja allied with the Fulani scholar Shehu Alimi; after Afonja's death in the 1820s Alimi's son Abdulsalami became the first emir under Gwandu. It is the southernmost emirate of the former Sokoto Caliphate, with a largely Yoruba-speaking population ruled by a dynasty of Fulani origin. The current emir, Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, has reigned since 1995.

authority.text: A fused office: the Emir of Ilorin is both a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the emirate, which styles itself a centre of Islamic learning in Yorubaland. He leads Eid prayers and festivities and oversees the emirate's Islamic hierarchy, including the chief imam, under the spiritual primacy of the Sultan of Sokoto. His customary role includes conferring titles and chairing the Kwara State Council of Traditional Rulers.

sections.history:
In the late eighteenth century Ilorin was a provincial town of the Oyo Empire. Afonja, the Oyo general who held the military title Are Ona Kakanfo, rebelled against the Alaafin and made Ilorin his base. Around 1810 he allied with Shehu Alimi (Salih Janta), a Fulani Islamic scholar who had moved there from Oyo, and Alimi's network brought in Muslim fighters (the Jama'a), including Hausa and Fulani, who were linked to Usman dan Fodio's movement.

After Alimi's death, tensions between Afonja and the Jama'a led to fighting in which Afonja was killed, during the reign of Alimi's son Abdulsalami, who became the first emir in about 1823–24 and accepted the overlordship of Gwandu. Ilorin then played a central part in the collapse of the Oyo Empire, attacking and burning Oyo-Ile. Its push south was checked by Ogbomoso and by Ibadan at Osogbo in 1838, and it took part in the long nineteenth-century wars among Yoruba states.

In 1897 forces of the Royal Niger Company attacked Ilorin, and the emirate was soon brought into the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria with relatively little fighting, unlike the rest of Yorubaland, which became part of the Southern Protectorate. This left Ilorin a predominantly Yoruba-speaking city in the Northern Region, a legacy that still shapes Kwara State's identity.

Kwara State was created in 1967 with Ilorin as capital. Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, a senior appeal court judge, became the 11th emir in 1995.
sections.selection: Emirs are drawn from the descendants of Shehu Alimi. When the throne is vacant, the four Baloguns, who head the city's main quarters (Balogun Gambari, Balogun Fulani, Balogun Ajikobi and Balogun Alanamu), together with the Mogaji Aare (head of Afonja's family) and the Baba Isale, elect and install a new emir. The governor of Kwara State must approve the choice. The longest-serving Balogun holds the title Balogun Agba and is second in rank to the emir.
sections.council: Ilorin's traditional government reflects its mixed origins. The four Balogun quarters represent the Hausa (Gambari), Fulani and Yoruba (Ajikobi and Alanamu) communities, and the Mogaji Aare preserves Afonja's lineage. Alongside them are Islamic office-holders such as the chief imam, and district heads in the emirate's local government areas. The emir chairs the Kwara State Council of Traditional Rulers.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in the heart of old Ilorin beside the Ilorin Central Mosque, whose renovation the current emir led. Ilorin celebrates Eid with a durbar of horsemen from the Balogun quarters, and coronation anniversaries are marked with the conferment of titles. The banning of masquerades in Ilorin dates from the conflict over Afonja's era and still distinguishes the city's festivals from those of other Yoruba towns.
sections.today: The Emir of Ilorin is the most senior traditional ruler in Kwara State and chairs its Council of Traditional Rulers. Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, who turned 86 in 2026, remains active in public life, including as chancellor of Bayero University Kano since March 2024, and is an influential voice in Kwara politics and in national Muslim bodies.

rulers.bio: Ibrahim Kolapo Sulu-Gambari was born in Ilorin on 22 April 1940. He studied at Offa Grammar School and then in England, including at Oakham School, the City of Westminster College, the Middle Temple and the University of London, before qualifying at the Nigerian Law School. He became solicitor-general and permanent secretary in the former Gongola State, a judge of the Bauchi High Court in 1976 and a Justice of the Court of Appeal in 1978, rising to Presiding Justice of its Lagos Division. On 28 August 1995 he was appointed 11th Emir of Ilorin in succession to his uncle Aliyu Abdulkadir and was crowned on 11 November 1995. He has chaired the Kwara State Council of Traditional Rulers since 1995, led the renovation of the Ilorin Central Mosque, founded the Shehu Alimi Foundation for Peace and Development, and served as chancellor of Nnamdi Azikiwe University (2001–2015) and, from 2024, of Bayero University Kano.

thrones.title: Shehu of Borno
thrones.established: 1814 (al-Kanemi line; Shehu title dated by the dynasty to 1809). Successor to the Kanem-Bornu monarchy, whose Sayfawa Mais ruled for roughly a thousand years until 1846.
thrones.about: The Shehu of Borno heads the Borno Emirate and is the living successor of the Kanem-Bornu Empire, one of Africa's longest-lasting states. The office belongs to the al-Kanemi dynasty, founded by the scholar-soldier Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi, who saved Borno from the Fulani jihad and eclipsed the old Sayfawa kings. Since 1907 the Shehu has ruled from Maiduguri.

authority.text: The Shehu is both a traditional ruler and an Islamic leader. The title itself is the Kanuri form of the Arabic shaykh, reflecting the founder's standing as a Muslim scholar, and the dynasty's legitimacy has always rested on religious learning as much as on lineage. Today the Shehu is regarded as the foremost Muslim traditional authority in Borno: he presides over the emirate's religious life and ceremonies (such as the Sallah festivities that follow Eid prayers), and religious officials of the emirate, including the Chief Imam, sit within his council system. He has no formal executive power under the Nigerian constitution.

sections.history:
Before the al-Kanemi dynasty, Borno was ruled by the Sayfawa Mais, a royal line that had governed the Kanem-Bornu state from the region around Lake Chad for close to a thousand years, with its later capital at Ngazargamu in present-day Yobe State. In 1808 Fulani forces inspired by the Sokoto jihad sacked Ngazargamu, and Mai Dunama called on Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi, a Kanembu scholar settled at Ngala, for help.

Al-Kanemi rallied Kanembu spearmen and local forces, drove the jihadists back, and argued in a famous exchange of letters with Muhammad Bello of Sokoto that Borno, a long-established Muslim state, could not lawfully be attacked. He built a new capital at Kukawa in 1814 and took the title Shehu, keeping the Sayfawa Mais as figureheads while holding real power. After his death in 1837 his son Umar Kura succeeded; when the last Mai was killed in 1846 the Sayfawa line ended and the Shehus became sole rulers.

The late 19th century brought succession quarrels and then catastrophe: in 1893 the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr defeated Shehu Hashim, destroyed Kukawa and ruled from Dikwa, executing two Shehus who opposed him. After French forces killed Rabih in 1900, the al-Kanemi family was restored under colonial patronage. Borno was split among Britain, Germany and France; Abubakar Garbai accepted British recognition in 1902, ruling first from Monguno and Kukawa and, from January 1907, from the new town of Yerwa, now Maiduguri. A junior branch remained at Dikwa in German Kamerun.

The two lines were reunited in 1937 when Sanda Kyarimi, then Shehu of Dikwa, became Shehu of Borno. After independence the office continued under the Northern Region and later Borno State. In 2009 Abubakar ibn Umar Garbai el-Kanemi became the 20th Shehu (by the dynasty's count of reigns); his reign has been dominated by the Boko Haram insurgency, which displaced emirates across Borno and killed several district heads.
sections.selection: The Shehu is chosen from male descendants of Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi. When the throne falls vacant the emirate's kingmakers consider eligible princes and send their recommendation to the Borno State Government; the Governor makes the appointment and later presents the staff of office. In practice the throne has alternated among branches descended from Shehu Umar Kura, and the two most recent successions (1974 and 2009) passed to sons of earlier Shehus.
sections.council: The Shehu presides over the Borno Emirate Council, made up of senior titled officials of the Kanuri court, religious officials and district heads for the fifteen local government areas of the emirate. He also chairs the Borno State Council of Emirs and Chiefs, which brings together the state's emirs.
sections.palace: The Shehu's palace stands in the centre of Maiduguri facing the Maiduguri Central Mosque, the two buildings forming the ceremonial heart of the city. Royal ceremonies include the Sallah durbars after Eid, when district heads and horsemen in quilted armour and Kanuri regalia ride to pay homage, and the formal turbaning and presentation of a staff of office on accession.
sections.today: Under Borno State law the Shehu is an advisory traditional ruler with no executive power, but he is highly influential in peace-building, security and community affairs. During the Boko Haram insurgency he narrowly escaped a 2012 suicide bombing at the Central Mosque and repeatedly called for stronger security in the state; in 2020 he reported that 13 district heads had been killed. He also serves as chancellor of Nile University of Nigeria (since 2022).

rulers.name: Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi
rulers.note: Scholar-soldier who saved Borno from the Fulani jihad, founded Kukawa and ruled as Shehu while the Sayfawa Mais remained figureheads.
rulers.bio: Born around 1776, probably in Murzuk (Fezzan) to a Kanembu scholarly family, he studied widely and spent about a decade in the Middle East after a pilgrimage to Mecca. He settled at Ngala, attracted many students and married into the local ruling family. When Fulani jihadists sacked the Borno capital Ngazargamu in 1808, Mai Dunama summoned him, and his leadership and Kanembu spearmen helped retake the country. He defended Borno's cause in letters to Usman dan Fodio and Muhammad Bello, arguing that a Muslim state could not be lawfully attacked. In 1814 he founded Kukawa and took the title Shehu, steadily becoming the real power while keeping the Mais as titular kings. He received the British explorers Denham and Clapperton in 1823 and extended Borno's reach in the 1820s. He died at Kukawa on 8 June 1837.
rulers.dispute: The dynasty later dated his reign as Shehu from 1809; Wikipedia gives 1809–1837, while the founding of Kukawa and formal adoption of the title are usually placed in 1814. His birth year is approximate.
