rulers.note: Defeated by Rabih az-Zubayr in 1893 and fled Kukawa; deposed and later killed on his successor's orders.

rulers.name: Muhammad al-Amin ibn Abu Bakr (Kyari)
rulers.note: Rallied resistance against Rabih from Geidam; captured and executed by Rabih.

rulers.name: Sanda ibn Abu Bakr
rulers.parent: son of Bukar Kura; brother of Kyari
rulers.note: Proclaimed Shehu in opposition to Rabih; reigned less than a month before being captured and executed.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen places the reigns of Kyari and Sanda Wuduroma in 1893; Wikipedia in 1893–1894.

rulers.name: Umar Sanda ibn Ibrahim Kura
rulers.note: Installed by the French at Dikwa after Rabih's defeat in 1900, then removed by them later that year in favour of his brother.

rulers.name: Abu Bakr ibn Ibrahim Kura (Garbai)
rulers.parent: son of Ibrahim Kura; brother of Sanda Kura
rulers.note: After a turbulent start in which he lost and regained Dikwa, he accepted British recognition in 1902 and moved the capital to Maiduguri (Yerwa) in 1907.
rulers.bio: Abubakar Garbai first became Shehu in mid-1900 under French sponsorship, after his brother Sanda Kura was removed. He was driven out of Dikwa by Rabih's son Fadlallah in late 1900, returned in 1901 and, after Fadlallah's death, settled with the British, who formally appointed him Shehu of Borno on 2 April 1902. He ruled first from Monguno and then from the ruins of Kukawa, where Lugard invested him in 1904. Because Kukawa had poor water and lay far from British posts, he moved his court to Yerwa (Maiduguri) on 9 January 1907, founding the city that remains the seat of the Shehus. He ruled British Borno until his death in 1922, and his descendants have since provided several Shehus, including the present one.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia counts Garbai's four separate tenures (1900, 1901, 1901–02, 1902–22) as four numbered reigns. WorldStatesmen lists him at Kukawa from 1902 and gives his name as 'Ali ibn Ibrahim'.

rulers.name: Muhammad al-Mustafa ibn Umar
rulers.note: Proclaimed Shehu by refugees at Dikwa while Garbai was in flight; fled when Garbai returned in 1901.

rulers.name: Umar Sanda ibn Ibrahim Kura
rulers.note: Reinstalled after his brother Garbai's death and ruled British Borno until 1937.

rulers.name: Umar ibn Muhammad al-Amin (Sanda Kyarimi)
rulers.note: Previously Shehu of Dikwa (1917–1937); his accession reunited the two al-Kanemi lines. Ruled for three decades, through independence.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia gives his death as 29 December 1967; WorldStatesmen gives January 1968.

rulers.name: Umar ibn Abubakar Garbai al-Kanemi
rulers.note: A former teacher and district head; in 1972 he became the first reigning Borno ruler in generations to visit Sokoto.
rulers.bio: Born in Maiduguri in 1920, he was the youngest son of Shehu Abubakar Garbai. He trained as an elementary school teacher, became a headmaster, and from 1943 held posts in the Borno native administration, rising to district head of Maiduguri in 1957; he also took local government courses in Zaria and Britain. He was appointed Shehu on 27 March 1968 after the death of Sanda Kyarimi. In 1972 he visited Sokoto and met Sultan Siddiq Abubakar III, a symbolic reconciliation between the two historic rival states, and he promoted unity among Nigeria's traditional rulers. He died in his palace on 20 August 1974.

rulers.name: Mustafa ibn Umar el-Kanemi
rulers.note: Son of Sanda Kyarimi; named Shehu in 1974 and invested in 1975, he reigned for 34 years.

image.caption: Mustafa Umar el-Kanemi at his coronation

rulers.dispute: Named successor in 1974 but formally invested on 1 February 1975 (Wikipedia gives a reign start of 21 February 1975). His death is dated 21 February 2009 (Wikipedia) or 20 February 2009 (WorldStatesmen).

rulers.name: Abubakar ibn Umar Garbai el-Kanemi
rulers.parent: son of Shehu Umar ibn Abubakar Garbai
rulers.note: Current Shehu; a career local government administrator whose reign has been shaped by the Boko Haram insurgency.
rulers.bio: Born on 13 May 1957 at Damagum (now in Yobe State) and raised in Maiduguri, he was known as Abba Kyari before his accession. He studied local government administration at Kaduna Polytechnic and Ahmadu Bello University and later earned master's degrees in industrial and labour relations and public administration at the University of Maiduguri. Starting as a clerical officer in 1976, he held administrative posts in many Borno local governments and served as a permanent secretary in several state ministries; in October 2008 he became district head of Magumeri. Governor Ali Modu Sheriff appointed him Shehu on 2 March 2009, after the death of Shehu Mustafa. He survived a suicide bombing at the Maiduguri Central Mosque in 2012 and has repeatedly urged stronger action against the insurgency and attention to the Lake Chad basin. He was installed as chancellor of Nile University of Nigeria in December 2022.

rulers.dispute: Appointed 2 March 2009 and invested 4 March 2009 (WorldStatesmen gives 4 March).

thrones.title: Shehu of Dikwa (Emir of Dikwa)
thrones.established: 1900–1902 (junior al-Kanemi branch left at Dikwa when Borno was partitioned)
thrones.about: Dikwa was Rabih az-Zubayr's capital in the 1890s and, after Borno's partition, the seat of a junior branch of the al-Kanemi dynasty in German and then British Cameroons. Its rulers were styled Shehu, then Emir, and since 2010 Shehu again. The emirate today covers Dikwa, Ngala and Kala-Balge local government areas.

authority.text: Like the Shehu of Borno, the ruler of Dikwa is both a traditional ruler and the leading Muslim authority of his emirate, drawing legitimacy from the al-Kanemi scholarly dynasty. He presides over the emirate's Islamic ceremonies and religious officials, while holding only advisory status under Borno State law.

sections.history:
Dikwa rose to prominence when Rabih az-Zubayr, having destroyed Kukawa in 1893, made it his capital. After Rabih's defeat by French and Bornoan forces in 1900, the French installed al-Kanemi princes there. When Abubakar Garbai accepted British recognition in 1902 and left for British Borno, his relative Sanda Mandarama was left in charge at Dikwa, which fell within German Kamerun and became known as 'German Borno'.

The Germans briefly replaced Sanda Mandarama with Ibrahim (1905–1906) before restoring him. During the First World War Britain occupied the territory, which became part of the British Cameroons mandate; Sanda Kyarimi, who succeeded in 1917, adopted the style 'Shehu of Dikwa'. In 1937 Kyarimi was chosen as Shehu of Borno, ending the separate line of Dikwa Shehus; later rulers were styled emirs.

In 1942, at the request of the colonial administration, the emir's seat moved from Dikwa to Bama. In 2009–2010 the Borno State Government divided the emirate: a new Dikwa Emirate (Dikwa, Ngala and Kala-Balge LGAs) under a restored Shehu, Abba Tor Shehu Masta II, and a Bama Emirate under the sitting ruler, Kyari ibn Umar el-Kanemi. The split was controversial because the new Dikwa ruler was given precedence over the long-serving Kyari.

Boko Haram overran Dikwa in the mid-2010s and occupied the Shehu's palace, and Abba Masta II spent much of his reign in exile in Maiduguri, where he died. His successor was named in 2021 and formally crowned in Dikwa on 8 February 2025, marking the community's return.
sections.selection: The ruler is selected from the al-Kanemi princes of the Dikwa branch. The emirate's kingmakers recommend a candidate to the Borno State Government, which appoints the ruler and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The Shehu presides over the Dikwa Emirate Council of titled officials, religious leaders and district heads drawn from Dikwa, Ngala and Kala-Balge LGAs, and sits on the Borno State Council of Emirs and Chiefs.
sections.palace: The palace at Dikwa was built in the colonial era near the site of Rabih's former capital; it was occupied by insurgents and later restored. Coronation includes the turbaning of the Shehu and the presentation of the staff of office by the Governor, as at the 2025 ceremony in Dikwa.
sections.today: Dikwa is a first-class emirate. Its recent history is dominated by insurgency and displacement, the 2010 creation of the separate Bama Emirate, and the return of the court to Dikwa with the 2025 coronation of Shehu Ibrahim ibn Umar Ibrahim el-Kanemi.

thrones.title: Emir of Biu (Mai Biu)
thrones.established: c. 1535 (tradition of Yamta-ra-Wala); recognised as an emirate in 1920
thrones.about: The Mai Biu is the ruler of the Bura (Babur) and Pabir peoples of southern Borno. Tradition traces the kingdom to the conqueror Yamta-ra-Wala in the 16th century; the British recognised the Mai as an emir in 1920. The emirate covers Biu, Hawul, Kwaya Kusar and Bayo LGAs.

authority.text: The Biu kingship grew out of a Pabir/Bura state that predates the dominance of Islam in the area, and early Mais held a sacred, ritual position in the indigenous religion. Since the colonial-era recognition of the Mai as emir (1920) the office has been held by Muslims and carries the religious leadership expected of a northern emir, presiding over Islamic ceremonies of the court. Because the Bura population includes many Christians and followers of traditional religion, the emir's public role is also that of a cultural head for all Bura/Babur and Pabir people.

sections.history:
Oral tradition holds that Yamta-ra-Wala (also called Abdullahi, 'Yamta the Great'), a newcomer often linked with the Kanuri world, conquered the area in the mid-16th century and founded a capital at Dlimbur, now an archaeological site. His descendants formed rival royal centres at Kogu and Mandaragirau, and the state is described as settled by about 1670.

In the early 19th century the Fulani jihad under Buba Yero of Gombe pressed into the region; Mai Mari Watirwa (1793–1838), ruling from Kogu, eventually repulsed the invaders. Around 1870 Ari Paskur had Biu town walled, and in 1878 his son Mari Biya became the first Pabir king to rule from Biu itself.

British forces set up a post at Gujba in 1903; Biu became the traditional capital in 1904 and a separate division in 1918. In 1920 Mai Ari Dogo was acknowledged as the first emir of Biu. In 1957 the Shani and Askira districts were added and the area was known as the Biu federation.

In modern Borno State the emirate has remained one of the main traditional institutions of southern Borno, a counterweight to the Kanuri north; by convention the state's deputy governor has come from this zone. The long reign of Mai Umar Mustapha Aliyu (1989–2020) ended with his death, and his son succeeded him in September 2020.
sections.selection: The Mai is chosen from the royal descendants of Yamta-ra-Wala's line. Kingmakers of the emirate nominate candidates and the Borno State Governor appoints the emir and presents the staff of office, as Governor Zulum did for the current ruler.
sections.council: The emir presides over the Biu Emirate Council of titled officials and district heads for Biu, Hawul, Kwaya Kusar and Bayo LGAs, and sits on the Borno State Council of Emirs and Chiefs. Communities in Hawul, Kwaya Kusar and Bayo have at times petitioned for chiefdoms of their own.
sections.palace: The palace stands in Biu town. Accession ceremonies have been held publicly, such as the presentation of the staff of office to the 29th emir at Biu Central Stadium in January 2021, attended by the Shehu of Borno and other rulers.
sections.today: The Mai Biu is an advisory traditional ruler under Borno State law and an important voice for southern Borno, including in peace-building during the Boko Haram insurgency.

thrones.title: Emir of Fika (Moi Fika)
thrones.established: Tradition dates the Bole state to the 15th century; the present dynasty's list begins c. 1806
thrones.about: The Moi Fika is the paramount ruler of the Bole (Bolewa) people and heads the Fika Emirate, one of the major traditional states of Yobe. The emirate takes its name from its old capital, Fika, but its headquarters has been at Potiskum since 1924. The present emir is counted locally as the 43rd ruler.

authority.text: The Moi Fika is both a traditional ruler and a Muslim religious leader: the Bole had already converted to Islam by the early 19th century, and the emir presides over the emirate's Islamic institutions and ceremonies alongside its customary titles. As elsewhere in Nigeria the office is advisory under state law.

sections.history:
Bole tradition places the origins of the Fika state in the 15th century, with early rulers at a settlement called Daniski. The Bole, already Muslim, are said to have moved to their present heartland around 1805, after which the dated list of Mois begins with Buraima (from c. 1806).

In the 19th century Fika lay between the powers of Borno and the Fulani emirates founded during the Sokoto jihad, and its rulers succeeded one another rapidly in the 1860s–1880s. The British occupied the region at the start of the 20th century; in 1913 they merged the neighbouring Ngizim state of Potiskum into Fika, and in 1924 the emir's headquarters moved from Fika town to Potiskum, a growing trading town.

Muhammadu Gana ibn Idris reigned for over half a century (1922–1976). His son Abali Muhammadu Idrissa (1976–2009) saw the creation of Yobe State in 1991 and the restoration of a separate Potiskum Emirate for the Ngizim in January 2000, which he opposed in court before accepting. The current emir, his son, succeeded in March 2009.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from the royal family. Kingmakers nominate candidates (in 2009 three names were submitted) and the Yobe State Governor makes the appointment and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The emir presides over the Fika Emirate Council of titled officials (such as the Yerima, a title the current emir held before his accession) and district heads. He has served as chairman of the Yobe State Council of Chiefs.
sections.palace: The palace is in Potiskum. During Boko Haram attacks on Potiskum in 2009, many women and children took refuge in its grounds. Ceremonies include turbaning and the presentation of a first-class staff of office, which the current emir received in April 2010.
sections.today: The Moi Fika is an advisory first-class ruler in Yobe State. Relations with the restored Potiskum Emirate, which shares the same town, have produced disputes over land and heritage sites such as the old Potiskum prison. The current emir has argued for a formal constitutional advisory role for traditional rulers and holds the national honour CFR (2022).

He worked for the Nigerian Security Organization, rising to a senior intelligence post, then ran a security business and served as chief security officer of the Nigerian Railway Corporation (1998–2007). He was made Yerima of Fika in 2002 and district head of Potiskum in February 2009. Governor Ibrahim Gaidam chose him from three nominees on 16 March 2009, and he received a first-class staff of office in April 2010, also becoming chairman of the Yobe State Council of Chiefs. He was installed as chancellor of the University of Uyo and received the CFR national honour in 2022.

thrones.title: Mai Bade (Emir of Bade)
thrones.established: c. 1825 (Pan-Bade confederation under Lawan Babuje); clan chiefs (Dugums) from the mid-18th century
thrones.about: The Mai Bade (also written Mai Bedde) is the paramount ruler of the Bade people of northern Yobe, with his court at Gashua on the Yobe River. The kingdom was forged in the early 19th century when Lawan Babuje united Bade clans against Kanuri and Fulani pressure and declared independence from both. The British recognised Bade as an emirate in 1902.

authority.text: The Mai Bade is both a traditional ruler and the Muslim religious head of the emirate, presiding over its Islamic ceremonies and officials in the manner of other northern emirs. Before the 19th century Bade clan heads (Dugums) held authority rooted in clan and indigenous religious practice; the modern office is an emirship with advisory status under Yobe State law.

sections.history:
The Bade trace their origins to a migration from the east; tradition holds that four brothers parted at Dadigar (in present Bursari LGA), the eldest, Ago, becoming ancestor of the Bade while his brothers founded neighbouring groups including the Ngizim. By about the 14th century the Bade were settled near present-day Gashua under the authority of a Borno governor (galadima) based at Nguru.

By the 18th century the Bade were organised in clans under chiefs called Dugums, and the Gidgid dynasty rose to prominence. After Fulani jihadists scattered the Bade around 1808, they paid tribute to Borno. Around 1825 Lawan Babuje judged the tribute too heavy, formed a Pan-Bade confederation, built the walled town of Gorgoram (about 27 miles south-west of Gashua) as his capital, and declared independence from both Borno and the Fulani.

His son Mai Alhaji (1842–1893) defended Gorgoram against attacks, mainly from Hadejia and Borno. Under Mai Duna (1893–1897) the town fell to Rabih az-Zubayr's forces. When British rule was established in 1902, Mai Saleh was recognised as emir of an independent Bade. The seat later settled at Gashua, the emirate's largest town.

The current Mai, Abubakar Umar Suleiman, succeeded his uncle in November 2005 and has served as deputy chairman of the Yobe State Council of Chiefs.
sections.selection: The Mai is chosen from the royal descendants of Lawan Babuje's line. Kingmakers recommend a candidate and the Yobe State Governor appoints him; in 2005 Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim appointed the current Mai after the death of his uncle.
sections.council: The Mai presides over the Bade Emirate Council of titled officials and district heads and sits on the Yobe State Council of Chiefs, where the current Mai has been deputy chairman.
sections.palace: The Mai's palace and court are at Gashua. The earlier walled capital of Gorgoram remains a historic site of the Bade state.
sections.today: The Mai Bade is an advisory ruler under Yobe State law. The current Mai has been active in public-health campaigns, notably promoting polio immunisation with the World Health Organization when vaccine fears were widespread in the north.

rulers.bio: Born in January 1962 in Gashua, he studied at Ahmadu Bello University (diploma in insurance) and later earned an advanced diploma in public administration from the University of Maiduguri. He worked in banking from 1984, then joined the Yobe State public service, becoming chief accountant in the Governor's office and later Director of Finance and Supply (1996–2005). Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim appointed him Mai Bade, and he was turbaned on 12 November 2005 after his uncle's death. He has served as deputy chairman of the Yobe State Council of Chiefs and campaigned for polio immunisation.

thrones.title: Emir of Hadejia
thrones.established: 1808 (Fulani emirate); earlier the Hausa kingdom of Biram
thrones.about: Hadejia, once the Hausa kingdom of Biram counted among the 'seven true Hausa states', became a Fulani emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate in 1808. Under Emir Buhari it broke away from Sokoto in the mid-19th century, and in 1906 it resisted British occupation. The Emir of Hadejia today chairs the Jigawa State Council of Chiefs.

authority.text: The Emir of Hadejia is both a traditional ruler and an Islamic leader. The emirate was founded during the Sokoto jihad, and the emir traditionally serves as the Muslim head of his domain, presiding over religious ceremonies and appointing religious officials such as the Chief Imam. Like other emirs he historically owed allegiance to the Sultan of Sokoto as Amir al-Mu'minin. Under Jigawa State law he holds an advisory, not executive, role.

sections.history:
Hadejia stands on the site of Biram, a Hausa kingdom whose rulers claimed descent from Bayajidda and Daura, which made it one of the Hausa Bakwai. Its Hausa kings (Sarkin Biram) are remembered from around 1700.

During the Fulani jihad, local Fulani leaders led by Umaru, son of Ardo Abdua, took control (1805–1808), and in 1808 Hadejia became an emirate under the Sokoto Caliphate. Sambo Digimsa reigned for nearly four decades. His son Buhari, who held power in 1848–1850 and 1851–1863, renounced allegiance to Sokoto in 1851 and raided neighbouring emirates including Kano, Katagum, Gumel, Bade and Jama'are, enlarging Hadejia before it returned to the caliphate after his death.

In 1906 Hadejia, under Emir Muhammadu, resisted British occupation by force; he is remembered as Mai Shahada ('the martyr') and his reign ended that year. The British installed Haruna II, and the emirate was later administered as part of Kano Province and, after 1967, Kano State.

When Jigawa State was carved from Kano in 1991, Hadejia became one of its emirates. The present emir, Adamu Abubakar Maje, succeeded his father in September 2002.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from the descendants of the jihad-era ruling family. On a vacancy the emirate's kingmakers screen princes and recommend candidates to the Jigawa State Governor, who appoints the emir.
sections.council: The emir presides over the Hadejia Emirate Council, including titled officials (for example the Iya, a title the current emir held before accession), religious officials and district heads. He chairs the Jigawa State Council of Chiefs.
sections.palace: The Emir's Palace in Hadejia dominates the old town, near the Hadejia Museum and colonial-era sites associated with the 1906 conflict. Sallah durbars with mounted cavalry are held after Eid.
sections.today: The emir is an advisory first-tier ruler in Jigawa State and chairman of its Council of Chiefs. The current emir also serves as chancellor of the University of Uyo (since 2015). The emirate has marked the memory of those killed during the 1906 British campaign.

rulers.bio: Born in Hadejia on 15 October 1960, he attended Federal Government College, Ikot Ekpene, and later studied rural and social studies in Kano, public administration at Ahmadu Bello University and peace and conflict studies at the National Open University. He worked as a social welfare officer in Kano State and spent many years with the Kano and Jigawa pilgrims' welfare boards. In 1999 he became Iyan Hadejia and a member of the emirate council. He was crowned the 16th Emir on 13 September 2002 (WorldStatesmen: 14 September) after his father's death, becoming chairman of the Jigawa State Council of Chiefs. In 2015 he was appointed chancellor of the University of Uyo.

thrones.title: Emir of Gumel
thrones.about: Gumel was founded in the mid-18th century by Dan Juma and his Manga (a Kanuri subgroup) followers, and was long a tributary of Borno rather than part of the Sokoto Caliphate. Its present town site dates from 1845. In September 2026 Lawan Ahmed Muhammad Sani became the 17th emir after his father's 46-year reign.

authority.text: The Emir of Gumel is both a traditional ruler and the Muslim religious head of the emirate, presiding over Islamic ceremonies and religious officials. Unusually among the northern emirates, Gumel never belonged to the Sokoto Caliphate, having been a tributary of Borno; its emirs nonetheless hold the same fused traditional and Islamic role. The office is advisory under Jigawa State law.

sections.history:
Gumel's ruling line descends from Dan Juma, leader of Manga settlers, who established the state around 1749–1750. Soon after his death it became a tributary of Borno. Gumel survived the Fulani jihad of the early 19th century without being absorbed into the Sokoto Caliphate.

From 1828 Gumel fought frequent wars with its neighbours Hadejia, Kano and Danzomo and with the Damagaram sultanate of Zinder, whose slave raids were a persistent threat. In 1845 the capital moved from Tumbi (in present-day Niger) to the present site of Gumel.

Emir Ahmadu accepted British rule in 1903, and the colonial border with French territory cut Gumel off from part of its hinterland. The emirate later belonged to Kano Province and Kano State, and from 1991 to Jigawa State.

Ahmed Muhammad Sani II, a former Kano State commissioner, reigned from December 1980 until his death in September 2026, one of the longest reigns among Nigeria's current emirs. His son Lawan was appointed the 17th emir three days later.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from the descendants of Dan Juma's line. Kingmakers screen applicants (nine aspirants applied in 2026) and recommend a candidate to the Jigawa State Governor, who approves the appointment.
sections.council: The emir presides over the Gumel Emirate Council of titled officials and district heads. Senior titles include the Chiroma, held by the current emir before his accession.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in Gumel town. Accession is marked by turbaning and the presentation of a staff of office; Sallah durbars are held after Eid.
sections.today: Gumel is one of Jigawa State's emirates. The death of Ahmed Muhammad Sani II on 3 September 2026, after 46 years on the throne, and the swift appointment of his son on 6 September were widely reported, alongside the near-simultaneous death of the Emir of Zurmi.

He worked for the Gumel Native Authority and the Nigeria Immigration Service before moving into divisional administration. In 1978 he ran unsuccessfully for the Senate, and from 1978 to 1980 he was Kano State Commissioner for Information, Internal Affairs and Culture, overseeing the founding of The Triumph newspaper and a state television station. He was selected emir on 16 December 1980, three days after his father's death. He died in a hospital in Egypt on 3 September 2026, aged about 85, after 46 years on the throne.

After his father's death on 3 September 2026, the kingmakers considered nine aspirants and recommended him; the Jigawa State Government approved him as the 17th Emir of Gumel on 6 September 2026.

thrones.title: Emir of Kazaure
thrones.about: Kazaure was founded in 1819 by Ibrahim Dan Tunku, a Yerimawa Fulani warrior and one of the flag-bearers of Usman dan Fodio's jihad, who carved it out of land claimed by Kano, Katsina and Daura. Sultan Muhammad Bello recognised it as a separate emirate after years of conflict with Kano. The current emir, Najib Hussaini Adamu, has reigned since 1998.

authority.text: The Emir of Kazaure is both a traditional ruler and an Islamic leader, as the emirate was founded by a flag-bearer of the Sokoto jihad and historically owed allegiance to the Sultan as Amir al-Mu'minin. The emir presides over religious ceremonies and officials in his domain; in 2025 the current emir was appointed Jigawa State's Amirul Hajj, leading the state's pilgrims to Mecca. The office is advisory under Jigawa State law.

sections.history:
Tradition says the Kazaure area was first settled around 1300 by Hausa hunters under a leader named Kutumbi, but an organised state came only with the Yerimawa Fulani. Dan Tunku, from Dambatta, received a flag from Usman dan Fodio during the jihad, seized a stockaded village and named it Kazaure, establishing his headquarters there in 1819.

Kano disputed Dan Tunku's independence, and about five years of fighting followed until Sultan Muhammad Bello arbitrated in Kazaure's favour and fixed its boundaries. Under Dambo (1824–1857) the emirate grew, partly at its neighbours' expense.

The British reached Kazaure in the early colonial period, and Emir Muhammad Mayaki submitted without bloodshed. Kazaure later formed part of Kano Province and Kano State and, from 1991, of Jigawa State.

The present emir, Najib Hussaini Adamu, a lawyer, was appointed in 1998 after the death of his father, Hussaini Adamu.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from the descendants of Dan Tunku. Kingmakers recommend candidates to the Jigawa State Governor, who appoints the emir.
sections.council: The emir presides over the Kazaure Emirate Council of titled officials and district heads (for example Roni, a district several emirs have headed before accession) and sits on the Jigawa State Council of Chiefs.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in Kazaure town. Accession involves turbaning and installation ceremonies; the current emir was formally installed in December 1998.
sections.today: The emir is an advisory traditional ruler in Jigawa State. The current emir also serves as chancellor of Benue State University, Makurdi, and led Jigawa's official Hajj delegation in 2025.

He is chancellor of Benue State University, Makurdi, and in 2025 was appointed Jigawa State's Amirul Hajj.

thrones.title: Emir of Katagum
thrones.established: c. 1807 (town of Katagum founded 1814)
thrones.about: Katagum was founded during the Sokoto jihad by Ibrahim Zaki, the Fulani commander who sacked the Borno capital Ngazargamu. Its seat moved from Katagum town to Azare in the early colonial period. It is the second-largest emirate in Bauchi State, spanning six local government areas.

authority.text: The Emir of Katagum is both a traditional ruler and an Islamic leader. The emirate was created by a commander of the Sokoto jihad and historically owed allegiance to the Sultan of Sokoto as Amir al-Mu'minin; the emir presides over religious ceremonies and the emirate's religious officials. Under Bauchi State law he is an advisory first-class ruler.

sections.history:
The founder, Ibrahim Zaki (Malam Zaki), was a son of Malam Lawan, a Fulani scholar whose tomb at Yayu near Chinade is a historic site. Zaki fought in the jihad against Borno and in 1808 sacked Ngazargamu, the Kanem-Bornu capital; Usman dan Fodio reportedly recognised him as leader of the campaign in Borno. He returned west and founded the walled town of Katagum around 1814, where his tomb lies outside the old walls.

Under Dankauwa (1816–1846) the emirate became a significant power on the eastern frontier of the caliphate, often in conflict with Borno and Hadejia. After the British took Kano in 1903, Katagum briefly gave its name to a province, then became a division of Kano Province. The capital was moved from Katagum to Azare in the early colonial period, and about a decade later the emirate was placed under Bauchi Province.

In the 20th century the emirate produced prominent national figures; Muhammadu Kabir Umar, who reigned from 1980 to 2017, had earlier been a Northern Nigeria minister in the First Republic. His son Umar Farouq II succeeded him in December 2017.
sections.selection: Under Bauchi State law, when the throne falls vacant the emirate's traditional kingmakers select three names from the royal family and submit them to the Governor. The list is reviewed by the State Council of Traditional Leaders (chaired by the Emir of Bauchi), and the Governor appoints one candidate. In 2017 the Governor chose the first name on the list, the Sarkin Shira, following a pattern in which many past emirs held that district title before accession.
sections.council: The emir presides over the Katagum Emirate Council, comprising kingmakers, titled officials and district heads (such as Shira and Madara) across six LGAs of Bauchi North, and sits among Bauchi State's six first-class emirs.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in Azare. Earlier emirs are buried at Katagum (the founder's tomb lies outside its defensive walls). Sallah durbars are held after Eid, and the emirate confers traditional titles on public figures.
sections.today: Katagum is one of Bauchi State's six first-class emirates and Azare is the headquarters of Bauchi North senatorial district. The emir takes part in the state's council of traditional leaders and in security and community consultations with the state government.

He began as a scribe in the Katagum Native Authority in 1949, became a councillor, and was elected to the Northern House of Assembly. In the First Republic he served as Minister of State in the Premier's Office and as Minister of Internal Affairs of Northern Nigeria. He was appointed the 11th Emir on 25 November 1980 after his father's death, and later served as chancellor or pro-chancellor of several universities. He is one of Bauchi State's six first-class emirs.

thrones.title: Emir of Gombe
thrones.about: The Gombe Emirate was founded in 1804 by Buba Yero, a follower of Usman dan Fodio, who campaigned from Gombe Abba against the Jukun and neighbouring peoples. The British moved its capital to Nafada and then, in 1919, to present-day Gombe. The emir chairs the Gombe State Council of Emirs and Chiefs.

authority.text: The Emir of Gombe is both a traditional ruler and an Islamic leader. The emirate was established through the Sokoto jihad and historically owed allegiance to the Sultan of Sokoto as Amir al-Mu'minin; the emir presides over Islamic ceremonies and religious officials, and appointments are often formally announced at the Gombe Central Mosque. Many communities in southern Gombe have separate chiefdoms with Christian or traditional-religion populations, over which the emir has no religious role.

sections.history:
Buba Yero (Abubakar dan Usman Subande), a Fulani follower of Usman dan Fodio, launched the jihad in the Gongola valley in 1804 and made Gombe Abba his base for campaigns against Jukun settlements, raiding as far as Adamawa and Biu. His brother Hamman Ruwa held authority over the territory that became Muri until Buba Yero had him executed in 1833.

Muhammadu Kwairanga (1844–1882) enlarged the emirate. At the end of the century Mallam Jibril Gaini resisted from Burmi until his defeat and exile in 1902, and the British conquered Gombe at the Battle of Tongo in 1902. The colonial government moved the capital to Nafada in 1913 and then to the present site of Gombe (Gombe Doma) in 1919.

Waja was separated as a district in 1930, and in 1976 the Native Authority area was divided into Gombe, Akko and Dukku LGAs. Shehu Usman Abubakar (1984–2014) chaired the state's council of emirs and chiefs and led the campaign for Gombe State, created in 1996.

In 2002 the Gombe State Government restructured the emirate, creating second-class emirates and senior district headships and reducing the Emir of Gombe's direct territory. Abubakar Shehu-Abubakar III succeeded his father in June 2014.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from the descendants of Buba Yero. Kingmakers recommend candidates and the Gombe State Governor appoints the emir; in 2014 the letter of appointment was presented at the Gombe Central Mosque.
sections.council: The emir presides over the Gombe Emirate Council and chairs the Gombe State Council of Emirs and Chiefs, which includes the emirs of Dukku, Funakaye, Akko, Nafada, Pindiga, Gona, Yamaltu and Deba and chiefs such as the Mai Tangale, Mai Kaltungo, Mai Tula and Dala Waja.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in Gombe city; the late Emir Shehu Abubakar was buried in its grounds in 2014. Coronation and Sallah durbars feature mounted horsemen.
sections.today: The Emir of Gombe is the senior traditional ruler in Gombe State and chairman of its council of emirs and chiefs. The 2002 restructuring of the emirate remains a significant change to his historic domain. The current emir received the CFR national honour in 2022.

He was a supervisory councillor in Gombe Local Government, then personal assistant to a director at the Ministry of Defence in Abuja, and later worked in business. He received his letter of appointment as the 11th Emir at the Gombe Central Mosque on 6 June 2014, about ten days after his father's death. He received the CFR national honour in 2022.

thrones.title: Emir of Muri (Lamido Muri)
thrones.established: 1817 (independent of Gombe from 1833)
thrones.about: Muri was established by Hamman Ruwa, a brother of Buba Yero of Gombe, who brought the middle Benue region under Fulani rule by 1817. It became an independent emirate after 1833, and its seat has been at Jalingo, now the Taraba State capital, since 1917. The 1986 deposition of Emir Umaru Abba Tukur became a landmark court case.

authority.text: The Emir (Lamido) of Muri is both a traditional ruler and the Muslim religious head of the emirate, founded in the Sokoto jihad and historically linked to the caliphate. He presides over the emirate's Islamic ceremonies and officials. Many of the peoples within the old emirate's territory (such as the Jukun, Mumuye and others) are not Muslim and have their own traditional rulers, so his religious authority applies to the Muslim community.

sections.history:
The middle Benue region was once part of the Jukun kingdom of Kwararafa. During the jihad, Hamman Ruwa, a brother of Buba Yero of Gombe, consolidated Fulani control by 1817, at first under Gombe's authority. After Buba Yero had him executed in 1833, the local Fulani sought and obtained independence, and Muri (also called Hamaruwa) became a separate emirate ruled by Hamman Ruwa's descendants.

The mid-19th century was a period of disunity in which districts such as Gassol and Wurio acted almost independently. Emir Muhammadu Nya (1874–1896) signed an 1885 treaty allowing the Royal Niger Company to trade at Ibi, but conflict with the company led him to accept a short-lived French protectorate in 1892–1893 under Louis Mizon. In 1893 he moved the capital to Jalingo, originally a war camp.

Emir Hassan submitted peacefully to the British, who established control around 1900–1901; Muri became a province and the emir lived at Lau until 1910 and Mutum Biyu until 1917, after which Jalingo became the permanent seat. Muhammadu Mafindi (1903–1953) reigned for half a century and was honoured with a KBE.

In 1986 the military governor of Gongola State, Col. Yohanna Madaki, deposed Emir Umaru Abba Tukur and banished him to Mubi; the emir's legal challenge reached the Supreme Court in 1997. Abbas Njidda Tafida, a grandson of Mafindi, was installed in 1988 and Jalingo became capital of Taraba State in 1991.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from the descendants of Hamman Ruwa, in recent times from the line of Muhammadu Nya. Kingmakers recommend a candidate and the state government (Gongola, now Taraba) appoints him; the 1986 deposition showed the state's power to remove an emir by order.
sections.council: The emir presides over the Muri Emirate Council of titled officials and district heads; the 1986 crisis followed the dissolution of this council by the Gongola State government. He sits on the Taraba State Council of Chiefs alongside rulers such as the Aku Uka of Wukari.
sections.palace: The palace is in Jalingo, a town founded as a war camp and made the capital in 1893. Traditional ceremonies include turbaning, Sallah durbars and the Lamido's public audiences.
sections.today: The Emir of Muri is an advisory traditional ruler in Taraba State, a state with deep ethnic and religious diversity in which farmer-herder conflict is a recurrent issue; the current emir has publicly addressed criminal herders operating in the state's forests.

rulers.note: Deposed by the Gongola State military governor in 1986 and banished to Mubi.
rulers.bio: Installed as the 11th Emir of Muri on 6 November 1965, he reigned for two decades. After a running dispute with the military governor of Gongola State, Col. Yohanna Madaki, the government dissolved the emirate council and on 12 August 1986 issued an order deposing him, citing alleged misconduct; a banishment order to Mubi followed in September. He challenged the deposition in court, and the case (Tukur v. Government of Taraba State) was decided by the Supreme Court on 27 June 1997, largely on the question of which court had jurisdiction. He was later honoured as OFR.

rulers.name: Abbas Njidda Tafida
rulers.parent: grandson of Muhammadu Mafindi; son of Njidda Tafida
rulers.note: Current (12th) emir; a grandson of Mafindi and former hotel manager.
rulers.bio: Born in Jalingo on 10 June 1953, he received Qur'anic education before attending Muhammadu Nya Primary School and Government College, Keffi, and studied business administration at Ahmadu Bello University. He worked for the New Nigeria Development Company and then as a manager with Nigeria Hotels (1979–1988), and also farmed. He was installed as the 12th Emir of Muri in July 1988, after the throne had been vacant following his predecessor's deposition. During his long reign Jalingo became the capital of the new Taraba State (1991).

thrones.title: Etsu Nupe
thrones.established: Nupe kingdom c. 1531 (traditional); Fulani emirate at Bida c. 1835
thrones.about: The Etsu Nupe is the paramount ruler of the Nupe people, reigning from Bida. The title goes back to the old Nupe kingdom said to have been founded by Tsoede, but since the 19th century it has been held by descendants of the Fulani scholar Mallam Dendo, rotating among three ruling houses.

authority.text: The Etsu Nupe is both a traditional ruler and an emir: as head of a former Sokoto Caliphate emirate (originally under Gwandu) he is the senior Islamic leader of his domain, appointing imams and leading major Muslim festivals. The pre-Fulani Etsu of Tsoede's line held a sacred kingship tied to royal regalia and ancestral rites. Today the office is a fused traditional–Islamic one, and the current Etsu also chairs the board of the Abuja National Mosque.

sections.history:
Nupe tradition traces kingship to Tsoede (also Edegi), described as a son of the Attah of Idah and a Nupe mother, who returned north, united the Nupe settlements between the Niger and Kaduna rivers and established a dynasty; the king list dates his reign to 1531–1591. His successors ruled from a succession of capitals, and Etsu Jibiri in the 18th century is remembered as the first Nupe king to embrace Islam.

In the late 18th and early 19th centuries the kingdom was torn by civil war between rival princes such as Jimada and Majiya II. The Fulani cleric Mallam Dendo, a follower of Usman dan Fodio, gained influence at court and, after the wars of succession, his sons took power under the protection of Gwandu. Usman Zaki became the first Fulani Etsu, and Bida became the capital in the 1850s.

Under Masaba (second reign 1859–1873) and Umaru Majigi, Bida became one of the strongest emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate's southern frontier, with a large cavalry army and wide tributary territories. Branches of the old Tsoede dynasty survived elsewhere, and Agaie, Lapai, Pategi and Lafiagi emerged as separate Nupe-area emirates.

In 1897 the Royal Niger Company stormed Bida, and in 1901 the emirate was absorbed into the British Protectorate of Northern Nigeria, with Etsu Abubakar exiled and Muhammadu (Makun) installed. Under indirect rule the Etsu ran the Bida Native Authority, and Muhammadu Ndayako (1935–1962) is remembered as its most successful ruler.

After independence the office lost formal executive power. Since the creation of Niger State in 1976 the Etsu Nupe has been the state's leading traditional ruler, and the annual Nupe Day keeps both the Tsoede legacy and the Fulani-era court traditions in public view.
sections.selection: Succession is restricted to the descendants of Mallam Dendo's three sons — the houses of Usman Zaki, Masaba and Umaru Majigi — which have rotated the throne. When a vacancy occurs, the emirate's kingmakers screen princes of the eligible house and recommend a candidate to the Niger State Government, whose governor approves the appointment and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The Etsu presides over the Bida Emirate Council, made up of senior titled chiefs, district heads and Islamic officials. The senior royal title is the Shaba Nupe, regarded as second-in-command of the kingdom, while other titles such as Kusodu Nupe are held by princes before any accession; district heads administer the emirate's districts.
sections.palace: The Etsu's palace is in the centre of Bida, a walled city entered by traditional gates such as Ban Gaye and Ban Wuya. Court ceremonial includes durbars with cavalry at the Sallah festivals and the annual Nupe Day celebration, at which the Etsu receives homage from Nupe communities across Niger, Kwara and Kogi states.
sections.today: Under Niger State law the Etsu Nupe is a first-class traditional ruler and chairs the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers; he has also chaired the coordinating committee of the National Council of Traditional Rulers. The current Etsu, Yahaya Abubakar, has championed the creation of a Nupe-majority Edu State with Bida as its capital.

rulers.name: Muhammadu (Makun) dan Umaru Majigi
rulers.note: Installed by the British after Abubakar's removal; ruled under the new Northern Nigeria Protectorate.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Ndayako
rulers.note: Remembered as the most successful Etsu of the colonial era; ancestor of the prominent Ndayako family of the Majigi house.
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Ndayako, nicknamed 'Baba Kudu', came from the Majigi royal house and was installed in February 1935. His 27-year reign spanned late colonial indirect rule, the rise of party politics and independence in 1960. He is widely described in Nupe memory as the most successful Etsu of modern times. Several of his descendants have held senior titles, and his son Umaru Sanda Ndayako later became Etsu. He died in office in October 1962.

rulers.name: Usman Sarki dan Malam Sa'idu
rulers.note: Left the throne in 1969; the Niger State government describes his exit as an abdication, followed by a short interregnum.

rulers.name: Musa Bello
rulers.note: Died in January 1975.

rulers.name: Umaru Sanda Ndayako
rulers.note: Reigned about 28 years and died on 1 September 2003.
rulers.bio: Umaru Sanda Ndayako was a son of Etsu Muhammadu Ndayako of the Majigi house and was turbaned in January 1975. Daily Trust counts him as the 12th Etsu Nupe of the Fulani line. His reign of nearly three decades covered the creation of Niger State in 1976 and the return to civilian rule in 1999. A state general hospital in Bida is named after him. He died on 1 September 2003 and was succeeded by his nephew Yahaya Abubakar.

rulers.name: Yahaya Abubakar
rulers.parent: Nephew of Umaru Sanda Ndayako (son of his sister)
rulers.note: Retired brigadier general; chairman of the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers.
rulers.bio: Yahaya Abubakar was born in Bida on 12 September 1952 into the Usman Zaki ruling house; his mother, Princess Habiba, was a daughter of the Ndayako line. He was educated at Government College Sokoto and the Commercial College Kano before entering the Nigerian Defence Academy in 1973. He served in the Nigerian Army, his last post being director of foreign operations at Defence Headquarters, and retired as a brigadier general in 2003. Before accession he held the title Kusodu Nupe. He was appointed Etsu Nupe in September 2003 after his uncle's death. He chairs the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers and the management board of the Abuja National Mosque, and has led the campaign for a Nupe-majority Edu State.
rulers.dispute: Sources differ on the date (20 August vs 11 September 2003) and on whether he is the 12th or 13th Etsu of the Fulani line.

thrones.title: Emir of Kontagora (Sarkin Sudan)
thrones.about: Kontagora was carved out in the mid-19th century by Umaru Nagwamatse, a Sokoto prince, who subdued small chiefdoms of the Kambari, Dukawa and others. Its ruler carries the unusual title Sarkin Sudan and the throne has stayed within the Nagwamatse line.

authority.text: The Sarkin Sudan of Kontagora is an emir of the Sokoto Caliphate tradition: besides his role as traditional ruler he is the Islamic leader of the emirate, responsible for Islamic affairs, imams and the Eid prayers. The emirate also governs many non-Muslim Kambari, Dukawa and other communities, whose own village chiefs serve under the emir.

sections.history:
Between the late 1850s and 1864 Fulani forces led by Umaru Nagwamatse, a grandson of Usman dan Fodio's line from Sokoto, overran the minor chiefdoms of the area — among them Kambari, Dukawa, Dakka-Karri, Aguarra and Ngaski communities — and founded Kontagora as a frontier emirate dependent on Sokoto. The founder took the title Sarkin Sudan.

Under Ibrahim Nagwamatse (from 1880) Kontagora became notorious for large-scale slave raiding across the Niger–Kaduna region. In January 1901 British forces attacked the emirate; Ibrahim fled and was later captured, and the throne was declared vacant until the British reinstated him in 1903.

Kontagora was then administered as a province and later a division of the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. Emirs Umaru Maidubu (1929–1961) and Mu'azu presided over the transition to independence.

Sa'idu Namaska, a grandson of the founder and a former police officer and judicial official, ruled for almost five decades until his death in 2021. His successor's appointment by the Niger State government was contested in court before being upheld.
sections.selection: Princes of the Nagwamatse dynasty are eligible. The emirate's council of kingmakers screens candidates and elects one, whose name is forwarded to the Niger State Government for approval and the presentation of the staff of office. In 2021 over 40 princes applied for the vacancy.
sections.council: The Kontagora Emirate Council includes senior title-holders, district heads and Islamic officials. Its area spans Kontagora, Mariga, Magama and Rafi LGAs and includes subordinate chiefdoms such as Wushishi and the Kagara area.
sections.palace: The emir's palace stands in Kontagora town. As in other Hausa–Fulani emirates, turbaning ceremonies and the Sallah durbars with mounted horsemen are the main public displays of the throne.
sections.today: The Sarkin Sudan is a first-class ruler on the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers. The 2021 succession was challenged by rival princes, and a court briefly halted the appointment before later proceedings upheld Muhammad Bara'u Mu'azu II.

rulers.name: Sa'idu Namaska
rulers.note: Sixth emir; reigned about 47 years.
rulers.bio: Sa'idu Namaska (born Saidu Umaru, 31 December 1937, in Old Kontagora) was a grandson of the emirate's founder through his father, Umaru Sarkin Kudu. He studied at Bida Middle School and later at Ahmadu Bello University. He joined the Nigeria Police in 1961 and later rose to be a senior judicial official in the old North-Western State. He was turbaned as Sarkin Sudan in January 1974. During his long reign he became one of the senior members of the Niger State traditional council. He died at the National Hospital, Abuja, on 9 September 2021, aged 83.

rulers.name: Muhammad Bara'u Mu'azu II
rulers.note: Seventh emir; announced by the Niger State Government on 7 October 2021.
rulers.bio: Muhammad Bara'u Mu'azu II was born in Kontagora in 1974 and is a grandson of the fifth emir, Mu'azu. He was educated in Ibeto and at Government Secondary School Kontagora, then earned an NCE at the Federal College of Education, Kontagora. He worked in business before his selection. In 2021 the kingmakers chose him from more than 40 applicants, and the Niger State Government announced him as seventh Sarkin Sudan in October 2021. Losing contestants went to court, which briefly halted the appointment, but he was later confirmed and received his staff of office in February 2023.

thrones.title: Emir (Etsu) of Agaie
thrones.established: 1822 (conquest by Malam Baba); first emir installed 1832
thrones.about: Agaie is one of the three emirates (with Bida and Lapai) that grew out of the old Nupe kingdom after the Fulani jihad. Its ruler, styled Etsu Agaie, descends from the Fulani scholar-warrior Malam Baba.

authority.text: The Etsu Agaie is a traditional ruler and an emir in the Sokoto Caliphate tradition (historically under Gwandu), and so also the Islamic leader of the emirate, overseeing imams and Muslim festivals. There is no separate priestly role attached to the office.

sections.history:
Malam Baba, a Fulani cleric and warrior, conquered the Nupe communities around Agaie in 1822, during the jihad that broke up the old Nupe kingdom. His son 'Abd Allahi was installed as the first emir in 1832, with Malam Baba acting as regent until his death in 1848.

Agaie remained a tributary of Gwandu within the Sokoto Caliphate. Its rulers alternated between sons and brothers of earlier emirs, with the title Etsu reflecting the Nupe character of the state.

After the British conquest of Nupe in 1897–1901, Agaie was administered as a separate native authority in Niger Province. From 1989 the throne was disrupted by succession disputes: Etsu Muhammad Attahiru was removed in 1994, the office lay vacant at times, and he was restored in 2001 before dying in 2004.
sections.selection: Candidates come from the descendants of Malam Baba. The emirate kingmakers recommend a prince to the Niger State Government, which confirms the appointment and issues the letter and staff of office.
sections.council: The Etsu presides over the Agaie Emirate Council, which includes titled chiefs, district heads and Islamic officials of the emirate.
sections.palace: The palace is in Agaie town. Court ceremonial follows the Nupe–Fulani pattern of the region, with turbaning at accession and durbars at the Sallah festivals.
sections.today: The Etsu Agaie is a member of the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers. Etsu Muhammadu Kudu Abubakar was attacked by a mob in 2010 during a dispute over a police operation; he died in 2014 and was succeeded by Yusuf Nuhu.

rulers.bio: Muhammadu Kudu Abubakar came from the Ubandoma branch of the royal family and was appointed Etsu Agaie on 30 April 2004, aged about 42. He held diplomas in animal health and public administration from Ahmadu Bello University. He was grand patron of an education foundation for the emirate and backed the campaign, led by the Etsu Nupe, for a separate Edu State for the Nupe. In July 2010 he was attacked by a mob in Agaie who accused him of siding with police in a security operation; one person died in the unrest. He died in an Abuja hospital on 30 March 2014 after a long illness.

thrones.title: Emir (Etsu) of Lapai
thrones.about: Lapai emirate was founded in the 1820s in former Gbagyi (Gbari) country by Daudu Maza, a lieutenant of Malam Baba of Agaie, and became a Nupe-speaking emirate tributary to Gwandu. Its ruler is styled Etsu Lapai.

authority.text: The Etsu Lapai is a traditional ruler and an emir of the Sokoto Caliphate tradition, and so also the Islamic head of his emirate. He has no separate priestly role; Gbagyi communities in the emirate retain their own local chiefs.

sections.history:
The Lapai area was originally Gbagyi (Gbari) land. It came under Nupe influence in the 18th century and later under the Hausa state of Zazzau. During the jihad Malam Baba of Agaie sent his lieutenant Daudu Maza to subdue the area; Daudu succeeded but kept it for himself, and Lapai was separated from Zaria and Agaie around 1825.

The early emirs were sons of Jaura, and later the Jantabo and 'Abd al-Qadiri branches supplied rulers. The emirate paid tribute to Gwandu until the British took control in the early 1900s.

Muhammadu Kobo, a teacher and broadcaster who ruled from the mid-1950s to 2002, wrote a short history of the emirate and was one of Northern Nigeria's best-known traditional rulers. His nephew Umaru Bago Tafida succeeded him.
sections.selection: Eligible princes come from the descendants of the founding Jaura family. Kingmakers nominate a candidate to the Niger State Government, which approves the appointment; Umaru Bago Tafida was appointed by Governor Abdulkadir Kure in 2002.
sections.council: The Etsu presides over the Lapai Emirate Council of titled chiefs, district heads and Islamic officials.
sections.palace: The palace is in Lapai town. Turbaning ceremonies draw national figures — the 2002 turbaning was attended by Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and former head of state Ibrahim Babangida.
sections.today: The Etsu Lapai sits on the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers and has supported the movement for an Edu State. The emirate has seen farmer–herder clashes, including a deadly one in 2010.

rulers.name: Da'udu Maza dan Jaura
rulers.note: Founder; lieutenant of Malam Baba who kept Lapai for himself.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Kobo dan Aliyu Gana
rulers.note: 11th Etsu Lapai; died 13 June 2002 aged about 92.
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Kobo was born in 1910 into the Lapai royal house and educated at Agaie, Bida Provincial School and Katsina Teachers' College. He taught and served as a headmaster in several provinces before entering politics in 1948, when he was elected to the Northern House of Assembly. He held the title Tswaidan Lapai, headed the Northern Nigeria Broadcasting Corporation in the 1950s and chaired its board of governors in the 1960s. In 1958 he led a delegation to Libya and Pakistan to study penal codes. He became Etsu Lapai in the 1950s and reigned for about 48 years, writing a short foundation history of the emirate in 1981. He held the OBE and CON honours and was Chancellor of Kano State University in 1992–93. He died on 13 June 2002.
rulers.dispute: Start of reign given as 1953 or 1954 in different parts of the sources.

rulers.name: Umaru Bago Tafida II
rulers.note: 12th Etsu Lapai, appointed 10 August 2002.
rulers.bio: Umaru Bago Tafida, born in 1954, is a nephew of his predecessor Muhammadu Kobo. Niger State governor Abdulkadir Kure appointed him the 12th Etsu Lapai in 2002, and his turbaning was attended by senior national figures. He has been active on the Niger State Council of Chiefs and was among the delegation led by the Etsu Nupe in 2009 that asked lawmakers to consider a new Edu State. His reign has seen farmer–herder violence in the emirate, notably in 2010.

thrones.title: Emir of Borgu
thrones.established: Bussa kingdom by the 18th century (dated rulers from c. 1730); Borgu Emirate 1954
thrones.about: The Emir of Borgu rules from New Bussa and continues the line of the kings (Kibe) of Bussa, one of the old Borgu states of the Busa (Bisã) and Bariba peoples. The modern emirate was formed in 1954 by joining Bussa and Kaiama.

authority.text: Today the Emir of Borgu is a traditional ruler who also serves as the Islamic leader of his Muslim subjects, in the manner of other northern emirs. Unlike the Fulani emirates, however, Bussa was never conquered in the jihad: its kingship is older, and Borgu tradition links its royal houses to the legendary hero Kisra, so the office also carries non-Islamic ceremonial heritage.

sections.history:
Bussa was one of the kingdoms of Borgu, a region straddling today's Nigeria–Benin border whose ruling houses trace descent from the legendary Kisra. Its rulers bore the title Kibe; dated lists begin with Kiseru Brodi before 1730. Bussa remained independent of both the Oyo empire and the Sokoto Caliphate.

In 1898 Borgu was partitioned between France (Dahomey, now Benin) and Britain, with Bussa, Kaiama and Illo falling to Nigeria. Bussa was briefly placed under Yauri between 1915 and 1917, after the British removed Kitoro Gani, who was later restored.

In 1954 the Bussa and Kaiama emirates were merged as Borgu Emirate. In 1968 the old town of Bussa was flooded by the lake of the Kainji Dam, and the emir's seat was moved to the planned town of New Bussa.

In 2000–2002 the throne was disputed: Isiaku Musa Jikantoro was removed after two years and Haliru Dantoro, a former federal minister and senator, became emir. His son succeeded him in 2015.
sections.selection: The throne passes among the recognised royal houses of Bussa, which descend from earlier kings. Kingmakers nominate a candidate to the Niger State Government, which approves the appointment.
sections.council: The Emir presides over the Borgu Emirate Council of titled chiefs and district heads of Borgu and Agwara LGAs.
sections.palace: The palace was rebuilt at New Bussa after the old town was submerged by Kainji Lake. The emirate's ceremonial calendar includes the Sallah durbars and Borgu cultural festivals.
sections.today: The Emir of Borgu is a first-class member of the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers. The Kainji Dam relocation and the 2000–2002 succession dispute remain the main modern episodes in the throne's history.

rulers.name: Haliru Dantoro Kitoro III
rulers.note: Former FCT minister and senator; died 30 October 2015.
rulers.bio: Haliru Dantoro was born in 1938 at Bussa into the House of Gbemusu. Under the Gowon regime he served as a Kwara State commissioner for agriculture, finance and trade, and he later chaired the Niger River Basin Authority. In the Second Republic he was deputy state chairman of the NPN and briefly Minister of the Federal Capital Territory in 1983. He was elected a senator on the NRC platform in 1992. He became Emir of Borgu on 26 February 2002 after his predecessor was removed, and reigned until his death in a German hospital on 30 October 2015, aged 77.

thrones.title: Emir of Suleja (Sarkin Zazzau Suleja)
thrones.established: 1804 (exile court at Zuba); town of Abuja founded 1828
thrones.about: The Emir of Suleja heads the Hausa (Habe) dynasty of Zazzau that fled Zaria during the Fulani jihad and refounded its kingdom in the south at Zuba and then Abuja. The ruling line is Hausa, while most of the original rural population were Gbagyi (Gwari) and Koro.

authority.text: The emir is a traditional ruler and also the Islamic leader of the emirate's Muslims, presiding over Islamic affairs and the Sallah prayers. Unusually, the dynasty is a pre-jihad Hausa (Habe) line that was never part of the Sokoto Caliphate; it keeps the old title Sarkin Zazzau. The emirate's Gbagyi and Koro communities have their own chiefs under it.

sections.history:
When Fulani jihadists captured Zaria, capital of the Hausa kingdom of Zazzau, around 1804, Sarkin Zazzau Muhammadu Makau led his court south to the Koro town of Zuba. His brother Jatau, known as Abu Ja, founded a new walled town in 1828 that took his name — Abuja — and ruled it as Sarkin Zazzau.

Abuja survived as an independent Hausa refuge, resisting Fulani Zaria. Its rulers came from the sons of Ishaqu Jatau and their descendants, and the town became a centre of trade and craft between the Niger and Benue.

The British occupied Abuja in 1902. Under Emir Musa Angulu (1917–1944) tin mining began, and Sulaimanu Barau (1944–1979) presided over decolonisation.

In 1976 most of the emirate's territory was taken for the new Federal Capital Territory, which also borrowed the name Abuja. The old town and its emirate were renamed Suleja and remained in Niger State.

The late 20th century brought bitter succession disputes: Awwal Ibrahim, a former governor, became emir in 1993, was deposed by General Sani Abacha in 1994 and restored in 2000, both events sparking violence.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from princes of the Zazzau (Abuja) royal houses descended from the Jatau family. Kingmakers make a recommendation and the Niger State Government approves the appointment; the federal military government's direct intervention in 1994 was exceptional.
sections.council: The Suleja Emirate Council comprises titled Hausa officials, district heads and Islamic officials, together with representatives of Gbagyi and Koro communities in the emirate.
sections.palace: The emir's palace stands in the old walled city of Suleja. Durbars at the Sallah festivals continue the traditions of the Zazzau court.
sections.today: The Emir of Suleja is a first-class member of the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers. His restoration in 2000 was followed by clashes, a curfew and arrests, but he has remained on the throne since then.

rulers.name: Awwal Ibrahim (restored)
rulers.note: Restored 17 January 2000.
rulers.bio: Mohammed Awwal Ibrahim was born in Abuja (now Suleja) on 8 September 1941. He studied at Provincial Secondary School Bida and Abdullahi Bayero College, Kano, and became a language lecturer at Ahmadu Bello University and later an administrator at Bayero University. He rose to permanent secretary in the new Niger State civil service and in 1979 was elected the state's first civilian governor on the NPN platform. After the 1983 coup a military tribunal convicted him, and he was banned from public office in 1986. He became emir in 1993 amid riots, was deposed by General Abacha in May 1994, and was restored on 17 January 2000, again amid unrest that led to a curfew. He later chaired a Niger State committee on the reform of almajiri education.

thrones.title: Emir of Argungu (Sarkin Kabi)
thrones.established: Kebbi kingdom c. 1516; Argungu seat from c. 1827–1849
thrones.about: The Emir of Argungu is the heir of the Kanta dynasty of the Kebbi (Kabi) kingdom, the Hausa-speaking Kabawa state that dominated the region in the 16th century. After losing Birnin Kebbi in the jihad, the Kabawa kings held out at Argungu and kept their independence from Gwandu for much of the 19th century.

authority.text: The Sarkin Kabi of Argungu is a traditional ruler who is also the Islamic leader of his Muslim subjects and leads Islamic observances in the emirate. Unlike most northern emirs, his dynasty is a pre-jihad Hausa line that fought the Sokoto Caliphate rather than descending from it. Older Kabawa customs, including those surrounding the Argungu fishing festival on the Matan Fada river, survive alongside the Islamic role.

sections.history:
Kebbi emerged as a strong state when Kanta Kuta of Leka broke from the Songhay empire around 1516; his successor Muhammadu Kanta Kotal defeated Songhay forces, built the walled capital Surame, and made Kebbi the leading power among the western Hausa states. Kebbi declined after Kanta's death, and Birnin Kebbi became its capital.

In the Fulani jihad, Abdullahi dan Fodio took Birnin Kebbi (1805–08) and made it the base of Gwandu. The Kabawa under Muhammadu Hodi and then Karari kept fighting from the Zamfara valley and Argungu. Karari's son Yakubu Nabame submitted in 1831 and lived in Sokoto, but in 1849 he returned and proclaimed himself Sarkin Kebbi at Argungu.

Decades of war with Gwandu followed until a treaty in 1867 recognised Kebbi's independence. Sokoto reasserted control in 1892, but the arrival of the French explorer Monteil (1891) and British forces (1898–1902) changed the balance; Argungu provided a base for the British advance on Sokoto in 1903.

Under colonial rule the emirate became a native authority of Sokoto Province, and in 1934 Emir Muhammadu Sama staged a fishing contest for the visiting Sultan of Sokoto — the origin of the Argungu Fishing Festival, now an international event. Argungu became part of Kebbi State on its creation in 1991.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from princes descended from the Kanta dynasty. The emirate's kingmakers recommend a candidate to the Kebbi State Government, which makes the appointment.
sections.council: The Argungu Emirate Council includes senior title-holders, district heads and Islamic officials. Kebbi State's four emirate councils (Gwandu, Argungu, Yauri and Zuru) form the state council of chiefs.
sections.palace: The emir's palace stands in Argungu near the Kanta Museum, housed in the old palace building. The Argungu Fishing Festival — held on the Matan Fada river, with durbar, archery, wrestling and the hand-fishing contest — is the throne's best-known ceremony.
sections.today: The Emir of Argungu is a first-class member of the Kebbi State Council of Chiefs and chairs the festival's traditional committee. The festival lapsed between 1999 and 2004 for political reasons and was later revived; in 2025 the Kebbi governor named the emir the state's Amirul Hajj. Amid rural banditry the emir has publicly urged communities to defend themselves.

thrones.title: Emir of Yauri
thrones.established: 1411 (traditional king list)
thrones.about: Yauri is an old Niger-river kingdom in southern Kebbi whose king list begins in the early 15th century. Its population mixes Gungawa (Reshe) river people, Kambari, Hausa and others, and its rulers became tributaries of Gwandu after the jihad.

authority.text: The Emir of Yauri is a traditional ruler and Islamic leader of the emirate's Muslims, following the pattern of emirs tributary to Gwandu since the early 19th century. The kingship itself is pre-jihad, and the river communities (Gungawa/Reshe) and Kambari preserve customs older than the Islamic period.

sections.history:
The Yauri area along the Niger was settled by Kambari groups between about 1000 and 1200 AD; later the island-dwelling Gungawa (Reshe) rose to dominance and in the early 1500s expanded through war with the Kambari. A brief Songhay incursion left Songhay elements in the population. The king list dates the first Sarkin Yauri to 1411, and tradition credits a ruler named Yauri with founding Bin Yauri.

Slave raiding weakened the kingdom in the 1700s, and after the Fulani jihad Yauri became a tributary of Gwandu. The British took control in 1904, and in 1915–1917 Bussa was temporarily placed under Yauri.

The building of the Kainji Dam in the 1960s flooded old Yelwa and other riverside settlements, forcing resettlement. Yauri became part of Sokoto State and, from 1991, of Kebbi State.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from princes of the Yauri royal family. The emirate kingmakers nominate a candidate whom the Kebbi State Government appoints.
sections.council: The Yauri Emirate Council includes titled chiefs, district heads (covering Yauri, Shanga and Ngaski LGAs) and Islamic officials.
sections.palace: The emir's court is at Yelwa. River traditions are central: the emirate maintains a royal boat, and the Kebbi government approved funds for a new one in the 2020s.
sections.today: The Emir of Yauri is one of the four first-class emirs of Kebbi State. The current emir, Muhammad Zayyanu Abdullahi, has reigned since 1999.

thrones.title: Emir of Zuru
thrones.established: Colonial era (exact date not confirmed in sources consulted)
thrones.about: The Zuru Emirate covers the hill country of southern Kebbi inhabited mainly by the Dakarkari (Lela) and related peoples, spanning Zuru, Fakai, Sakaba and Danko-Wasagu LGAs. Its emirs carry the dynastic name Sami Gomo.

authority.text: Although the ruler bears the title emir and recent holders have been Muslims, Zuru was not founded through the jihad and governs a religiously mixed population of Lela (Dakarkari), Kambari and other communities with many Christians and adherents of traditional religion. Its role is primarily that of a civil traditional ruler; sources consulted do not attribute formal Islamic offices to the throne beyond leading Muslim subjects.

sections.history:
The Zuru area was home to the Dakarkari (Lela) and neighbouring peoples who largely stayed outside the jihad states of Gwandu and Yauri. Under British rule the district was organised as a native authority with its seat at Zuru, which later became an emirate.

The best-known modern holder was Major-General Muhammadu Sani Sami (Sami Gomo II), a former military governor of Bauchi State, who became the 11th Emir of Zuru in 1995 and reigned for 30 years. After his death in London in August 2025, the Kebbi State Government appointed Sanusi Sami as his successor.
sections.selection: Kingmakers of the Zuru Emirate screen candidates from the royal family and vote; a government committee reviews the outcome and the Kebbi State governor makes the appointment. In 2025 three candidates were screened and the one with the most kingmakers' votes was appointed.
sections.council: The Zuru Emirate Council covers four LGAs — Zuru, Fakai, Sakaba and Danko-Wasagu — with district heads and titled chiefs drawn from the area's communities.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in Zuru town. The Uhola festival of the Dakarkari (Lela) is the emirate's best-known cultural celebration.
sections.today: The Emir of Zuru is one of the four first-class emirs on the Kebbi State Council of Chiefs. The area has been badly affected by banditry in recent years.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Sani Sami (Sami Gomo II)
rulers.note: Retired major-general and former Bauchi military governor; died in London on 16 August 2025.
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Sani Sami was born in Zuru on 24 October 1943 into the emirate's royal lineage. He joined the army in December 1962, trained at Mons Officer Cadet School in Aldershot and was commissioned in 1963, later attending the Command and Staff College, Jaji. He served in the civil war, commanded the Brigade of Guards and led troops that expelled Chadian incursions from Borno. After the 1983 coup he was military governor of Bauchi State (1984–85). He retired as a major-general in 1990 and in 1995 became the 11th Emir of Zuru, taking the name Sami Gomo II. He died after a brief illness in London on 16 August 2025, aged 81.
rulers.dispute: The ten earlier emirs are not listed here: their names and dates could not be confirmed from accessible sources.

rulers.name: Sanusi Sami
rulers.note: Appointed by Governor Nasir Idris in August 2025 after winning the most votes among the kingmakers.

thrones.title: Emir of Lafia
thrones.established: c. 1804 (traditional); emir recognised by the British 1903
thrones.about: Lafia, capital of Nasarawa State, is ruled by an emir from a Kanuri (Beriberi/Bare-Bari) dynasty founded by Dunama, a migrant from Borno. The emirate governs a mixed population of Kanuri, Gwandara, Alago, Migili (Koro), Eggon, Fulani and Hausa.

authority.text: The Emir of Lafia is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the emirate's Muslims; the chief imam is one of the five kingmakers. Recent emirs have held national Islamic posts — Isa Mustapha Agwai I was a national vice-chairman of both Jama'atu Nasril Islam and the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs. Many of his subjects are Christian or follow traditional religion under their own chiefs.

sections.history:
Lafia grew on the site of a small Alago settlement. Tradition credits its founding to Dunama, a Kanuri leader from Borno, around the start of the 19th century; his descendants formed the royal lineages. The town became the capital of a significant chiefdom in the 19th century.

Under Mohamman Agwai (1881–1903) Lafia's market became one of the most important in the Benue valley, and a trade route was opened to the river port of Loko.

In 1903 the British recognised Musa as the first Emir of Lafia, and the emirate formed most of Lafia Division of Benue Province. It later passed to Benue-Plateau State (1967), Plateau State (1976) and, in 1996, the new Nasarawa State, with Lafia as state capital.

Isa Mustapha Agwai I reigned from 1974 to 2019, the longest reign in the emirate's history, and chaired the state council of chiefs from 1996. He was succeeded in 2019 by the Supreme Court justice Sidi Bage.
sections.selection: The Nasarawa State Government has gazetted two ruling houses, Ari and Dalla, both descended from Dunama; other Dunama lineages have contested this. Five kingmakers — the Makwangiji, Salanke, Moyi, Sarkin Fada and the Chief Imam — screen candidates and send names through the Ministry of Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs to the governor and state council of chiefs for approval.
sections.council: The Lafia Emirate Council includes the five kingmakers, senior titled princes (such as the Ubangari, Madaki and Kachalla) and district heads.
sections.palace: The emir's palace is in central Lafia. Turbaning, Sallah durbars and the conferment of titles are the main ceremonies.
sections.today: The Emir of Lafia is a first-class ruler and has chaired the Nasarawa State Council of Chiefs. Succession in 2019 attracted about 40 contenders, and in 2022 the emirate removed a son of the late emir from the Ubangari title in a dispute.

rulers.name: Isa Mustapha Agwai I
rulers.note: Longest-reigning Emir of Lafia; chaired the Nasarawa State Council of Chiefs.
rulers.bio: Isa Mustapha Agwai was born in Lafia on 15 February 1935 into the Aliyu Ari royal house. He attended Lafia Elementary School and the Benue Provincial Middle School at Katsina-Ala, then took an accountancy diploma at the Institute of Administration, Zaria, in 1959. He worked for the Lafia Native Authority as assistant treasurer and paymaster, and held the title Dan Galadiman Lafia as district head of Obi. He became the 16th emir in 1974 and reigned for 44 years, through the transfer of Lafia from Benue-Plateau to Plateau and then to Nasarawa State, whose capital it became in 1996. He chaired the state council of chiefs from 1996, was national vice-chairman of JNI and the NSCIA, and served as chancellor of two federal universities. He died in Abuja on 10 January 2019, aged 83.

rulers.name: Sidi Dauda Bage
rulers.note: Former Justice of the Supreme Court; appointed 26 March 2019.
rulers.bio: Sidi Dauda Bage was born in Lafia on 22 May 1956. He became a High Court judge in 1992 and was elevated to the Court of Appeal in 2007 and to the Supreme Court in December 2016. In March 2019 the Lafia kingmakers selected him from many contenders, and Governor Umaru Tanko Al-Makura appointed him the 17th Emir of Lafia on 26 March 2019, after which he left the bench. He has since been named chancellor of a Kano State university.

thrones.title: Emir of Keffi
thrones.about: Keffi was founded around 1800 by the Fulani warrior Abdu Zanga as a vassal emirate of Zaria. It is remembered for the 1902 killing of the British Resident in the town, which helped trigger the British conquest of Kano.

authority.text: The Emir of Keffi is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the emirate's Muslims, in the tradition of the Sokoto Caliphate emirates (historically under Zaria). The emirate also includes non-Muslim communities whose chiefs serve under the emirate council.

sections.history:
Abdu Zanga (Abdullahi), a Fulani leader from the north, founded Keffi around 1800–1802 and made it the seat of a small emirate subject to Zaria, to which it paid annual tribute in slaves. Keffi itself suffered slave raids, and wars with neighbouring Nasarawa under Emir Sidi Umaru (1877–1894) increased its payments to Zaria.

In 1902 the British moved the headquarters of Nassarawa Province to Keffi to protect the trade route from the Benue. That year Zaria's representative in Keffi, the Magaji, killed the British Resident and fled to Kano, giving Lugard a pretext for the 1903 attack on Kano.

Under colonial rule Keffi was a native authority in Nassarawa (later Plateau) Province. It passed to Plateau State in 1976 and to Nasarawa State in 1996.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen by the emirate's kingmakers from eligible princes of Abdu Zanga's dynasty and approved by the Nasarawa State Government.
sections.council: The Keffi Emirate Council comprises titled officials, district heads and Islamic officials.
sections.palace: The palace is in old Keffi town. Sallah durbars and turbaning ceremonies are the main royal public events.
sections.today: The Emir of Keffi is a first-class member of the Nasarawa State Council of Chiefs. In December 2025 the current emir marked ten years on the throne, an event attended by the Vice-President.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Chindo Yamusa II
rulers.note: Enthroned 11 May 1978; died 4 December 2015.
rulers.bio: Muhammadu Chindo Yamusa was born in Keffi in January 1940 and trained as a teacher, studying at the Higher Teachers' Training College in Ilorin, Ahmadu Bello University and Bristol University. He taught and served as a headmaster before becoming education officer for Keffi District (1965–72) and later secretary of education boards and local government councils in Plateau State. The kingmakers chose him after the death of Emir Ahmadu Maikoto, and he was enthroned on 11 May 1978. He reigned for 37 years, remembered for promoting peaceful coexistence and education. He died on 4 December 2015 after a brief illness.
