thrones.title: Emir of Nasarawa
thrones.established: 1835 (c. 1838 per Britannica)
thrones.about: Nasarawa emirate was founded in the 1830s by Umaru Makama Dogo, a dissident official of Keffi, who conquered Bassa and Afo communities and placed his new state under Zaria. The state of Nasarawa takes its name from the town.

authority.text: The Emir of Nasarawa is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the emirate's Muslims, in the tradition of the Zaria-linked emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate. The emirate's Bassa, Afo (Eloyi) and other communities, many Christian or traditionalist, have chiefs under the emirate council.

sections.history:
Umaru, known as Makama Dogo, came from Ruma in Katsina and served as an official in Keffi before breaking away. Around 1835–1838 he conquered the Bassa kingdom of Ikereku and Afo territory and founded Nasarawa, which he placed under Zaria as a vassal.

Emir Muhammadu Umaru Dan Waji (1878–1923) enlarged the emirate by further conquest and in 1900 was among the first northern emirs to accept British authority, earning the nickname Maje-Lokoja.

Nasarawa was a native authority of Nassarawa Province, then part of Benue-Plateau, Plateau (1976) and finally Nasarawa State (1996), which took its name from the emirate.
sections.selection: The emir is chosen from the descendants of Umaru Makama Dogo by the emirate kingmakers and appointed by the Nasarawa State governor.
sections.council: The Nasarawa Emirate Council includes titled officials, district heads and Islamic officials across Nasarawa and Toto areas.
sections.palace: The palace is in Nasarawa town; turbaning and the Sallah durbar are the main royal ceremonies.
sections.today: The Emir of Nasarawa is a first-class member of the Nasarawa State Council of Chiefs. The current emir is a former federal minister.

rulers.name: Umaru Usman (Makama Dogo)
rulers.note: Founder; a former official of Keffi who conquered the Bassa (Ikereku) and Afo country.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia dates the founding to 1835; Britannica to about 1838.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Sani
rulers.note: Reigned about 40 days.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Umaru Dan Waji (Maje-Lokoja)
rulers.note: Expanded the emirate and in 1900 was among the first emirs to pledge allegiance to Britain.
rulers.dispute: Britannica gives his reign as 1878–1922.

rulers.name: Ibrahim Usman Jibril
rulers.note: Former Minister of State for Environment; appointed 7 December 2018.
rulers.bio: Ibrahim Usman Jibril was born in Nasarawa town on 27 January 1958, a descendant of the founder Umaru Makama Dogo through the eighth emir, Umaru Maje-Haji. He studied education and geography at Bayero University Kano and later took a master's in land resources. After teaching, he spent about 25 years in FCT land administration, rising to director of the Land Administration Department. He was Minister of State for Environment from November 2015 to December 2018 under President Buhari. On 7 December 2018 Governor Umaru Tanko Al-Makura appointed him the 12th Emir of Nasarawa. He received the national honour CON in 2022.

thrones.title: Emir of Wase
thrones.about: Wase, below the striking Wase Rock in southern Plateau State, was founded as a Fulani emirate around 1820 by Hassan, a commander from Bauchi. It is the only historic jihad-era emirate in Plateau State.

authority.text: The Emir of Wase is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of the emirate's Muslims; the emirate was founded under Bauchi with permission from Sokoto. Non-Muslim communities in the area keep their own chiefs.

sections.history:
Giwa, a Fulani from Wuro Mayo in Bauchi, settled at Wase around 1813. His eldest son Hassan, a student of Usman dan Fodio and Madaki (cavalry commander) of Bauchi's founder Yakubu, founded the emirate around 1817–1820 in an area of the Basherawa people then under Jukun rule. Sokoto is said to have permitted the town on condition that it lie north of Wase Rock.

Wase expanded by conquest and recognised the Emir of Bauchi as overlord. Royal Niger Company troops entered the walled town in 1898, and after the British took Bauchi in 1902 Wase was declared independent and its ruler given the title emir.

Wase was part of Plateau Province under colonial rule and is today an LGA of Plateau State.
sections.selection: Princes of Hassan's dynasty are eligible. The emirate kingmakers nominate a candidate to the Plateau State Government for approval; in 2010 six princes contested the vacancy.
sections.council: The Wase Emirate Council includes titled officials and district heads; the emir also oversees lead and zinc mining interests in the area.
sections.palace: The palace is in Wase town, below Wase Rock, a notable landmark and bird habitat.
sections.today: The Emir of Wase is a first-class member of the Plateau State Council of Chiefs. The area has suffered banditry and farmer–herder violence in recent years.

rulers.name: Hassan dan Giwa
rulers.note: Founder; former Madaki of Bauchi.
rulers.dispute: Emirs 2–12 and their dates could not be confirmed from accessible sources.

rulers.name: Haruna Abdullahi Maikano
rulers.note: Nominated after his father's death in September 2001 and confirmed in 2002; died September 2010 aged 64.

rulers.name: Muhammadu Sambo Haruna
rulers.note: Appointed with effect from 28 October 2010.

thrones.title: Etsu Patigi
thrones.about: Pategi emirate was created in 1898 for Idrisu Gana, leader of the Yissazhi faction of the old Tsoede (Edegi) royal line of Nupe, who sided with the British against Fulani Bida. It is the seat of the Etsu Patigi and home of the Pategi Regatta.

authority.text: The Etsu Patigi is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of his mostly Muslim Nupe subjects; the Kwara government even named the Etsu Amirul Hajj (leader of the state's pilgrims) in 2023. The dynasty claims descent from the pre-Fulani Nupe kings of Tsoede's line rather than from the jihad leaders.

sections.history:
After Mallam Dendo's sons took power in Nupe, branches of the older Tsoede (Edegi) royal family continued to resist. The Yissazhi faction, led first by Jimada and from 1897 by Idrisu Gana, refused to fight for Bida when the Royal Niger Company attacked it in 1897.

As a reward the British allowed Idrisu Gana to form his own emirate at Pategi in 1898, south of the Niger. Under colonial rule Pategi was a district of Ilorin Province, and the first successful Sudan Interior Mission station was established there.

Etsu Umaru Bologi's council conceived the Pategi Regatta in 1949–50, first held in the early 1950s, a festival of canoe racing on the Niger. Pategi is now in Kwara State.
sections.selection: The Etsu is chosen from the royal house descended from Idrisu Gana (the Edegi line). Kingmakers recommend a prince and the Kwara State Government appoints him.
sections.council: The Patigi Emirate Council comprises titled chiefs, district heads and Islamic officials of Patigi LGA.
sections.palace: The palace is in Pategi town. The Pategi Regatta on the Niger, with canoe races and cultural displays, is the throne's showcase festival.
sections.today: The Etsu Patigi is a first-class ruler and member of the Kwara State Council of Chiefs; Ibrahim Umaru Chatta served as its vice-chairman. The current Etsu, appointed in 2019 aged 37, was named Amirul Hajj in 2023.

sources.label: VON – Kwara governor appoints Etsu Patigi as Amirul Hajj 2023

rulers.name: Idrisu Gana I
rulers.note: Founder; leader of the Yissazhi branch of the Tsoede line.

rulers.name: Umaru Ibrahim Bologi I
rulers.note: His council conceived the Pategi Regatta.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia gives him birth and death years (1939–2018) that are hard to reconcile with a reign beginning in 1949.

rulers.name: Idrisu Gana II
rulers.note: Reigned from 26 October 1966.

rulers.name: Ibrahim Umaru Chatta
rulers.note: Vice-chairman of the Kwara State Council of Chiefs; died 19 March 2019.
rulers.bio: Haliru Ibrahim Bologi Umaru Chatta was born in Pategi on 1 September 1958 and attended Government Secondary School, Ilorin. He was installed as Etsu Patigi in October 1999 after the death of Idrisu Gana II. During his twenty-year reign he served as vice-chairman of the Kwara State Council of Chiefs. He died after a brief illness in Abuja on 19 March 2019 and was succeeded by his son.

rulers.name: Umar Bologi II
rulers.note: Former customs officer; appointed 16 April 2019.
rulers.bio: Umar Bologi was born in Pategi on 8 February 1982 into the royal House of Bologi. He graduated in public administration from the University of Abuja in 2005 and joined the Nigeria Customs Service in 2010, serving in liaison, communication and protocol roles. On 16 April 2019, shortly after his father's death, Governor Abdulfatah Ahmed appointed him Etsu Patigi, and he was crowned that month, aged 37. In 2023 the Kwara government appointed him Amirul Hajj.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia counts him as both the 7th and 8th Etsu in different places.

thrones.title: Emir of Lafiagi
thrones.established: 1810 (town); first emir 1824
thrones.about: Lafiagi was founded in 1810 by the Fulani leaders Malam Maliki and his brother Manzuma, who came from Gwandu into Nupe country. The emirate governs a mainly Muslim Nupe population south of the Niger in Kwara State.

authority.text: The Emir of Lafiagi is a traditional ruler and the Islamic leader of his mostly Muslim Nupe subjects, in the tradition of the Gwandu-linked emirates founded during the jihad.

sections.history:
Malam Maliki and his brother Manzuma, Fulani leaders from Gwandu, founded Lafiagi as a fortified town in Nupe territory in 1810. After Maliki's death in 1824 the Emir of Gwandu named Manzuma the first Emir of Lafiagi.

The emirate withstood Nupe revolts in the late 1820s and again in the late 1890s, the latter with help from Royal Niger Company forces. Under colonial rule it formed part of Ilorin Province. In 1949 the ruler's title was changed from emir to chief, and from 1954 he chaired a federated council of Lafiagi, Sharagi and Shonga.

Saadu Kawu Haliru reigned from 1975 to 2021, one of the longest reigns in Kwara State. He was succeeded by the banker Mohammed Kudu Kawu, the 14th emir.
sections.selection: All ruling houses descend from a common ancestor and any eligible prince may contest. The kingmakers review applications, shortlist candidates and send names to the Kwara State Government, which makes the final appointment.
sections.council: The Lafiagi Emirate Council includes titled princes (such as the Ubandoma) and district heads of Edu LGA, and historically federated with Sharagi and Shonga.
sections.palace: The palace is in Lafiagi town; the presentation of the staff of office by the Kwara governor and Sallah celebrations are the main royal ceremonies.
sections.today: The Emir of Lafiagi is a first-class member of the Kwara State Council of Chiefs. The current emir, a former bank executive, was crowned in December 2021.

rulers.name: Malam Maliki
rulers.note: Co-founder of Lafiagi; not counted as emir.

rulers.name: Manzuma
rulers.note: Named first emir by the Emir of Gwandu.
rulers.dispute: Emirs between Manzuma and Saadu Kawu Haliru could not be confirmed from accessible sources.

rulers.name: Saadu Kawu Haliru
rulers.note: Reigned about 45 years; died 8 July 2021 aged 86.

rulers.name: Mohammed Kudu Kawu
rulers.note: Former banker; crowned 10 December 2021.
rulers.bio: Mohammed Kudu Kawu was born on 28 May 1969 to Mallam Abubakar Kawu, a Lafiagi prince. He studied business administration at Ahmadu Bello University and holds postgraduate degrees from ABU and Bayero University, Kano, and is a Fellow of the Chartered Institute of Bankers. His banking career of over two decades took him through Standard Chartered, Ecobank, Prudent/Skye (Polaris) Bank, where he became regional director for the North, and Wema Bank, where he was a deputy general manager. He held the title Ubandoman Lafiagi before the kingmakers shortlisted him and the Kwara government appointed him in late 2021. He received his staff of office as the 14th emir on 10 December 2021.

thrones.title: Tor Tiv
thrones.about: The Tor Tiv (also styled Begha U Tiv) is the paramount ruler of the Tiv, one of Nigeria's largest peoples, with his seat at Gboko in Benue State. The office was created in 1946, at the request of Tiv war veterans and educated Tiv, for a people who had traditionally been governed by lineage elders rather than kings. By state law the stool rotates between the two great Tiv lineages, Ipusu and Ichongo.

sources.label: Latest Nigerian News: History of kingship in Tiv land (2015)
Intervention: Value shift in Tivland as intellectual emerges king (2016)
Guardian NG: New dawn as Tiv land crowns Prof. James Ortese Iorzua Ayatse
Tiv Heritage Archive: Tor Tiv (historical figures)
Tiv Heritage Archive: James Akperan Orshi
Tiv Heritage Archive: Alfred Akawe Torkula

rulers.name: Makir Zakpe
rulers.born: 11 April 1896, Mbayar (Nyumagbagh), Mbaduku District, now Vandeikya LGA
rulers.note: First Tor Tiv, chosen in September 1946 from the Ipusu line (Kunav clan) by 25 votes to 11 over Gondo Aluor, and installed in November 1947. He died in office in October 1956.
rulers.bio: Makir Zakpe was born in 1896 in Mbaduku District in the Kunav clan of the Ipusu lineage. He enlisted in the Royal West African Frontier Force at Calabar in 1918, served through the Second World War and rose to battalion sergeant major, then served as a police officer, latterly as police chief of the Tiv Native Authority at Gboko. With other Tiv veterans he campaigned against the division of the Tiv into separate administrative zones and for a single Tiv ruler. In 1946 the chiefs chose him by 25 votes to 11 over Gondo Aluor, with 18 abstentions. As Tor Tiv he worked to settle disputes across Tivland, approved the building of the Tor Tiv office at Gboko and suppressed the Garyo movement of 1948. He died at Gboko on 11 October 1956 and was buried at Abagu, which became the burial ground of later Tor Tivs.
rulers.dispute: Selection on 19 September 1946 is agreed. Installation is given as 1 November 1947 (Tiv Heritage Archive) or 3 April 1947 (a Wikipedia variant).

rulers.name: Gondo Aluor
rulers.note: First Tor Tiv from the Ichongo line, installed in December 1956 after serving as chief scribe and deputy Tor Tiv. His 22-year reign spanned the Tiv disturbances of 1960 and 1964 and the creation of Benue State.
rulers.bio: Gondo Aluor, born in 1906, became a teacher in 1924, was made chief scribe of the Tiv Native Authority in 1940 and deputy Tor Tiv in 1948. He had been the Ichongo candidate in 1946 and lost to Makir Zakpe. On Makir's death he was installed as Tor Tiv II (Wikipedia gives 12 December 1956), which began the alternation of the stool between Ichongo and Ipusu. His reign covered the violent political disturbances of 1960 (Nande-Nande) and 1964 (Atem Tyough) and the creation of Benue-Plateau and then Benue State, and he became chairman of the Benue State Council of Chiefs. He died in 1978.
rulers.dispute: Death date given as 17 Sept 1978 (Gondo Aluor article) or 19 Nov 1978 (Tor Tiv list); year agrees.

rulers.name: James Akperan Orshi
rulers.ended: died (per the Tiv Heritage Archive, which lists him as late; date not given)
rulers.note: A lawyer and senior civil servant from the Ipusu line, enthroned in 1979. Wikipedia gives his reign as 10 March 1979 to 16 October 1990.
rulers.bio: James Akperan Orshi was born at Gboko in 1925. He trained and worked as a teacher and headmaster, studied at the University of London Institute of Education and the Institute of Administration, Zaria, and was called to the English Bar (Middle Temple) in 1963. He served as magistrate and senior magistrate, Solicitor-General, and Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Benue-Plateau State (1974–76), then briefly as Secretary to the Benue State Military Government and Head of Service in 1976; he also chaired Nigeria Airways. He was enthroned as Tor Tiv III in 1979. Sources consulted record little about the events of his reign.
rulers.dispute: Enthronement is given as 10 March 1979 (Wikipedia list) or April 1979 (Tiv Heritage Archive). Wikipedia's end date of 16 October 1990 is not explained; the Tiv Heritage Archive describes him as late but gives no date of death.

rulers.name: Alfred Akawe Torkula
rulers.born: 10 July 1944, Tse-Torkula, Mbadwem District, Guma LGA
rulers.note: An Ichongo-line scholar-king, he worked to calm the Tiv–Jukun crisis and internal boundary disputes, restructured the traditional council with new graded stools, and campaigned against costly bride-price and burial practices. He wrote on Tiv cosmology and burial customs and died in Abuja in November 2015, aged 71.
rulers.bio: Alfred Akawe Torkula, of the Ihyarev clan (Ichongo), was educated at Mount Saint Michael's, Aliade, and the University of Besançon in France, and later earned a doctorate in cultural anthropology. He spent over two decades in the Benue-Plateau and Benue civil service, rising to permanent secretary, and was Benue Commissioner for Local Government from 1989. Installed in 1991, he also chaired the Benue State Council of Chiefs. He inherited the Tiv–Jukun crisis and internal boundary disputes and threatened to remove chiefs who incited violence; he reorganised the traditional council with new graded stools and introduced honorary titles. He served as chancellor of the Universities of Ibadan and Calabar and of Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, and wrote on Tiv cosmology and burial customs. He died in Abuja in November 2015, aged 71, and was buried at Abagu.

image.caption: Tor Tiv IV, Alfred Akawe Torkula

rulers.dispute: Start given as 14 Jan 1991 in the article body and 21 Apr 1991 in the infobox; year agrees.

rulers.name: James Ortese Iorzua Ayatse
rulers.note: A professor and former vice-chancellor, he was elected by the kingmakers (39 of 46 votes) on 20 December 2016 and crowned at Gboko on 4 March 2017. The coronation was marked by a man sitting on the royal stool beforehand, who was jailed and banished; the new Tor Tiv later asked for his pardon.
rulers.bio: James Ortese Iorzua Ayatse studied biochemistry at the University of Ibadan, took an MSc at Calabar and a doctorate at the University of Surrey, and in 1993 became, at 37, the first Tiv professor of biochemistry. He was vice-chancellor of the University of Agriculture, Makurdi (2001–2006) and pioneer vice-chancellor of the Federal University Dutsin-Ma (2011–2016), and later chancellor of Abia State University. Elected Tor Tiv V by 39 of 46 kingmakers on 20 December 2016, he was crowned at Gboko on 4 March 2017 and received the staff of office from Governor Samuel Ortom. He chairs the Tiv Traditional Council and the Benue State Council of Chiefs and was made CFR in 2022.
rulers.dispute: Elected 2016, crowned 2017; 2017 used as start.

thrones.grade: First class (paramount ruler of the Tiv; chairs the Benue State Council of Chiefs)

authority.text: The Tor Tiv is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office: he presides over the Tiv Traditional Council (Ijir Tamen), arbitrates disputes and represents the Tiv to government. The office has a ritual dimension rooted in Tiv tradition rather than a priestly one: the coronation oath has customarily been sworn on Swem, the ancestral hill and sacred emblem invoked in Tiv oaths and cleansing rites. The Tiv Heritage Archive notes that two holders (Orshi and Ayatse) took the oath on the Bible instead.

sections.history:
Tiv tradition traces the whole people to a single ancestor, Tiv, and his two sons, Ichongo and Ipusu, whose descendants form the two great lineages that still order Tiv kinship and land. Oral history places the ancestors at Swem, a hill near the source of the Katsina-Ala River on the present Nigeria–Cameroon border, from where they moved in stages into the Benue Valley; the Tiv Heritage Archive dates settlement near Swem to about 1600 and a major outward expansion to roughly 1750–1800, after the Kwararafa confederacy declined. Language evidence (Tiv is a Tivoid, Bantoid language whose relatives are spoken along that same border) supports a south-eastern origin.

Before colonial rule the Tiv had no king. Authority lay with the elders of each lineage and with the eldest man of a clan, and leadership rested on age, influence and wealth. Settlement was dispersed, with compounds spread over high ground rather than walled towns.

British contact began with Hugh Trenchard's expedition of 1907–08, and pacification reached southern Tivland in 1911, remembered locally as 'the eruption'. Because indirect rule needed chiefs, the administration experimented with placing Tiv under neighbouring rulers and with elders' councils; in 1927 a non-Tiv, Audu Dan Afoda of Makurdi, was put at the head of the Tiv council at Abinsi, which Tiv chiefs and the educated class resented. Resistance to colonial taxation and forced labour during the 1920s ended in armed confrontations around 1929.

After the Second World War, returning soldiers led by Makir Zakpe and Lawrence Igyuse Doki, with educated Tiv officials, campaigned for a single Tiv ruler. The colonial government agreed, and in September 1946 the chiefs voted between the Ipusu candidate, Makir Zakpe, and the Ichongo candidate, Gondo Aluor; Makir won 25 votes to 11, with 18 abstentions, and was formally installed in November 1947. Under colonial oversight the Tor Tiv collected poll tax, carried government messages and presided over Ijir Tamen as chief judge.

The office passed through the turbulent politics of the First Republic, including the Tiv disturbances of 1960 and 1964, and the creation of Benue-Plateau (1967) and Benue (1976) states. Later holders were drawn from law, the civil service and universities. Tor Tiv IV, Alfred Akawe Torkula, steered the institution through the Tiv–Jukun conflicts of the 1990s and 2000s and restructured its chieftaincy grades; Tor Tiv V, Professor James Ayatse, was crowned in 2017.
sections.selection: Benue State law (the law establishing the Council of Chiefs and Traditional Councils) provides that the stool rotates between the Ipusu and Ichongo ruling houses, a principle the Tiv Heritage Archive calls ya na angbian. Candidates from the lineage whose turn it is are put to a vote of the kingmakers of the Tiv Traditional Council: in December 2016, for example, James Ayatse won 39 of 46 votes. The governor of Benue State then approves the choice and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The Tor Tiv presides over Ijir Tamen, the Tiv Traditional Council, which the Tor Tiv Wikipedia article describes as the highest policy body of the Tiv and which includes all chiefs in Tivland. Under it are graded chiefs, district heads and clan heads; Torkula created 14 second-class stools and proposed first-class stools and some 60 third-class chiefdoms. The Tor Tiv also chairs the Benue State Council of Chiefs. The office confers titles such as Zege Mule U Tiv, the highest Tiv chieftaincy title.
sections.palace: The Tor Tiv's seat and office are at Gboko; the first holder approved the building of the Tor Tiv office there. Past Tor Tivs are buried at Abagu, Gboko, starting with Makir Zakpe in 1956. Coronations are public events at Gboko before the kingmakers, with the governor presenting a staff of office; at the 2017 coronation in J.S. Tarka Stadium, a man who sat on the prepared royal stool was jailed for impersonating the Tor Tiv. Torkula chose a leopard-skin cap and beads, instead of the turban worn by many northern rulers, to mark a distinct Tiv identity. Tiv Day and festivals such as Kwagh-hir puppet theatre are major occasions of Tiv culture.
sections.today: The Tor Tiv has no constitutional powers but is the main voice of the Tiv to federal and state governments, chairs the Benue State Council of Chiefs and is often called on in farmer–herder violence, inter-communal boundary disputes and Tiv–Jukun relations. James Ayatse, a biochemist and former vice-chancellor, has held the stool since March 2017 and was made a Commander of the Order of the Federal Republic (CFR) in 2022.

thrones.title: Och'Idoma
thrones.established: 1948 (organised under the Idoma Native Authority, 1947–48)
thrones.about: The Och'Idoma is the paramount ruler of the Idoma of southern Benue State, with his palace at Otukpo. The office was created under British rule, when the chiefs of the Idoma Native Authority elected the first holder in 1948 to stand above the 22 formerly independent Idoma groups. He chairs the Idoma Area Traditional Council.

I Am Benue: Idoma people of Benue State

rulers.name: Ogiri Oko
rulers.note: Former district head of Adoka, he was elected the first Och'Idoma by the newly formed Idoma traditional council, giving the colonial administration a single intermediary for the Idoma districts.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia and World Statesmen give 1948–1959 (World Statesmen notes the office was organised in 1947). The throne was vacant 1959–1960.

rulers.name: Abraham Ajene Okpabi
rulers.note: Of Igede descent and formerly head of the Native Authority dispensary at Adoka, he is credited with the longest tenure of any Och'Idoma and with keeping Idoma land united; he helped settle a long-running boundary dispute by retracing colonial beacons. He was son-in-law to Ogiri Oko.
rulers.dispute: World Statesmen gives March 1960–1995, followed by a vacancy 1995–1996.

rulers.name: Edwin Ogbu
rulers.note: Reigned only from January to April 1996 (World Statesmen); he died in April 1996 (IdomaLand).
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia and I Am Benue give 1996–1997, which conflicts with his April 1996 death and his successor's December 1996 installation. Corrected here to January–April 1996 per World Statesmen and IdomaLand.

rulers.name: Elias Ikoyi Obekpa
rulers.note: A tax administrator who had chaired the Benue State Board of Internal Revenue, he was installed on 7 December 1996 and reigned for nearly 25 years. He died on 9 October 2021 and was buried according to Idoma traditional rites for chiefs.
rulers.bio: Elias Ikoyi Obekpa trained as a teacher at St Enda's Teachers College, Zaria, and taught in Samaru before joining the Benue-Plateau civil service as a tax administrator. He took a BSc in business administration at Ahmadu Bello University (1974) and an MSc in management in Cambridge, Massachusetts (1982), became Director of Tax Administration, and in 1994 chairman of the Benue State Board of Internal Revenue. The kingmakers chose him after Edwin Ogbu's death, and he was installed at Otukpo on 7 December 1996. He was known for reconciling Idoma politicians and improving relations with neighbouring peoples, was made CON in 2006, and served as chancellor of the Federal University of Kashere. He died on 9 October 2021 and was buried the next day under Idoma traditional rites for chiefs.

rulers.name: John Elaigwu Odogbo Obagaji
rulers.note: Elected by 19 of 28 kingmakers on 30 December 2021 and crowned by Governor Samuel Ortom at Otukpo on 30 June 2022. He is from Agatu LGA. Some Idoma groups have contested his selection.

image.caption: Och'Idoma V, John Elaigwu Odogbo Obagaji

rulers.dispute: Elected December 2021 (World Statesmen dates his reign from 30 Dec 2021), crowned June 2022.

authority.text: The Och'Idoma is a traditional ruler with no formal religious office. In the older Idoma polities the local king (Oche) was also chief priest of the earth (Aje) shrines and was called Ond'aje, 'owner of the land', and the Alekwu ancestral cult played a central role in justice and community life. The paramount office created in the colonial period is administrative and representative rather than priestly, although its holders are buried with Idoma traditional rites for chiefs.

sections.history:
The Idoma comprise many groups in southern Benue State, several of which trace their origin to Apa, a polity associated with the Kwararafa (Okolofa) confederacy of the Benue valley; Idoma traditions describe migrations away from Apa roughly three centuries ago under pressure from northern invaders.

Before British rule each of about 22 Idoma groups governed itself. A council of elders, including hereditary title-holders (igabo), advised the local Oche, who was chosen for qualities such as strength of character, war leadership and fairness in mediation, and who served as priest of the earth shrines.

The British grouped these chiefdoms in the Idoma Native Authority. Its chiefs formed a council which, in 1948, elected Ogiri Oko, district head of Adoka, as the first Och'Idoma, giving the colonial administration a single intermediary.

Abraham Ajene Okpabi (from 1960) held the throne for some 35 years and is credited with holding Idoma land together and settling a long boundary dispute. After a brief reign by Edwin Ogbu in 1996, the tax administrator Elias Ikoyi Obekpa reigned from December 1996 until his death in October 2021. John Elaigwu Odogbo Obagaji was elected in December 2021 and crowned in June 2022.
sections.selection: The Och'Idoma is chosen by election among kingmakers drawn from the Idoma traditional council, and the Benue State government approves the choice and presents the staff of office. In December 2021, 28 kingmakers voted: John Elaigwu Odogbo received 19 votes, Sunday Echono 8 and Andrew Idakwu 1. Sources consulted do not describe a fixed rotation among Idoma districts.
sections.council: The Och'Idoma chairs the Idoma Area Traditional Council, made up of the chiefs and district heads of the Idoma-speaking areas of southern Benue State. The council issues collective positions on security, land and culture, and it has, for example, declared void chieftaincy titles conferred by the Ny'Igede of the neighbouring Igede.
sections.palace: The palace is at Otukpo; at the 2022 coronation the governor said a new palace was about 90 per cent complete. The coronation took place at the Och'Idoma Square in Otukpo, where the governor presented the staff of office. Holders are styled Agabaidu. The five-day Alekwu ancestral festival in December is a major event of the Idoma calendar.
sections.today: The Och'Idoma has no constitutional powers but represents the Idoma to the state and federal governments and speaks on security, farmer–herder violence and Idoma unity. Some Idoma groups have contested the legitimacy of the 2021 selection. The current holder, Agabaidu John Elaigwu Odogbo Obagaji, has issued annual addresses to the 'Idoma nation' and declared 23 December as Idoma Day.

thrones.title: Attah Igala
thrones.established: c. 16th century (traditional; Wikipedia gives Abutu-Eje as founder, with uncertain dates)
thrones.about: The Àtá (Attah) Igala is the sacred king of the Igala, with his seat at Idah on the Niger in Kogi State. The kingship, which tradition traces to the 16th century, is regarded as the spiritual centre of the kingdom, and the Àtá is chosen in rotation from four royal houses descended from Àtá Ayegba Oma Idoko. Two figures loom over its memory: Princess Inikpi, who in legend gave her life for the kingdom's victory, and Àtá Ameh Oboni, who died in 1956 rather than submit to British deposition.

rulers.ended: died rather than accept deposition and exile by the British
rulers.parent: son of Oboni (per the Ọm patronymic in the Wikipedia list)
rulers.note: Installed on 1 May 1945, he resisted British indirect rule and defended Igala ritual practice. Facing deposition and exile in 1956, he died by his own hand at Dekina.
rulers.bio: Ameh Oboni was born in 1911 and lost his father in infancy, growing up partly among his mother's relatives in Itobe district. In the 1930s he worked for the colonial waterworks at Lokoja and Okene; after the death of his brother in 1938 he was recalled as heir. Installed on 1 May 1945, he is credited with expanding Native Authority schools and dispensaries, road building and Idah's first airstrip. He resisted being subordinated under British indirect rule and the northern establishment, and popular accounts describe clashes over royal protocol in Kaduna. After a petition alleged human sacrifice at a royal festival, the festivals were banned and his deposition and exile were ordered; he died by suicide at Dekina on 26 June 1956. Igala memory treats him, with Ayegba, as the most revered Àtá, and the British afterwards required future Àtás to have Western education.
rulers.dispute: World Statesmen places the 1945–1956 dates against 'Obaje om Oceje' and is unclear on Ameh Oboni's tenure; Wikipedia, the Igala people article and WithinNigeria give 1945–1956 to Ameh Oboni. Some details of the popular account (WithinNigeria) are oral tradition.

rulers.bio: Aliyu Ocheje Obaje, son of Otulukpe Obaje, was installed by the colonial administration after Ameh Oboni's death, at about 46. ThisDay describes the appointment as bypassing the normal rotation, since his house was not among those in contention; the expected candidate, Opaluwa Oguche, challenged it in court until 1972. ThisDay also notes that he never went through the full traditional rites of an Igala king. He reigned through independence, the civil war and the creation of Kogi State, chaired the state council of traditional rulers, held the GCFR honour and conferred many chieftaincy titles. He died on 16 July 2012, aged about 101, and was buried at Idah.
rulers.dispute: Installation is given as 2 November 1956 (Wikipedia: Aliyu Obaje) or 20 October 1956 (World Statesmen).

rulers.bio: Matthew Alaji Opaluwa was educated at St Peter's College, Idah, and Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria (BSc 1986, MBA 1997). He joined the Independent National Electoral Commission in 1988 and served for over two decades as an electoral officer and unit head in Kogi, Kaduna, Katsina and the FCT, rising to deputy director. A grandson of Opaluwa Oguche of the Aj'Ameacho house, he was named Àtá-designate by the Igala Traditional Council on 28 April 2021, approved by the Kogi State Executive Council on 18 October 2021 and crowned with the staff of office at Idah on 4 March 2022.

authority.text: The Àtá is not only a ruler but the 'national father' and spiritual head of the Igala in traditional religion. He oversees the kingdom's principal sacred objects, shrines and festivals, and performs key rites of the farming year, such as opening the earth festival with a communal hunt in which he spears an animal for the national earth shrine. The Igala Mela, the nine kingmaker chiefs, are custodians of the sacred earth shrine. Regalia including oka and okwu beads, the robe, the red cap and the flywhisk mark his ritual status.

sections.history:
Igala tradition names Abutu-Eje as the founder of the kingdom in the 16th century, under a dynasty linked to Kwararafa (Jukun), and remembers a woman, Ebulejonu, as the first Àtá of the independent line; she was followed by her brother Aganapoje and then by Idoko. Wikipedia's list also preserves an earlier 'Aji' series of names with indicative dates from 1507.

Idoko's son Ayegba is the kingdom's great hero: tradition credits him with a war that ended outside domination. In the best-known legend an oracle demanded the life of his daughter Inikpi, who volunteered and was buried alive near the Niger at Idah; her statue stands at Ega market. Sources disagree on the enemy: Igala Kingdom and Igala people articles frame the war as liberation from the Jukun, while the Princess Inikpi article places it in the Igala–Benin war of 1515–16. Benin influence on Igala is also recorded, including suzerainty under Oba Esigie and Benin-style brass masks.

The four present royal houses descend from Ayegba's sons and grandsons. In the 19th century Idah was an important river kingdom on the lower Niger, and the dated list begins with Ekele in about 1835. British rule was established around 1900.

Àtá Ameh Oboni, installed in 1945, opposed indirect rule and defended Igala ritual practice. After a petition alleged human sacrifice at a royal festival, colonial authorities moved to depose and exile him, and he died on 26 June 1956 at Dekina; Igala accounts treat his death as a refusal to submit. The British then installed Aliyu Obaje outside the usual rotation, and he reigned for about 56 years, through independence and the creation of Kogi State in 1991.

Obaje's death in 2012 restarted the rotation: Idakwo Michael Ameh Oboni II (2012–2020) was followed, after a year-long contest within the Aj'Ameacho house, by Matthew Alaji Opaluwa, crowned at Idah in March 2022.
sections.selection: The stool rotates among four royal houses of Ayegba Oma Idoko's line, in order of seniority: Aj'Ameacho, Aj'Aku, Aj'Akogu and Aj'Ocholi. When an Àtá dies, the Achadu (the kingdom's prime minister) declares the stool vacant. The house whose turn it is chooses a candidate, usually preferring the eldest qualified son of its last king; a later amendment ('Wada Law') widened eligibility to grandsons, nephews and grand-nephews. The Igala Mela kingmakers, led by the Etemahi, verify the nominee, and the Achadu forwards the name for approval by the Kogi State government.
sections.council: The Achadu is chief executive or prime minister of the kingdom and declares vacancies. The Igala Mela are nine high chiefs, headed by the Etemahi, who are kingmakers and custodians of the earth shrine. Beneath the Àtá are traditional councils with their own rulers (onu) in areas such as Ankpa, Ajaka, Ugwolawo, Egume, Dekina, Omala and Olamaboro, and the Igala Traditional Council selects the Àtá-designate.
sections.palace: The Àtá's palace is at Idah, the ancestral capital on the Niger. His regalia include oka and okwu beads, a robe, a red cap and a flywhisk. The ritual calendar includes the earth festival that opens the farming year and the Ibegwu festival honouring the ancestors before the yam harvest; Ameh Oboni's last years were bound up with colonial bans on royal festivals. The 2022 coronation was held at the Civic Centre, Idah, attended by other monarchs including the Olu of Warri. Inikpi's statue at Ega market is a major memorial site.
sections.today: The Àtá chairs the Igala Traditional Council and is a leading member of the Kogi State Council of Traditional Rulers. Kogi State law governs approval of the Àtá-designate, and the 2020–21 succession saw a long contest among Opaluwa Oguche's descendants. When approving Matthew Opaluwa's appointment in 2021, the state government also upgraded 74 traditional stools in Igala land.

thrones.established: Wukari dynasty list from 1833; Jukun tradition dates the Wukari chiefdom to 1596
thrones.about: The Aku Uka is the sacred king of the Jukun (Wapan) at Wukari in Taraba State and the heir of the Kwararafa kingship that once dominated the Benue valley. In Jukun belief he is a divine king, son of a god, who 'does not die but joins his ancestors'. The throne alternates between two royal houses and is filled by kingmakers through secret Jukun rites before state recognition.

rulers.bio: Shekarau Angyu Masa Ibi, son of Aku Uka Angyu Masa Ibi, was born at Wukari in 1937. He worked as a personal assistant in the Northern Region government in Kaduna, including to a parliamentary secretary, and from 1963 to the chairman of the Electricity Corporation of Nigeria in Lagos; after the 1966 coup he left the civil service for business in Makurdi. Crowned at Byepi in 1976 as Kuvyon II, he reigned 45 years, chaired the Taraba State Council of Traditional Rulers and was chancellor of the Federal University Dutse. His reign saw the Tiv–Jukun conflicts of 1990–92 and 2001–02, and in 2020 he linked the long land dispute to an unresolved boundary adjustment. He celebrated 40 years on the throne in 2017 and died at Wukari in October 2021, aged 84.

He holds a Higher National Diploma in forestry and retired in 2000 after 35 years in the civil service. Chosen by the kingmakers after Kuvyon II's death, he was crowned in Pankan rites at Bye Vyi on 28 January 2022, then performed rites at Jukun sacred sites before entering Wukari as Aku Uka. He later received the staff of office from the Taraba State governor; a public celebration was held in November 2022.

authority.text: The Aku Uka is a sacred king in Jukun traditional religion: he is regarded as divinely sanctioned and the son of a god, with the sun god paramount in the Jukun pantheon. His accession is completed through Pankan rites at Bye Vyi and other Jukun spiritual sites (Puje, Kuntsa, Akwana, Arufu, Wapan Nghaku), and Jukun tradition holds that the king does not die but joins his ancestors. Wukari also keeps a sacred crocodile shrine in the Marmara pond. C. K. Meek's 1931 ethnography 'A Sudanese Kingdom' is the classic study of this divine kingship.

sections.history:
The Jukun regard themselves as the heirs of Kwararafa, a confederacy of the Benue valley whose existence is recorded in Hausa chronicles from the 15th century. Its old capital is remembered as Api or Bie-Pi. The Jukun were established at Wukari by the 17th century, and Jukun tradition dates the Wukari chiefdom to 1596.

Wukari lay on a trade route linking the Benue to Bauchi and to Katsina, Kano and Borno, and its king had regional prestige: in 1780 a migrant leader from Borno sought the Aku Uka's endorsement to rule at Lafia. After the Fulani jihad of 1804–1810 broke the remains of Kwararafa, Wukari emerged in the 1840s as the leading Jukun power; the dated king list begins in 1833.

Wukari came under British rule around 1900. In the 1910s the colonial administration encouraged Tiv migration into the area and placed Tiv settlers under the Aku Uka's authority, laying the ground for later disputes. Christian missions arrived in 1905–06. In 1958 the Aku Uka was one of four Northern Region traditional rulers made ministers without portfolio in the regional government.

In the First Republic, Jukun–Tiv rivalry ran along party lines. Kuvyon II, crowned in 1976, reigned for 45 years, during which the Jukun–Tiv conflicts of 1990–92 (over whether Wukari should belong to Benue or Taraba State) and of 2001–02 cost thousands of lives; he attributed the dispute to an unresolved boundary question. After his death in 2021, Manu Ishaku Adda Ali of the Ba Ma house was crowned in January 2022.
sections.selection: The throne alternates between two royal houses, Ba Ma and Ba Gya. On a vacancy, the kingmakers (named in 2022 as the Abon-Achuwo, Abon-Ziken, Kinda-Achuwo, Kinda-Ziken and Kun-Vyi) choose a successor through spiritual and traditional rites and submit a single name to the governor for approval; Daily Trust reported that the governor cannot interfere in the choice. The new king is crowned in Pankan rites at Bye Vyi before receiving the state staff of office.
sections.council: The kingmakers listed above are among the senior ritual and court officials of Wukari. The Aku Uka heads the Wukari Traditional Council, with district and village heads under him, and chairs the Taraba State Council of Traditional Rulers.
sections.palace: The palace is at Wukari. Coronation rites take place at Bye Vyi, followed by rites at Puje, Kuntsa, Akwana, Arufu and Wapan Nghaku; the public celebration of Manu Ishaku Adda Ali's accession was held in November 2022. The Nwonyo fishing festival on Lake Nwonyo, with canoe racing, diving and a prize for the heaviest fish, is the best-known Wukari festival.
sections.today: The Aku Uka has no constitutional powers but chairs the Taraba State Council of Traditional Rulers and is the chief voice of the Jukun in state and federal affairs, particularly on Tiv–Jukun and other inter-communal conflicts in southern Taraba. Kuvyon II also served as chancellor of the Federal University Dutse. The present holder, Manu Ishaku Adda Ali, was installed in 2022.

thrones.established: 1935 (stool created at Riyom; recognised 22 Feb 1936); moved to Jos in 1947
thrones.about: The Gbong Gwom Jos ('most eminent king of Jos' in Berom) is the paramount ruler of the Berom of Jos and Greater Jos, with his palace at Jishe in Jos. The stool began in 1935 as a colonial-era Berom paramountcy at Riyom, moved to Jos in 1947 and became first class in 1970. Its holder chairs the Plateau State Council of Chiefs.

rulers.note: Installed at Riyom as head of the Berom tribal council (styled Gwom Gbong Duk Shot). His authority covered the other Berom districts.

rulers.name: Rwang Pam
rulers.note: A former headmaster who moved the vacant stool to Jos with colonial backing, first as a third-class Sarkin Jos. During the 1966–67 crisis he reportedly urged calm in Jos. His family alleges he was poisoned, but this is unproven.
rulers.dispute: Sources differ on which governor renamed and upgraded the title.

rulers.name: Fom Bot
rulers.note: Acceded on 26 Aug 1969. At his 1970 coronation the stool was raised to first class. He chaired the Plateau State Traditional Council and was the longest-reigning holder, at 33 years.

rulers.name: Victor Dung Pam
rulers.note: A retired Deputy Inspector-General of Police, he took the throne on 1 Apr 2004 after a two-year vacancy. He campaigned against illicit gin among Berom youth and promoted rural schooling.

rulers.name: Jacob Gyang Buba
rulers.born: 10 October 1951, Madu village, Du District, Jos South
rulers.note: A former Comptroller-General of Customs, he chairs the Plateau State Traditional Council. He has publicly pressed for action on killings in Plateau. In 2019 a court stopped an attempt to reduce his status.
rulers.bio: Jacob Gyang Buba was educated at Provincial Secondary School, Kuru, and took a diploma in banking at Ahmadu Bello University's Institute of Administration in 1975. After working at the Federal Pay Office, he joined the Nigeria Customs Service in 1975 and rose to Comptroller-General (2004–2008), overseeing the adoption of the ECOWAS common external tariff and scanning equipment at ports and borders, and chairing an African Union customs sub-committee. He became the fifth Gbong Gwom in 2009, succeeding Victor Pam, and chairs the Jos traditional council and the Plateau State Council of Chiefs. He was a delegate to the 2014 National Conference and has pressed governments on insecurity in Plateau. In 2019 a court stopped an attempt to reduce his status, and he received the CFR in 2022.
rulers.dispute: His accession is given as 1 Aug 2009 (coronation) or 1 Apr 2009 (swearing-in).

authority.text: The Gbong Gwom Jos is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office. His role is to lead the Berom traditional institution, preside over the Jos traditional council and represent the Berom and Plateau rulers to government. Sources consulted do not attribute a priestly or ritual function to the office.

sections.history:
The Berom are the largest indigenous people of the Jos Plateau, living in Jos North, Jos South, Riyom and Barkin Ladi and in parts of southern Kaduna. Before colonial rule they were organised in village and district polities under their own heads rather than a single king.

In 1935 the British set up a Berom tribal council at Kwallak, Riyom, with Dachung Gyang as its head (styled Gwom Gbong Duk Shot); the stool was recognised on 22 February 1936 under the Plateau Province Resident. The growing tin-mining town of Jos, however, was administered largely through non-Berom intermediaries.

In 1947, after a vacancy, the former headmaster Rwang Pam moved the stool to Jos as a third-class Sarkin Jos with colonial backing. The title was later renamed Gbong Gwom Jos, and at Fom Bot's coronation in 1970, under military governor Joseph Gomwalk, it was raised to first class. Fom Bot reigned 33 years, the longest of any holder.

After a two-year vacancy Victor Dung Pam, a retired Deputy Inspector-General of Police, reigned 2004–2009. Jacob Gyang Buba, a former Comptroller-General of Customs, succeeded him in 2009 and has reigned through repeated cycles of violence in Jos and rural Plateau.
sections.selection: Succession is not hereditary: the kingmakers (Be Gwom Rweis) select a candidate and the Plateau State government approves him. No Gbong Gwom since 1935 has been followed by his own heir, and the governor in office at the time of a vacancy has had strong influence on the outcome.
sections.council: The Gbong Gwom presides over the Jos Joint Traditional Council (Jos traditional council of chiefs), covering the Berom districts of Jos North, Jos South, Riyom and Barkin Ladi, and chairs the Plateau State Council of Chiefs and Emirs, which formally receives newly installed Plateau rulers such as the Ngolong Ngas in 2024.
sections.palace: The palace is at Jishe, Jos. The 1970 coronation of Fom Bot marked the stool's elevation to first class.
sections.today: The Gbong Gwom chairs the Plateau State Council of Chiefs and Emirs and has been a prominent voice on killings and displacement in Plateau. In 2019 attempts under Governor Simon Lalong to redefine traditional boundaries and reduce the Gbong Gwom's status led to litigation, and a court restrained the change. Jacob Gyang Buba was also chancellor of Nnamdi Azikiwe University from 2016 and was made CFR in 2022.

thrones.title: Ohinoyi of Ebiraland
thrones.established: 1902–04 (colonial chiefs of Igbirra, titled Atta from 1903); title Ohinoyi from the 1950s
thrones.about: The Ohinoyi is the paramount ruler of the Ebira, with his palace (the Azad Palace) at Okene in Kogi State. Colonial-appointed chiefs, titled Atta, ruled Igbirra from 1902–03; the throne later took the title Ohinoyi and is filled by kingmakers, traditionally rotating among the major Ebira clans. The latest appointment (2024) was voided by the Kogi State High Court in 2025, and an appeal was pending.

rulers.name: Ouda Adidi
rulers.note: First colonial-recognised chief of Igbirra, per World Statesmen; sources consulted give no details of his tenure.

rulers.name: Isa Husaini Omadiva (Omadivi of Abonika)
rulers.note: First ruler to bear the title Atta under colonial rule, until January 1917.
rulers.dispute: World Statesmen gives 1903–Jan 1917; the earlier version of this entry gave c. 1904.

rulers.name: Arudi Adano (Arudi Odano)
rulers.note: Held the title briefly, from January to November 1917.

rulers.name: Ibrahim Onoruoiza (Chugudo Onoruo Ibrahima)
rulers.ended: Abdicated and was banished in 1954 after a popular revolt
rulers.note: Installed in November 1917 under colonial rule. Late in his reign, opposition to him and to colonial rule grew, and a 1954 uprising forced him out.
rulers.dispute: He held the title Atta, and some sources count him as the second Atta rather than the first Ohinoyi.

rulers.name: Muhammad Sani Omolori
rulers.note: Chosen after a stalemate over the British-favoured candidate. He stayed neutral in 1950s party rivalries, and Okene gained hospitals and many schools during his four-decade reign.
rulers.dispute: Accession is given as 1954 (World Statesmen), 1956 or 1957 (Wikipedia, Blueprint); his end as 1996 (World Statesmen: vacant from July 1996) or 1997 (Wikipedia).

rulers.name: Abdulrahman Ado Ibrahim
rulers.note: Installed on 2 June 1997. He built the Azad Palace in Okene, upgraded the grading of clan chiefs, and promoted Ebira cultural festivals and peaceful relations with neighbouring groups.
rulers.bio: Abdulrahman Ado Ibrahim, a son of Atta Ibrahim Onoruoiza of the Omadivi lineage, attended the Native Authority school in Okene, Ondo Boys' High School and Oduduwa College, then took a degree in economics at the London School of Economics (1954) and a master's at Harvard Business School (1959). He became a Lagos-based entrepreneur before being installed as Ohinoyi on 2 June 1997. He built the Azad Palace in Okene, upgraded clan chieftaincies, offered scholarships and promoted peaceful relations between the Ebira and neighbouring peoples of Kogi Central, as well as Ebira festivals and mining livelihoods. He died on 29 October 2023 after a reign of about 26 years.
rulers.dispute: He is omitted from Wikipedia's Ohinoyi page but appears in World Statesmen and newspaper sources.

rulers.name: Ahmed Tijani Anaje
rulers.note: Appointed by the state governor on 8 Jan 2024 after 70 candidates were screened, and given the staff of office on about 25 Jan 2024.
rulers.dispute: On 3 February 2025 the Kogi State High Court (Lokoja) voided his appointment and ordered a fresh selection by the kingmakers. The state government announced an appeal; no appeal outcome was found.

authority.text: The Ohinoyi is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office. He heads the Ebira traditional council, mediates disputes and represents the Ebira to government, and the office has no formal role in Islamic, Christian or traditional religious institutions.

sections.history:
The Ebira (Igbirra) of the Okene area were organised in clans without a single paramount king before colonial rule. In 1902 the British recognised Ouda Adidi as chief, and from 1903 a series of colonial-appointed rulers bore the title Atta: Isa Husaini Omadiva (of Abonika), Arudi Adano briefly in 1917, and from November 1917 Ibrahim Onoruoiza.

Onoruoiza ruled for 37 years from Okene. Opposition to his rule, entangled with resentment of colonial administration, grew in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and a popular uprising in 1954 forced him to abdicate; he went into exile.

His successor, Muhammad Sani Omolori of the Oziada clan, was chosen after a stalemate over the British-favoured candidate and is the first holder generally styled Ohinoyi. He reigned four decades, avoided partisan alignment in the 1950s, and saw schools and hospitals built in Okene.

After a vacancy, Abdulrahman Ado Ibrahim, a son of Onoruoiza educated at the London School of Economics and Harvard, was installed in 1997. He built the Azad Palace, regraded clan chieftaincies and promoted Ebira culture until his death in October 2023. In January 2024 Governor Yahaya Bello appointed Ahmed Tijani Anaje after screening 70 candidates, but on 3 February 2025 the Kogi State High Court voided the appointment.
sections.selection: Wikipedia notes that elders choose the Ohinoyi and that, in the absence of a single royal line, the throne has traditionally rotated among the major Ebira clans. Under Kogi State's 2006 chiefs law, kingmakers select and the governor approves. The 2024 appointment was challenged on the ground that the procedure in section 4(1) of that law was not followed; the court ordered a fresh selection by the kingmakers, and the state government said it would appeal.
sections.council: The Ohinoyi heads the Ebira traditional council, with clan chiefs (some upgraded to higher grades under Ado Ibrahim) and district heads, and sits on the Kogi State Council of Traditional Rulers.
sections.palace: The Ohinoyi's seat is the Azad Palace in Okene, built during Ado Ibrahim's reign and named after one of his sons; it is often described as one of the most striking palaces in West Africa. Staff-of-office ceremonies are performed by the Kogi State governor. Ebira cultural festivals, encouraged by recent holders, are major occasions in Okene.
sections.today: The Ohinoyi has no constitutional powers but is the leading traditional voice of the Ebira in Kogi State politics, security and inter-ethnic relations. The throne's legitimacy has been in dispute since the Kogi State High Court voided Ahmed Tijani Anaje's appointment in February 2025; no appeal outcome was found in the sources consulted.

thrones.title: Agwatyap
thrones.grade: First class from 2007; the Kaduna State government's current list shows the Zangon Kataf Traditional Council as second class
thrones.about: The Agwatyap ('monarch of the Atyap' in Tyap) is the paramount ruler of the Atyap chiefdom in southern Kaduna State, with his palace at Atak Njei near Zangon Kataf. The chiefdom was created in 1995 after a long Atyap campaign to leave the Zazzau (Zaria) emirate system, sharpened by the deadly Zangon Kataf crisis of 1992. Three Agwatyaps have reigned.

authority.text: The Agwatyap is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office. He heads the Atyap Traditional Council, which deals with custom, land, culture and peace-building, and represents the Atyap to the Kaduna State government. Sources consulted describe no priestly role for the office.

sections.history:
Before colonial rule the Atyap were governed by clan heads, each with a designated heir (nggwon), and elders met in council on land and community matters. Princes oversaw security and land at the Zangon Katab market under a trading pact with Hausa merchants.

Zaria's influence grew through tribute, raids and alliances with some lineages, but the Atyap refused tribute in 1894 and during the wars of 1899–1902. Under British rule they were placed in 1907 under Kauru (Katuka District) and from 1912 in a Zangon Katab District headed by Hausa officials responsible to the Emir of Zaria. Revolts against taxation and forced labour broke out in 1910, 1922 and 1946, when the Atyap demanded separation from Zaria and their own chiefdom on the model of Kagoro, Moroa and Kwoi.

After the Hausa district head died in 1967, Bala Ade Dauke became the first indigenous District Head of Zangon Kataf. Tension over land and the relocation of the Zango market erupted in 1992: clashes in February killed over 60 people and violence in May killed about 400, with reprisals in Kaduna. A tribunal sentenced 17 people to death, including the retired general Zamani Lekwot; the sentences were later commuted.

Following a committee chaired by Air Vice Marshal Usman Mu'azu, the Atyap chiefdom was created in 1995 and Bala Ade Dauke became Agwatyap I. It was upgraded to first class in 2007. In 2017 the state government reduced its 16 districts to four.
sections.selection: Wikipedia describes the stool as an elective monarchy. Four royal houses correspond to the four Atyap clans: Agbaat (sub-clans Akpaisa, Jei, Akwak), Aminyam (Afakan, Ason), Aku and Ashokwa. The Kaduna State governor approves the choice and presents the staff of office, as Governor el-Rufai did for Agwatyap III in November 2016. Sources consulted do not set out the kingmakers' procedure in detail.
sections.council: The Agwatyap heads the Atyap Traditional Council, which had 16 districts from 1995 to 2017 and four government-approved districts afterwards, together with some 61 approved village units. The Atyap Community Development Association works alongside the council on community affairs.
sections.palace: The palace (Magwatyap) is at Atak Njei, on the outskirts of Zangon Kataf; the state government has questioned its location, which the Atyap Community Development Association has defended. The Atyap flag and ensign are symbols of the chiefdom, and Atyap culture is showcased at events such as the Southern Kaduna festival (SK Fest).
sections.today: The Agwatyap has no constitutional powers but is central to peace efforts in Zangon Kataf, an area repeatedly hit by attacks and reprisals. The Kaduna State government's list now names the 'Agwam Zangon Kataf' of the Zangon Kataf Traditional Council as second class, reflecting the regrading of southern Kaduna stools under Governor el-Rufai. Agwatyap III, Dominic Gambo Yahaya, has reigned since 2016.

rulers.name: Bala Ade Dauke
rulers.note: The first indigenous District Head of Zangon Kataf (1967–96) became the first Agwatyap when the chiefdom was created, reigning until his death on 1 January 2005.
rulers.bio: Bala Ade Dauke served in the Nigeria Police (1951–56) and as a Native Authority social welfare officer (1961–63), and stood unsuccessfully for the Northern House of Representatives in 1959. In 1967 he became District Head of Zangon Kataf, the first Atyap to hold the post after decades of Hausa district heads. He held it until 1996, through the 1992 Zangon Kataf crisis. When the Atyap chiefdom was created he became its first paramount ruler, Agwatyap I, from May 1996. He died on 1 January 2005, aged 73.
rulers.dispute: The chiefdom was created in 1995 and Wikipedia's Atyap Chiefdom article dates his reign from 1995; his own article gives May 1996. His birth year is 1931 on his tomb but 1935–36 in his autobiography.

rulers.name: Harrison Yusuf Bungwon
rulers.note: An engineer (FNSE), he succeeded Dauke in 2005 and reigned until 6 April 2016.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia's Dominic Yahaya article says his successor was chosen after his death; the exact circumstances are not given in sources consulted.

rulers.name: Dominic Gambo Yahaya
rulers.note: A retired permanent secretary and town planner, he received the staff of office from Governor el-Rufai at Atak Njei on 12 November 2016.
rulers.bio: Dominic Gambo Yahaya joined the Kaduna State government in 1976 as a town planner and rose to Director of Town and Country Planning, General Manager of the Kaduna State Urban Planning and Development Authority and permanent secretary in several ministries, retiring in 2010. He was among Atyap men detained without charge after the May 1992 Zangon Kataf disturbances. He later chaired the Zangon Kataf interim local government committee (2011–12) and sat on the NYSC governing board. Chosen after Agwatyap II's death, he was presented with the staff of office on 12 November 2016. In 2023 he launched a foundation to support the education of victims of attacks in the chiefdom.

thrones.title: Agwam Bajju (Agwam Kajju)
thrones.grade: Second class (Kajju Traditional Council, per the Kaduna State government list)
thrones.about: The Agwam Bajju, now officially styled Agwam Kajju, is the paramount ruler of the Bajju (Kaje) people of southern Kaduna, with his seat at Zonkwa. The Kajju chiefdom was created in 1995 in the reorganisation that followed the 1992 Zangon Kataf crisis. Two rulers have held the stool.

authority.text: The Agwam Bajju is a traditional ruler appointed by the Kaduna State government, without a formal religious office. His role is customary leadership, dispute resolution, cultural promotion and representation of the Bajju to government. Sources consulted describe no priestly function.

sections.history:
The Bajju live mainly around Zonkwa in Zangon Kataf LGA of southern Kaduna. Like their Atyap neighbours, they were administered in the colonial period within the Zazzau (Zaria) emirate system and pressed for chiefdoms headed by their own rulers.

The Kajju (Bajju) chiefdom was created in 1995, after the 1992 Zangon Kataf crises, as one of several new southern Kaduna chiefdoms. Nuhu Bature Achi, a businessman known for a bookshop in Jos, became the first Agwam Bajju and reigned until his death in December 2021. In 2012 he noted that, 17 years after its creation, the chiefdom still had no palace.

In December 2022 Governor Nasir el-Rufai appointed Luka Kogi Yabwat, district head of Bvokpat (Ungwar Rimi), as Agwam Kajju II. His appointment came during a round of southern Kaduna coronations in which several stools were regraded, which critics described as a downgrading of the traditional institutions.
sections.selection: Kingmakers drawn from the chiefdom deliberate and recommend a candidate, and the Kaduna State governor appoints and presents the staff of office. The 2022 selection drew public disquiet, reported by Leadership, over how the new Agwam was chosen.
sections.council: The Agwam heads the Kajju Traditional Council at Zonkwa, with district and village heads beneath him, and sits on the Kaduna State Council of Chiefs and Emirs.
sections.palace: The seat is the chief's palace at Zonkwa (Azunkwa), where Agwam Bajju I was buried in 2021. The Bajju Cultural Festival is the chiefdom's major cultural gathering.
sections.today: The Agwam Kajju has no constitutional powers. The Kaduna State government's list now names the Kajju Traditional Council as second class, after the regrading of southern Kaduna stools under Governor el-Rufai, which groups such as SOKAPU criticised. The current holder, Luka Kogi Yabwat, has reigned since December 2022.

sources.label: TheCable: Nuhu Bature, Kaduna monarch, is dead (2021)
Leadership: Disquiet over selection of new Agwam Bajju (2022)
Punch: Interview with Agwam Bajju I

rulers.name: Nuhu Bature Achi
rulers.note: First paramount ruler of the Kajju chiefdom from its creation in 1995 until his death in Kafanchan on 18 December 2021. He was buried at the palace in Zonkwa.
rulers.bio: Nuhu Bature Achi was an entrepreneur who founded a well-known bookshop on Rwang Pam Street in Jos before becoming the first Agwam Bajju when the chiefdom was created in 1995. He reigned for about 26 years, through repeated insecurity in southern Kaduna, and spoke publicly on Bajju customs and history. In 2012 he lamented that the chiefdom still lacked a palace. He died after a brief illness at a hospital in Kafanchan in December 2021 and was buried at the palace in Zonkwa.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia's infobox gives 1995 as the start of his reign (coronation 1995); its regnal table gives 1996.

rulers.name: Luka Kogi Yabwat
rulers.note: A retired correctional service officer and former district head of Bvokpat, he was appointed by Governor el-Rufai and capped on 24 December 2022.
rulers.bio: Luka Kogi Yabwat holds a master's degree in public administration from Ahmadu Bello University and retired as a deputy superintendent of the Nigerian Correctional Service. He then served as district head of Bvokpat (Ungwar Rimi). Governor Nasir el-Rufai appointed him in December 2022 and he was capped on 24 December 2022 as the second paramount ruler of the Bajju. His appointment came amid controversy over the regrading of southern Kaduna chiefs.

thrones.title: Agwam Agworok (Chief of Kagoro)
thrones.about: The Agwam Agworok (Oegwam Oegworok) is the paramount ruler of the Agworok (Kagoro) people, with his palace at Fadan Kagoro (Ucyo) in Kaura LGA. Created in 1905, Kagoro was one of the few southern Zaria chiefdoms outside emirate control in colonial times, and it is now a first-class stool. Six chiefs have reigned, including Gwamna Awan, whose 63-year reign (1945–2008) was among the longest in Africa.

authority.text: The Agwam Agworok is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office. In Kagoro tradition, ritual duties belong to separate office-holders: at the Afan festival it is the chief priest (Agwam Abvwoi) who climbs the hills to pray to the god Agwaza (Uza), while the Ankwai clans handle war-related and festival rites. The Agwam hosts the festival at his palace.

sections.history:
The Agworok trace the older Ankwai clans to the Jos–Bauchi plateau around 1500, with the Kpashang clans arriving later as migrant groups. They long lived on the Kagoro hills for safety; British authorities later moved many communities to the foot of the hills.

In 1905 the British created the Gworok (Kagoro) chiefdom as one of three independent districts in southern Zaria province, outside the authority of the emirs. Bala Bishut of the Kamang lineage was the first chief (1905–26), followed by Aluwong Benyan (1926–29), Mugunta Atin (1929–32) and Biya Kaka (1932–44).

After a succession dispute, Gwamna Awan, a former teacher and assistant scribe of the Kagoro Native Authority, became chief in 1945. In 1946 he moved the Afan festival to 1 January, and the same year colonial officials and the Emir of Zaria blamed him for encouraging the Atyap revolt in Zangon Katab, where the Atyap were demanding a chiefdom on the Kagoro model. He reigned until his death in 2008.

Ufuwai Bonet succeeded in 2008 and has served as deputy chairman of the Kaduna State Council of Chiefs and Emirs. His reign has been marked by recurrent attacks in southern Kaduna, during which he has called for restraint and for government action.
sections.selection: Paramount rulership belongs to the Kpashang sub-clans, and Wikipedia describes the stool as an elective monarchy. Four of the six chiefs listed by the Kagoro History blog came from the Kamang lineage, with one each from Tukum and Afwai. The Kaduna State government approves the selection and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The Agwam heads the Kagoro Traditional Council at Fadan Kagoro, with district and village heads under him, and has been deputy chairman of the Kaduna State Council of Chiefs and Emirs. Ankwai clan elders hold customary responsibilities for war matters and festival rites.
sections.palace: The palace stands at Fadan Kagoro (Ucyo); Gwamna Awan helped oversee its construction in 1943. Each 1 January the palace grounds host the Afan National Festival, which marks the end of the farming season and the start of hunting: the chief priest prays on the hills, hunters set out the next day and return to dancing and freshly brewed beer. The Agwam has addressed his people at the palace and ridden through the town on horseback at past festivals.
sections.today: The Agwam Agworok has no constitutional powers but is one of the senior southern Kaduna rulers, listed by the Kaduna State government as first class. He is a prominent voice on insecurity in Kaura LGA and southern Kaduna. Ufuwai Bonet has reigned since 2008.

NICO: Afan National Festival, a celebration of heritage in Kagoro

rulers.name: Bala Bishut
rulers.note: First chief of the Kagoro chiefdom created by the British in 1905; of the Kamang lineage.

rulers.name: Aluwong Benyan
rulers.note: Of the Tukum lineage. Sources consulted give no details of his reign.

rulers.name: Mugunta Atin
rulers.note: Of the Afwai lineage. Sources consulted give no details of his reign.

rulers.name: Biya Kaka
rulers.note: Of the Kamang lineage; he died in August 1944.

rulers.name: Gwamna Awan
rulers.note: Installed in April 1945 after a succession dispute, he reigned 63 years, moved the Afan festival to 1 January and was blamed by the colonial authorities for encouraging the 1946 Atyap revolt.
rulers.bio: Gwamna Awan began teaching at the mission elementary school in Kagoro in 1936 and became assistant scribe of the Kagoro Native Authority in 1940; in 1943 he helped oversee the building of the present palace. After a succession dispute following Biya Kaka's death, he was made acting chief and formally installed on 11 April 1945, the first Christian chief in southern Zaria province. In 1946 the Emir of Zaria accused him of fuelling the Atyap revolt in Zangon Katab, and the British Resident warned him. He moved the Afan festival from April to 1 January, opening it to wider participation. Over 63 years on the throne he was an influential figure whose blessing politicians sought, and he was honoured with the MBE and OON. He died in Jos on 1 October 2008, aged 93; Gwamna Awan General Hospital is named after him.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia gives 1945 (acting chief, then installed 11 April 1945).

rulers.name: Ufuwai Bonet
rulers.note: Crowned in 2008, he has served as deputy chairman of the Kaduna State Council of Chiefs and Emirs and has spoken repeatedly on insecurity in southern Kaduna.
rulers.bio: Ufuwai Bonet succeeded Gwamna Awan in 2008 and holds the CON honour. As deputy chairman of the Kaduna State Council of Chiefs and Emirs (as of 2016) he has been a leading southern Kaduna ruler. After attacks in January 2017 he told the Chief of Defence Staff that his people would not retaliate, and he has used the Afan festival to speak on the security situation. During the 2020 COVID-19 lockdown he directed village and ward heads to enforce restrictions. Sources consulted do not give his date of birth.
rulers.dispute: Spelled Bonet (Wikipedia) or Bognet (Kagoro History blog).

thrones.title: Ponzhi Tarok (Ponzhi Taroh)
thrones.established: 1955 (single Tarok chiefdom under the Reak accord); selection rules gazetted 1975
thrones.about: The Ponzhi Tarok is the paramount ruler of the Tarok people of southern Plateau State, with his seat at Langtang. The Tarok became a single chiefdom in 1955, and the stool's selection rules were gazetted in 1975. Since the death of Edward Cirdap Zhattau in 2008 the stool has been mired in disputes and has had no fully installed holder; the state government said in 2025 that a new Ponzhi would be installed soon.

authority.text: The Ponzhi Tarok is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office. Tarok traditional religion centres on the orim ancestral cult, whose sacred groves lie outside most Tarok settlements and whose members (initiated men and post-menopausal women) represent the ancestors; sources consulted do not make the paramount ruler its priest.

sections.history:
The Tarok live around Langtang in southern Plateau State, about 186 km south-east of Jos. Their traditional institutions include the orim ancestral cult, and the annual Ilum Otarok festival is a major celebration of Tarok identity.

Under the Reak accord of 1955 the Tarok nation was united as a single chiefdom. The rules for choosing its paramount ruler were published in Benue-Plateau State Legal Notice No. 3 of 1975, and in that year Edward Cirdap Zhattau of the Ce clan was selected over Ayuba Kum of the Lagan family of Zini (Gazum).

In 1990 a separate Gazum chiefdom was created by Plateau State edict, which later became central to arguments over who may contest the Ponzhi stool. Zhattau died in November 2008.

In December 2010 the kingmakers selected the former Chief of Defence Staff Domkat Bali under a new Plateau State order of 2010. Supporters of another retired general, Jeremiah Useni of Gazum, challenged the process in court; the High Court upheld the 2010 order in April 2014, and the case went on to the Court of Appeal. Bali's widow later said he had never been installed and had resigned the position because of court orders; by 2016 the Tarok were asking the governor to begin a new selection. Bali died in December 2020. In May 2025 Governor Caleb Mutfwang told the Ilum Otarok festival that consultations were in their final stages and a new Ponzhi Tarok would soon be installed.
sections.selection: Kingmakers of the Tarok chiefdom select the Ponzhi under rules made by the Plateau State government. The original rules were Benue-Plateau Legal Notice No. 3 of 1975; they were replaced by the Plateau State Appointment and Deposition of Chiefs Order No. 4 of 2010, which the High Court in 2014 held to be the only valid procedure. Whether people of the separate Gazum chiefdom can contest has been a central point of dispute. The governor approves the choice and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The Ponzhi heads the Tarok traditional council at Langtang, with district and village heads across Langtang North and Langtang South, and sits on the Plateau State Council of Chiefs and Emirs, where the stool is listed as first class. Gazum has its own chiefdom.
sections.palace: The seat is at Langtang. The Ilum Otarok annual cultural festival, held at the Langtang North mini-stadium in 2025, is the main public celebration of the Tarok nation and the setting of the governor's 2025 pledge on the stool.
sections.today: The stool has had no settled occupant since 2008 because of the Bali selection dispute and related litigation. As of May 2025 the Plateau State government said it was finalising consultations to install a new Ponzhi Tarok; no installation was found in the sources consulted.

rulers.note: Of the Ce clan, he was selected in 1975 under the newly gazetted rules and reigned until his death in November 2008.
rulers.dispute: Spelled Zhattau or Zhato. Sources consulted do not say whether anyone held the paramountcy between the 1955 unification and 1975.

rulers.name: Domkat Yah Bali
rulers.note: The former Chief of Defence Staff was selected by the kingmakers in December 2010, but the selection was challenged in court and he gave up the stool.
rulers.bio: Domkat Bali joined the Nigerian Army in 1961, trained at Sandhurst and rose to general, commanding brigades and divisions and the Command and Staff College, Jaji. He was Minister of Defence and Chief of Defence Staff from 1984 to 1990 and sat on the Supreme Military Council and Armed Forces Ruling Council. In December 2010 the Tarok kingmakers selected him to succeed Edward Zhattau as Ponzhi Tarok, but supporters of Gen. Jeremiah Useni of Gazum challenged the process in court. A 2014 report called him the installed ruler, but his widow later said he was never installed and resigned because of court orders, and a 2016 report described him as having been forced to abdicate about two years earlier. He died in December 2020, aged 80.
rulers.dispute: Sources disagree on whether he was ever installed: Viewpoint Nigeria (2014) says the state government installed him; his widow (Daily Asset) says he was not and resigned; Viewpoint Nigeria (2016) says he abdicated around 2014. Death is given as 4 December (Wikipedia) or 5 December 2020 (Daily Asset).

thrones.title: Ngolong Ngas
thrones.about: The Ngolong Ngas is the paramount ruler of the Ngas (Angas) people of Pankshin and Kanke LGAs on the eastern Jos Plateau, with his seat at Pankshin. After the death of Joshua Dimlong around 2015 the stool stood vacant for about nine years, until Governor Caleb Mutfwang crowned Nde Jika Golit in January 2024.

authority.text: The Ngolong Ngas is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office. He leads the Ngas chiefdom's traditional council and represents the Ngas to government; sources consulted do not give him a priestly role in Ngas traditional religion.

sections.history:
Ngas tradition holds that the people migrated from Borno and settled on the highlands of the Jos Plateau, dividing into groups at Pankshin, Ampang, Amper and Kabwir; the Kabwir settlers were led by a chief named Gwallam and the Amper by Kendim. Pankshin is the main Ngas town, and terraced farming on the plateau edge is characteristic of the area.

The colonial administration grouped Pankshin as a federation of chiefdoms in the 1950s, and the Ngas paramountcy later became a first-class stool of Plateau State. Sources consulted do not give a dated list of early holders; Nigeria Galleria names Nde John Gowongji as a holder.

Joshua Dimlong, a first-class chief who ruled the Ngas of Pankshin and Kanke, died at Jos University Teaching Hospital aged 58, and the stool then stayed vacant for about nine years, with an acting Ngolong in place. On 5 January 2024 Governor Caleb Mutfwang crowned Nde Jika Golit at Pankshin Township Stadium after a peaceful selection by the kingmakers.
sections.selection: Kingmakers of the Ngas chiefdom select the Ngolong, and the Plateau State governor approves the choice and presents the staff of office and certificate of recognition. Sources consulted do not describe the ruling families or any rotation.
sections.council: The Ngolong heads the Ngas traditional council and the Pankshin/Kanke traditional council, with district and village heads under him, and is a member of the Plateau State Council of Chiefs and Emirs, whose chairman, the Gbong Gwom Jos, formally welcomes new members.
sections.palace: The seat is at Pankshin; the 2024 coronation was held at Pankshin Township Stadium. The major Ngas festival, Tsafi Tar or Mos Tar, is held around harvest and includes the 'shooting the moon' rite that marks the turn of the season.
sections.today: The Ngolong Ngas has no constitutional powers. During the nine-year vacancy local officials complained that Ngas cultural institutions had weakened; the 2024 coronation, held a week after mass killings in other Plateau LGAs, was presented by the governor as part of restoring traditional institutions. Nde Jika Golit has reigned since January 2024.
