thrones.title: Hama Bachama
thrones.about: The Hama Bachama (Homun) is the paramount ruler of the Bachama (Bwatiye) kingdom, with his administrative palace at Numan near the Benue–Gongola confluence and an ancestral seat at Lamurde, the people's spiritual home. The Bwatiye pride themselves as warriors never conquered. The present king, Daniel Shaga Ismaila, is counted as the 29th.

authority.text: The Hama Bachama is a traditional ruler whose office, as described in sources consulted, has no formal religious title. Lamurde, where the kingdom has a second palace, is regarded as the spiritual and ancestral home of the Bwatiye, and Bwatiye festivals honour the people's traditional deities, but sources consulted do not set out a priestly role for the king himself.

sections.history:
The Bwatiye (Bachama and Bata) live in Numan, Demsa, Lamurde, Girei and Fufore LGAs of Adamawa State and in parts of Cameroon. Their traditions trace an origin to Gobir, from which their ancestors were driven by Tuareg and later Bornu wars before settling along the upper Benue. They are known for having resisted conquest.

The Bwatiye are ruled by two kings sharing the title Hama: the Hama Bachama, with his palace at Numan, and the Hama Bata at Demsa. Lamurde is the traditional headquarters and spiritual home of the Bachama.

Sources consulted do not provide a dated list of early kings. In recent times Homun Asaph Zadok was succeeded in 2012 by Honest Irmiya Stephen, a retired army colonel, who received the staff of office in December 2013 and died in June 2020. Daniel Shaga Ismaila, a retired NDLEA officer, was elected by the kingmakers and approved by the governor in July 2020.
sections.selection: Kingmakers of the Bachama kingdom elect the Hama: in 2020 eight of the ten kingmakers voted for Daniel Shaga Ismaila. The Adamawa State governor then approves the choice and presents the first-class staff of office.
sections.council: The Hama Bachama heads the Bachama traditional council, with district heads across the Bachama area of Numan and Lamurde LGAs, and sits on the Adamawa State Council of Chiefs.
sections.palace: The Voti in Numan is the administrative palace; Lamurde has a second palace and is the ancestral and spiritual centre. The king's consort carries the title Mbamto. Bwatiye festivals include a seven-day spiritual and cultural festival honouring a deity for agricultural plenty, a wrestling and harvest thanksgiving festival around June–July, and the Farai-Farai festival that unites Demsa, Mbula, Numan and Lamurde at the start of farming.
sections.today: The Hama Bachama has no constitutional powers but is the chief voice of the Bwatiye in Adamawa State and is often involved in peace efforts during farmer–herder and inter-communal violence in Numan and Lamurde. Daniel Shaga Ismaila has reigned since 2020.

rulers.name: Honest Irmiya Stephen
rulers.note: A retired army colonel, he ascended in 2012, received the staff of office from Governor Murtala Nyako on 15 December 2013 and died at his palace in Numan on 28 June 2020, aged 66.
rulers.bio: Honest Irmiya Stephen retired from the Nigerian Army as a colonel and in 2007 sought the PDP nomination for a Senate seat. He ascended the Bachama throne in 2012 and received the staff of office from Governor Murtala Nyako on 15 December 2013. He reigned through a period of farmer–herder violence in Numan and Lamurde. He died after a brief illness at his palace in Numan on 28 June 2020, aged 66.

rulers.name: Daniel Shaga Ismaila
rulers.note: A retired NDLEA director, he was elected by eight of ten kingmakers and approved by Governor Ahmadu Fintiri on 29 July 2020.
rulers.bio: Daniel Shaga Ismaila, an accountant, joined the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency in 1994, rose to Director of Finance and Administration and retired in 2014 as Assistant Commander-General of Narcotics. About a month after Honest Irmiya Stephen's death, eight of the ten Bachama kingmakers elected him, and Governor Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri approved the appointment on 29 July 2020. He later received the first-class staff of office. His consort is Mbamto Rosaline Daniel Ismaila Shaga.

thrones.title: Mai Tangle (Mai Tangale)
thrones.established: c. 1295 (traditional king list)
thrones.about: The Mai Tangle (also Mai Tangale or Mai Yelli) is the paramount ruler of the western Tangale, with his seat at Billiri in Gombe State; the eastern Tangale have a separate Mai at Kaltungo. Tangale tradition keeps a list of 15 kings from about 1295 to 2021. The 2021 appointment of Danladi Sanusi-Maiyamba by the Gombe governor, against the kingmakers' vote, set off a dispute that continues.

authority.text: The Mai Tangle is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office in the sources consulted. Historically the Mai was head of state and commander-in-chief of the Tangale and chaired the Tangale Traditional Council through five councils; today the office is customary and representative. The 2021 succession dispute was widely reported as having a religious dimension in the choice of candidate, but this concerned the selection, not a religious role of the office.

sections.history:
Tangale tradition traces the people's origin to Yemen, with migrations dated variously from the 13th to the 15th century, possibly via Ngazargamu in Kanem-Borno, and contact with the Jukun kingdom of Kwararafa around 1350. Colonial-era British and German writers described the Tangale as among the earliest inhabitants of the area that became Gombe Emirate. The title Mai was used for the leader of the migrating group, and the king list begins with Mai Kiu around 1295.

Before colonial rule the Mai was head of state and commander-in-chief, presiding over a Tangale Traditional Council through five councils, and the kings were buried at Kumana on the hills. The list records an interregnum around 1680–1700.

Under British administration the seven pre-colonial Tangale districts were reduced to village areas and the Mai Tangle to the status of a district head; Kwaya was later added as an eighth area. From Mai Yamba (from 1912/1915) kings were buried at Poshiya. After independence, Gombe State governments expanded the districts to 18 and then reduced them to nine.

Abdu Buba Maisheru II reigned from 2001 to 2021 after a five-year vacancy. On his death the kingmakers' vote favoured Musa Idris Maiyamba, but on 3 March 2021 Governor Muhammad Inuwa Yahaya appointed Danladi Sanusi-Maiyamba. Protests and violence followed in Billiri, and many Tangale continue to reject him.
sections.selection: Candidates from the royal family contest before kingmakers drawn from the Tangale district heads (the Gombe State Government lists nine district heads under its kingmakers heading); the governor then approves and appoints. In 2021, 18 people contested; Musa Idris Maiyamba received five votes, and Ahmed Magaji and Danladi Sanusi two each, before the governor appointed Sanusi.
sections.council: The Mai chairs the Tangale Traditional Council at Billiri, with district heads (nine at present, after periods of seven, eight and 18 districts), and sits on the Gombe State Council of Chiefs. Historically the Mai ruled through five councils.
sections.palace: The seat is at Billiri. Pre-colonial kings were buried at Kumana on the hills, and kings from Mai Yamba onward at Poshiya.
sections.today: The Mai Tangle has no constitutional powers. The 2021 appointment remains contested: many Tangale groups refuse to recognise Danladi Sanusi-Maiyamba, and the dispute has been a source of tension between Billiri communities and the Gombe State government.

After Abdu Buba Maisheru II died in 2021, the kingmakers' vote gave Musa Idris Maiyamba five votes and Ahmed Magaji and Danladi Sanusi two each. On 3 March 2021 the governor nonetheless appointed Sanusi-Maiyamba, triggering protests in Billiri and calls from the Middle Belt Forum to respect the people's choice. Groups in Tangale land have continued to reject his authority.

thrones.title: Oba of Benin
thrones.established: c. 1200s (Oba dynasty; earlier Ogiso rulers before it)
thrones.about: The Oba is the hereditary sacred king of the Edo kingdom of Benin, ruling from the palace in the centre of Benin City. The present dynasty, founded by Eweka I in about the 13th century, followed an older line of Ogiso kings; it built one of West Africa's great forest states, famed for its walls and brass and ivory art. Since 1914 the Oba has reigned as a traditional monarch within Nigeria.

authority.text: The Oba of Benin is a sacred king in Edo traditional religion as well as a political ruler. Historically he was regarded as divine, lived largely secluded in the palace and appeared in public mainly for ceremonies; today the palace still describes him as the sacred custodian of the kingdom's customs and ancestral authority. He leads the rites for royal ancestors at the palace altars, and the annual Igue festival renews his spiritual power and blesses the land and people. He holds no Christian or Islamic office.

sections.history:
Edo tradition remembers an earlier line of rulers called the Ogiso, who governed a state known as Igodomigodo. According to the official account, after the last Ogiso was driven out the chiefs asked the ruler of Ile-Ife for a prince; Oranmiyan came, and his son by an Edo woman became the first Oba, Eweka I, in about the 13th century. An alternative story, first recorded in the 1970s, gives the founding king an Edo origin; most historians treat it as recent. The fourth Oba, Ewedo, moved the palace to its present site and set up a palace administration.

The kingdom's greatest expansion began with Ewuare, who took power in about 1440. He rebuilt the capital with earthen walls, ditches and gates, reorganised the chiefs and fixed succession on the king's eldest son. His successors, the 'warrior kings' Ozolua, Esigie, Orhogbua and Ehengbuda, extended Benin's influence west into Yoruba country, east to the Niger and south to the coast. Portuguese visitors arrived in the 1480s, followed by Dutch and English traders, and imported brass manillas fed a great age of palace casting. Esigie's mother Idia, credited with helping him win his wars, became the first Iyoba or queen mother.

After about 1600 the kings fought fewer wars, chiefs gained power and the kingdom lost its western lands. Under Oba Ewuakpe a revolt of chiefs led by the Iyase Ode sacked the city around 1700, and a succession war followed between his sons; Akenzua I won and restored royal authority, growing rich on trade. In the 19th century Benin traded palm oil, ivory and cloth and limited other exports to protect its independence.

In 1892 Oba Ovonramwen signed a treaty with Britain whose meaning the two sides disputed. In January 1897 some Benin chiefs attacked a British party that was advancing on the city without permission, killing most of its European members. A British punitive expedition captured Benin City in February 1897; the palace burned, thousands of brass and ivory works were taken and sold, and Ovonramwen was exiled to Calabar. The kingdom was absorbed into the Niger Coast Protectorate and later colonial Nigeria.

After Ovonramwen died in 1914 the British allowed his son to take the throne as Eweka II, who rebuilt the palace and revived the guilds. Akenzua II (1933–1978) began the long campaign to recover the looted art, and Erediauwa (1979–2016) and Ewuare II (from 2016) continued it. Since 2021 museums in Germany, Britain, the United States and elsewhere have returned many pieces, and a 2023 federal gazette recognised the Oba as their owner and custodian.
sections.selection: The throne passes by primogeniture: the Oba's eldest surviving son is the heir and has traditionally held the title Edaiken, introduced under Ewuare. Before he can be crowned, the heir must bury his father and complete a long series of royal rites; failure to do so could disqualify him, which is why burial of the late king has often been contested in succession disputes. The coronation is performed with the participation of the senior hereditary chiefs, and the new Oba takes a regnal name from among those of earlier kings. The Oba's mother may be installed as Iyoba, with her own palace at Uselu.
sections.council: Benin's chiefs fall into three historic orders. The Uzama Nihinron are the seven senior hereditary chiefs, regarded as the oldest order and kingmakers, who play a central part in coronation rites. The Eghaevbo n'Ore or town chiefs are led by the Iyase, the most senior non-royal chief and traditional head of the council of state. The Eghaevbo n'Ogbe or palace chiefs are organised in the palace associations such as Iwebo and Ibiwe, which manage the royal household, regalia and rituals. The palace today lists chiefs such as the Iyase n'Ore, the Esogban n'Edo (keeper of tradition) and the Ologbosere (war leader).
sections.palace: The palace (Eguae) stands at the centre of Benin City on the site chosen by Oba Ewedo; the present buildings date largely from Eweka II's rebuilding after 1914. Royal regalia include coral-bead crowns, collars and garments and scarlet cloth, and the ancestral altars hold cast-brass commemorative heads, bells and altar pieces. Hereditary guilds such as the brass casters (Igun Eronmwon) and carvers (Igbesanmwan) still serve the palace. The great annual ceremony is Igue, held in December, when the Oba blesses the land and honours past kings; other observances include Ugie Oro, which recalls Esigie's victory over the Igala, and the Emorho harvest celebration.
sections.today: The Oba has no executive power under Nigeria's constitution but remains one of the country's most influential traditional rulers and the head of the Benin Traditional Council. In 2024 an Edo State government created new traditional councils in Edo South and backed a separate museum for returned art; the next governor, Monday Okpebholo, reversed these steps in November 2024 and restored the Oba's statutory entitlements. The return of the Benin Bronzes remains the defining issue of the reign: the Smithsonian returned 29 works in 2022, more returns followed from other countries, and a Benin Royal Museum is planned to house them. In October–November 2026 the palace held events for Ewuare II's tenth coronation anniversary.

rulers.name: Ogun
rulers.parent: son of Ohen; elder brother of Uwaifiokun
rulers.note: Seized the throne from his brother with help from the market woman Emotan, rebuilt Benin City with walls and gates, and reorganised the chiefs and the royal succession.
rulers.bio: Born Prince Ogun, a son of Oba Ohen, he went into exile after Oba Orobiru died, and his younger brother Uwaifiokun took the throne. Tradition says he returned in secret, was sheltered by the food seller Emotan, and killed his brother during a festival procession; he then took the name Ewuare and, by one account, set the capital on fire. He rebuilt and enlarged the palace and is linked with the inner ring of walls and ditches and nine fortified gates. He reorganised the chiefs into town chiefs and palace chiefs who owed their rank to the king, which weakened the hereditary Uzama, and he introduced lineal succession through the heir's title, Edaiken. Coral-bead regalia, scarlet cloth and the Igue festival of royal renewal are all credited to his reign. His armies are said to have taken some 201 towns in Ekiti, Ikare and lands west of the Niger. Emotan was honoured after her death with a shrine and a tree in the market. He was buried at Esi near Udo.
rulers.dispute: Dates are reconstructions: Egharevba gives c. 1440–1473, while Millar puts his death about 1481. Traditions also differ on his mother's name.

rulers.note: Reigned for only 14 days. Tradition says he was struck by a poisoned arrow during his coronation.
Short reign. Warri tradition makes his eldest son Ginuwa the founder of the Itsekiri monarchy. After him the Uzama are said to have governed for about three years before Ozolua was recalled.

rulers.name: Okpame
rulers.note: Warrior king remembered as 'the Conqueror'. He received the first Portuguese visitors and was the husband of Idia, mother of Esigie.
rulers.bio: Born Okpame, a son of Ewuare, he was exiled to Ora after the killing of a rival prince and was recalled after Olua's death and a period of rule by the Uzama chiefs. He was crowned at Usama and spent much of his reign at war, especially in the Esan country, and also against Owo, Ondo and other towns, placing his sons over conquered places. Tradition credits him with receiving the Portuguese envoy João Afonso de Aveiro in about 1485–86, after which pepper, ivory and captives were traded through the port of Ughoton. In 1514 he is said to have asked the Portuguese for firearms, which they withheld. He noticed Idia at a dance and took her as a wife; their son Esigie succeeded him. He died near Uzea during or after a campaign against Uromi, with accounts disagreeing on whether he was poisoned or killed by his own soldiers.
rulers.dispute: Egharevba and Kaplan give c. 1481–1504; Blackmun c. 1480–1517. The list leaves a gap between 1480 and 1483.

rulers.name: Osawe
rulers.note: Won a civil war against his half-brother Arhuaran of Udo, defeated the Igala, and created the title of Iyoba (queen mother) for his mother Idia.
rulers.bio: Born Osawe, a son of Ozolua and Idia, he reached the throne after his father died away from the capital; his supporters smuggled the body past Udo, where his half-brother Arhuaran held power, so that Esigie could perform the burial rites that confer the right to rule. War with Arhuaran followed, and Udo was defeated. Benin tradition credits his mother Idia with raising soldiers and using ritual knowledge to win the war, and Esigie rewarded her with a new office, the Iyoba or queen mother, with her own palace at Uselu, chiefs and regalia. When the hereditary Uzama chiefs withheld their ritual services he appointed a substitute group, after which they submitted. He then defeated an invasion from the Igala kingdom, a victory still marked by the Ugie Oro festival. Portuguese traders and missionaries were at his court, and a Benin delegation reached Portugal in 1540. Brass plaques and other castings were produced on a large scale in this period, using metal from imported manillas.
rulers.dispute: Reign dates vary: Egharevba c. 1504–1550, Blackmun 1515–1550, Curnow 1517–1566. The Igala war is placed between about 1515 and 1521.

rulers.note: Ruled at the height of the warrior-king era.
Remembered as the last of the warrior kings. Western territories began to slip away and chiefs gained power during his reign.
His reign opened an era of weaker Obas and rival royal branches.
Reigned during the period of weaker central kingship.

rulers.note: Survived a rebellion by his brother Ogbewekon and ruled for four decades before British expansion reached Benin.
rulers.bio: Adolo succeeded his father Osemwende in the mid-19th century. In 1852–54 his brother Ogbewekon rebelled from Igueben in an attempt to take the throne, but the general Ebohon defeated the rebels. Benin forces later helped the Ekiti against Ibadan after Ibadan occupied Ilesha in 1879. His reign coincided with growing European interest in Benin's trade, and British envoys tried without success to secure a treaty between 1884 and 1886. He died in 1888 and was succeeded by his son Idugbowa, who became Ovonramwen.
rulers.dispute: Accession dated 1848 (Wikipedia list) or 1851 (WorldStatesmen).

rulers.name: Idugbowa
rulers.ended: deposed and exiled 1897; died in exile in Calabar 1914
rulers.note: Signed a treaty with Britain in 1892. After the 1897 British expedition captured and burned Benin City and looted the palace art (the Benin Bronzes), he was exiled to Calabar.
rulers.bio: Born Prince Idugbowa, the son of Oba Adolo, he had built up a household and armed following at Uselu and approached the capital in force when his father died, which helped him secure the throne over his brother Orokhorho. Several senior chiefs who opposed him were executed early in the reign. In 1892 the British vice-consul Henry Gallwey obtained a treaty with Benin, which Britain read as limiting the kingdom's independence while the Oba kept his trading monopolies. In January 1897 some of his chiefs attacked an unauthorised British party led by James Phillips, killing most of the Europeans; trial evidence later indicated the Oba had opposed the attack. A British force under Admiral Harry Rawson took Benin City in February 1897, the palace and much of the city burned, and thousands of brass and ivory works were carried off. Ovonramwen surrendered in August, was tried, and in September 1897 was sent into exile at Calabar, where he died in January 1914; his remains were not returned to Benin.

image.caption: Oba Ovonramwen in exile at Calabar, c. 1912

rulers.dispute: His accession is given as 1888 or 1889. His effective rule ended in 1897, though lists carry his reign to his death in January 1914.

rulers.name: Aiguobasimwin
rulers.note: Crowned in July 1914, ending the interregnum after his father's exile. He restored the monarchy under British colonial rule.
rulers.bio: Prince Aiguobasimwin, the eldest son of Ovonramwen, was allowed by the British to take the throne after his father died in exile, and was enthroned on 24 July 1914 as Eweka II, taking the name of the dynasty's founder. Ruling under colonial indirect rule, he rebuilt the royal palace destroyed in 1897 and restored the kingdom's titles and offices. He revived the craft guilds and commissioned new works to replace the looted regalia and altar pieces. He also founded the Benin Arts and Crafts School. He died in February 1933 and was succeeded by his son Akenzua II.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives his death as 2 February 1933.

rulers.name: Godfrey Edokparhogbuyunmwun Aguobasimwin Ovonramwen
rulers.note: Enthroned on 5 April 1933 and promoted Western education. From 1936 he campaigned for the return of the looted Benin Bronzes, and some royal coral regalia came back to him in the late 1930s.
rulers.bio: Born Prince Godfrey Edokparhogbuyunmwun Aguobasimwin in Lagos in 1899, he succeeded his father Eweka II and was enthroned on 5 April 1933. He encouraged Western schooling among the Edo while keeping palace rituals alive, and he merged several older ceremonies into the Igue festival so that people living away from Benin could attend. From 1936 he led efforts to bring back the art taken in 1897, and in the late 1930s two coral crowns and a coral-bead garment believed to be Ovonramwen's were returned to him by the son of a member of the expedition. When the British Museum declined to lend the ivory Idia pendant for FESTAC 77, he had the Igbesanmwan carvers' guild make copies. He reigned for 45 years, the longest reign of the 20th century in Benin.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia gives his death as 11 June 1978; WorldStatesmen gives 1 December 1978.

rulers.name: Solomon Aiseokhuoba Igbinoghodua Akenzua
rulers.note: Crowned on 23 March 1979. He often acted as a peacemaker among politicians, opened the palace to the press and marked his 30th anniversary in 2009 with a festival of Benin arts.
rulers.bio: Born in Benin City in 1923 as Prince Solomon Akenzua, he studied at Government College Ibadan and Yaba College and read law and administration at King's College, Cambridge. He joined the Eastern Nigeria civil service as a district officer in 1957 and moved to the federal service, retiring in 1973 as Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Health. He then worked briefly for Gulf Oil and served as Bendel State Commissioner for Finance from 1975. He was crowned on 23 March 1979, after his father Akenzua II died. As Oba he often mediated between quarrelling politicians, opened the palace to journalists with regular press briefings, and marked his 30th year on the throne in 2009 with a week of Benin arts. His death was announced on 29 April 2016, and he was posthumously made CFR in 2022.
rulers.dispute: His death was announced on 29 April 2016 without a stated date.

rulers.name: Eheneden Erediauwa
rulers.note: Crowned on 20 October 2016, his 63rd birthday. The return of looted Benin artworks has been a major theme of his reign.
rulers.bio: Born Prince Eheneden Erediauwa, eldest son of Oba Erediauwa, he attended Edo College and Immaculate Conception College in Benin City, took A-levels in London, studied economics at the University of Wales and earned a Master of Public Administration from Rutgers University. After working at the United Nations in 1981–82 he joined Nigeria's diplomatic service and served as ambassador to Angola, to Sweden (also covering Norway, Denmark and Finland) and to Italy. He was crowned on 20 October 2016, his 63rd birthday. In March 2018 he cursed traffickers who used shrine oaths to control victims and revoked such oaths, an act widely credited with weakening trafficking networks from Edo State. The return of the 1897 loot has dominated his reign: returned pieces began arriving in 2022, and a federal gazette of 23 March 2023 recognised the Oba as owner and custodian of repatriated Benin artefacts, settling a dispute with the Edo State government. In 2026 the palace marked his tenth coronation anniversary.
rulers.dispute: He is styled the 40th Oba by the palace and many news reports; Wikipedia's numbered list makes him the 39th.

thrones.title: Olu of Warri
thrones.about: The Olu of Warri is the paramount ruler of the Itsekiri people of the western Niger Delta. The kingdom (Iwere) was founded around 1480 by Ginuwa, a prince of Benin, and became a coastal trading state with early Portuguese ties. After a long interregnum from 1848 the throne was restored in 1936, and the present Olu, Atuwatse III, was crowned in 2021.

authority.text: The Olu is a traditional monarch without a formal priestly title. His accession nevertheless involves important ancestral rites: the late king's body is taken to the royal burial ground at Ijala, the Olu-designate spends a period of seclusion and instruction (Idanike) with elders, and the coronation takes place at the ancestral town of Ode-Itsekiri. From the late 16th century until 1848 the Olus were Catholic, a history the monarchy still emphasises, but the office does not carry a church title.

sections.history:
Itsekiri tradition says that Ginuwa, eldest son of Oba Olua of Benin, was sent away from Benin around 1480 with the sons of many Benin chiefs. After travelling through the creeks he reached Ijala, where the Itsekiri accepted him as their first Olu. His son Ijijen moved the capital to Ode-Itsekiri ('Big Warri') and drew the scattered Itsekiri communities together.

The kingdom traded with the Portuguese from the 16th century. Olu Atorongboye was baptised and his son, Atuwatse I, studied at Coimbra in Portugal and returned in 1611; Catholic missionaries worked in Warri for long periods, and European writers of the 17th and 18th centuries described Warri as independent of Benin. The Itsekiri exported palm oil, ivory and enslaved people and controlled many creeks and islands, reaching their widest influence under Erejuwa I (c. 1760–1795).

When Olu Akengbuwa died in 1848 his chosen heirs died soon after him, and no Olu was crowned for 88 years. Leading merchants acted as governors, the last and most famous being Nana Olomu, who dominated the palm-oil trade until the British defeated him in 1894. Itsekiri chiefs had signed a protectorate treaty with Britain in 1884, and Warri became part of colonial Southern Nigeria.

The monarchy was restored in 1936 with Ginuwa II, crowned as 'Olu of Itsekiri'. His son Erejuwa II won back the style 'Olu of Warri' in 1952, although some writers argue the 'Olu of Warri' style itself dates only from that year, a point still debated. From 1997 to 2003 disputes over local government headquarters and oil wealth led to violent conflict between Itsekiri and Ijaw communities. The throne passed from Atuwatse II (1987–2015) to his brother Ikenwoli (2015–2020) and then to Atuwatse III, crowned in 2021.
sections.selection: The Olu is chosen from the Ginuwa I Ruling House, descended from the founder. Succession follows a recognised order: the late Olu's sons, then his brothers, uncles and grandsons, and the candidate's mother must be Itsekiri or of Edo origin. A written succession declaration of 1979 governs the process. Custom requires that an Olu's death is not formally announced until a successor has been named. The Olu-designate takes the late king's body to Ijala for burial rites, spends about three months in seclusion (Idanike) learning custom from elders, and is then crowned at Ode-Itsekiri, where he picks up the sword (uda) that gives his regnal name.
sections.council: The Olu rules with a council of titled chiefs (the Ojoye). Its senior members include the Ologbotsere, the Olu's chief adviser and traditional prime minister, and the Iyatsere, who play leading parts in the succession process. Disagreements between these office holders were central to the 2021 succession dispute, during which the Ologbotsere was suspended.
sections.palace: Ode-Itsekiri remains the ceremonial capital where coronations are held, while the main palace in Warri city dates from the 1950s. The first crown, said to come from Ginuwa I, was a cone-shaped cap covered in coral beads; Atuwatse I added a Portuguese-style silver crown in 1611 and Oyenakpagha a diamond crown with a cross in 1645. These historic crowns were removed from the palace during the 2021 dispute, and new silver and gold crowns were made for Atuwatse III. Coronations are accompanied by a boat regatta, a custom traced to Olu Ojoluwa, and the Umalokun Olaja festival recalls Ginuwa's journey by water.
sections.today: The Olu has no executive powers under the Nigerian constitution but is one of the most prominent traditional rulers in Delta State and the Niger Delta. The history of the 'Olu of Warri' title and relations with neighbouring Ijaw and Urhobo communities in shared Warri remain sensitive after the conflicts of 1997–2003. Atuwatse III, crowned at 37, has travelled widely to promote Itsekiri culture and the kingdom, and has received several national and international honours, including the CFR in 2022.

rulers.dispute: The Warri Kingdom site calls him a great-grandson of Akengbuwa; the palace monarchy page calls him a grandson.

rulers.note: Crowned on 24 March 1951. The style 'Olu of Warri' was restored in 1952. He was deposed in 1964 and reinstated after the 1966 coup.
rulers.bio: The son of Ginuwa II, he was crowned on 24 March 1951 as Olu of Itsekiri; after protests the historic style 'Olu of Warri' was restored in 1952. He was active in the politics of the Western Region, serving as a regional minister without portfolio and as president of the Warri Divisional Traditional Council. In 1964 he was removed from the throne, and he was reinstated after the military coup of 1966. Tradition holds that, aggrieved at the treatment he had received, he laid a curse on Nigeria, which his grandson Atuwatse III formally lifted at his own coronation in 2021. He reigned until his death in the 1980s and was succeeded by his son Atuwatse II.
rulers.dispute: Deposed 1964–1966. His reign is given as ending in 1986 (ThisDay) or 1987 (Warri Kingdom site); his successor was crowned on 2 May 1987.

rulers.name: Godwin Toritseju Emiko
rulers.note: A lawyer who received the national honour CON. He reigned for nearly three decades.
rulers.bio: Born Godwin Toritseju Emiko at Ode-Itsekiri, the son of Olu Erejuwa II, he trained and practised as a lawyer before succeeding his father. He was crowned on 2 May 1987; the coronation is remembered as the last public engagement of Chief Obafemi Awolowo, who died a week later. His long reign covered the Itsekiri–Ijaw conflicts in Warri between 1997 and 2003, which centred on local government headquarters and oil wealth and displaced many thousands of people. He was honoured as Commander of the Order of the Niger (CON). He died in a Lagos hospital in 2015, aged 70, and was succeeded by his brother Ikenwoli.
rulers.dispute: The palace gives his death as 5 September 2015; the Wikipedia article on his successor says March 2015.

rulers.name: Ikenwoli Godfrey Emiko
rulers.parent: son of Erejuwa II; brother of Atuwatse II
rulers.note: Crowned on 12 December 2015 after his brother's death. He died in December 2020.
rulers.bio: Born Godfrey Ikenwoli Emiko in 1955 to Olu Erejuwa II and Olori Eyinagboluwade, he succeeded his elder brother Atuwatse II and was crowned Ogiame Ikenwoli I at Ode-Itsekiri on 12 December 2015, with national and state leaders in attendance. His reign was short. He died on 21 December 2020, reportedly of complications of COVID-19. In keeping with Itsekiri custom that an Olu's death is not formally proclaimed until a successor has been chosen, the Itsekiri traditional council announced his passing in April 2021, together with the name of his successor.

rulers.name: Utieyinoritsetsola (Tsola) Emiko
rulers.note: Crowned on 21 August 2021 as the 21st Olu after a succession dispute in which the old crowns were stolen. He introduced new silver and gold crowns.
rulers.bio: Born Utieyinoritsetsola Emiko in Warri, the son of Olu Atuwatse II, he attended Adesoye College, Offa, and studied international studies, political science and management at Case Western Reserve University in the United States. He worked in the oil, pension and maritime-security sectors and founded businesses before his selection. Nominated by the Ginuwa I Ruling House after his uncle Ikenwoli's death, he faced opposition from the then Ologbotsere, Chief Ayiri Emami, who was suspended and went to court; during the dispute the old crowns were taken from the palace. After completing the traditional rites he was crowned the 21st Olu at Ode-Itsekiri on 21 August 2021, choosing the regnal sword and name Atuwatse III, and at the ceremony he lifted his grandfather Erejuwa II's curse on Nigeria. New silver and gold crowns were made for his reign. In October 2022 he received the national honour CFR, the youngest person to do so.

thrones.title: Obi of Onitsha
thrones.established: c. mid-1500s (traditional)
thrones.about: The Obi of Onitsha is the traditional ruler of the old Onitsha community (Ndi Onicha) on the east bank of the Niger. The kingship traces back to Eze Chima and a migration from west of the river; Obis are chosen from the Umuezechima royal division. The present Obi, Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe, has reigned since 2002.

authority.text: The Obi is a ritual as well as a political figure in Igbo traditional religion. Before the annual Ofala festival he withdraws into seclusion, where he mourns the year's dead and communes with the earth deity (Ani Onicha), the ancestors and former kings, and he emerges to receive the homage of the town. He also proclaims dates in the customary calendar with his council. The office carries no Christian or Islamic title.

sections.history:
Onitsha tradition traces the kingdom to Eze Chima, whose followers left communities west of the Niger, an area long linked with Benin, and settled on the east bank; some versions say his descendant Oreze completed the crossing. Founders and early kings are placed from the mid-16th century, but dates before the 1800s are estimates from oral tradition.

The pre-colonial town had a dual leadership: alongside the Obi stood a female monarch, the Omu, who headed a women's council for markets and ritual. The last Omu, Nwagboka, was a party to the 1884 treaty and died in 1886, after which the office lapsed. European traders and missionaries settled at Onitsha in the 19th century, and on 9 October 1884 the British consul Edward Hewett signed a treaty of protection with the 'King, Queen and Chiefs of Onitsha'.

Under colonial indirect rule the Obi and his chiefs were drawn into native authority and town council structures; from 1956 the Obi was president of an urban council in which elected members, many from outside the old community, gradually gained a majority. Disputed interregna followed the deaths of Anazonwu (1899), Okosi I (1931) and Okosi II (1961). Okagbue reigned for three decades after the civil war, and Alfred Achebe emerged as Obi in 2002.
sections.selection: Eligibility is hereditary but the choice is elective. Candidates must be male-line descendants of Eze Chima within the Umuezechima royal division, and the throne does not pass automatically to the eldest son. Rival royal sub-lineages compete, and descent, seniority, titles, reputation and support all count; a strict rotation among royal kindreds has not been consistently followed. The chosen candidate must be accepted by the chiefs and the community, which can take time and explains the gaps between reigns. Installation proceeds through preliminary rites, seclusion, investiture with regalia and reintegration into the community, and the Obi reigns for life.
sections.council: The Obi presides over the Obi-in-Council, assisted by the Ndichie, chiefs recognisable by their red caps. The palace lists 52 Ndichie titles in three ranks: six senior Ndichie Ume, 23 Ndichie Okwa and 23 Ndichie Okwareze. The senior six are the Onowu Iyasele (the traditional prime minister), Ajie, Odu, Onya, Ogene and Owelle. Lineage priests (Di-Okpala) also take part in royal meetings, and the palace runs a customary court for civil disputes.
sections.palace: The palace, Ime Obi, stands at Ezechima Square in Onitsha. The high point of the year is the Ofala festival, after the Obi's period of seclusion: on Iru Ofala he appears in full regalia, dances to royal drums and receives homage, and on Azu Ofala age grades and other groups pay their respects. Royal regalia include the azuzu fan, abani sword, ogbanchi staff and akposi bag, along with the ufie slit drums that announce the king.
sections.today: The Obi has no formal powers under the Nigerian constitution, but he is among the most influential traditional rulers in the South-East. Obi Achebe has chaired the Anambra State Traditional Rulers Council and served as a university chancellor and in national public roles, and the Ofala festival has become a major public celebration of Onitsha and Igbo heritage.

rulers.bio: Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe was born in Onitsha in 1941 and attended Government Secondary School, Owerri. He studied chemistry at Stanford University (1966) and took an MBA at Columbia University. He joined Shell in Nigeria in 1972, rose to be a director of Shell Nigeria and of other Shell companies, and retired in 1995; he later chaired several companies, including Unilever Nigeria and International Breweries. He emerged as the 21st Obi in May 2002 (Onitsha custom speaks of an Obi 'emerging' rather than being crowned). Early in his reign he set up a community manpower development trust fund, and in 2004 he chaired a presidential enquiry into fuel shortages. He became chairman of the Anambra State Traditional Rulers Council in 2008, Chancellor of Kogi State University in 2010 and Chancellor of Ahmadu Bello University in 2015, and he was made CFR in 2004. He marked his 85th birthday in 2026.

thrones.title: Obong of Calabar
thrones.established: Efik kings at Duke Town from the 17th–18th century; style 'Obong of Calabar' from 1901–1903
thrones.about: The Obong of Calabar, also styled Edidem, is the paramount ruler of the Efik people of Calabar. The office grew out of the kingship of Duke Town (Akwa Akpa), one of the Efik trading towns of Old Calabar, and took its present title under a British arrangement in 1901–1903. Since 1970 a single Obong has represented all Efik, chosen by the heads of the ruling houses.

authority.text: The Obong is a traditional and ceremonial ruler without a formal priestly office today, though the institution grew from older Efik priest-kings and remains bound up with the Ekpe society, whose grades the Obong holds and which historically had authority even over kings. A new Obong is installed in two stages: esoteric rites performed by the royal houses at a sacred lodge (efe asabo), followed by a crowning at the Duke Town Presbyterian Church, and the palace has described the Obong as a 'defender of the Christian faith', a style it traces to the colonial era.

sections.history:
Efik tradition says the Efik lived among the Ibibio at Uruan before leaving after a dispute, settling for a time on the island of Ikpa Ene and then founding towns along the Calabar River: Creek Town (Ikot Itunko), Old Town (Obutong) and Duke Town (Akwa Akpa), together known to Europeans as Old Calabar. Families of the Efiom Ekpo line moved to Duke Town in large numbers in the 17th century, and by the early 1700s the Duke and Eyamba families led the town.

Calabar became one of the busiest slave-trading ports of the Bight of Biafra, with Efik merchants acting as middlemen between inland markets and European ships. Rivalry between the towns was fierce; in 1767 Duke Town leaders, with the help of English captains, trapped and killed or enslaved many Old Town chiefs. Trade was governed by the Ekpe society, which enforced debts and laws among the merchant houses. In 1841 King Eyamba V of Duke Town and King Eyo Honesty II of Creek Town agreed to stop exporting slaves, and palm oil and kernels became the main trade.

In 1884 the chiefs placed Calabar under British protection, and the town became the seat of the British protectorate administration until 1906. Under an arrangement completed in 1903 the Efik kings gave up the title of king and were styled Obong of Calabar, with much-reduced powers within colonial native councils. Duke Town and Creek Town continued to have separate rulers until December 1970, when the Efik agreed to have one Obong for all, chosen in turn from different communities.

Since 1999 the selection of the Obong has repeatedly been disputed. The 2001 choice of Professor Nta Elijah Henshaw broke the expected rotation and was settled by a compromise, and the 2008 selection of Ekpo Okon Abasi Otu led to fifteen years of court cases ending in a 2023 Supreme Court judgment and a renewed split between rival camps.
sections.selection: The Efik have twelve ruling houses, each headed by an Etubom. Only an Etubom who has been 'capped' by a sitting Obong, in a ceremony where the Obong-in-Council places a woven cap on him, may be chosen. The Etuboms' Traditional Council acts as kingmakers and elects the Obong under a written Palace Constitution (2002), and by agreement the stool alternates between Western and Central Calabar. The Obong-elect is presented to the state government for recognition before the coronation rites.
sections.council: The Obong rules with the Etuboms, the heads of the ruling houses, who also form the Etuboms' Traditional Council, the body that selects and advises him. The Ekpe society, organised in grades such as Nkanda, Oku Akama, Nyamkpe, Okpoho and Ebonko, remains a pillar of Efik authority; historically its decisions bound even kings, and senior Efik rulers hold its top grades.
sections.palace: The Obong's palace is in Duke Town, Calabar. The regalia include a crown, sword and orb that Efik tradition says were gifts from Queen Victoria; correspondence between an earlier king and the Queen is said to be kept at the National Museum in Calabar. At his coronation the Obong-elect wears the ikpaya, a royal raffia gown, and Ekpe masquerades and drumming are part of major royal ceremonies.
sections.today: The Obong is the head of the Efik within the Cross River State traditional institution and a symbol of Calabar's heritage, styled by his supporters the 'Treaty King' of the Efik. Since the Supreme Court's January 2023 judgment two camps have claimed the stool: the state government recognises Edidem Ekpo Okon Abasi Otu V, while the Etuboms' Traditional Council has backed Etubom Anthony Ani. Otu V continued to perform the Obong's public duties through 2025 and 2026.

rulers.name: Edem Ekpenyong Offiong Okoho
rulers.note: In 1841 he and King Eyo Honesty II of Creek Town agreed with the British to end their part in the slave trade; Calabar turned to palm-oil exports.

rulers.name: Effiom Okoho Asibong Ekpo
rulers.note: Chosen by Duke Town's leaders over a candidate favoured by the British. In 1850 the Calabar kings agreed with British officials to suppress human sacrifice at funerals.

rulers.name: Ededem Effiom
rulers.note: Duke Town king of the 1850s.

rulers.name: Eyo Asibong

rulers.name: Edem Asibong (Eyamba VIII)

rulers.name: Orok Edem-Odo

rulers.name: Edem Effiom Ededem (Adam Ephraim Adam)
rulers.parent: son of Ephraim Adam (Tete) of the Etim Efiom house
rulers.note: First ruler styled Obong of Calabar. Chosen after Prince Asibong Edem, selected in September 1900, died within weeks.
rulers.bio: Born around 1849 in Calabar, he was the eldest son of Ephraim Adam of the Etim Efiom royal house and Akwa Edem Itu of Big Qua Town. After his father's death in 1874 the household was run by his aunt, Queen Duke, until 1888, when he became its head. The stool fell vacant in 1896, and when the first choice, Prince Asibong Edem, died on 21 September 1900 before he could be crowned, Adam was installed in January 1901. Under the new British arrangement the Efik rulers gave up the style of king and became titular rulers styled Obong, and his powers were much reduced. He sat on the Native Council of Old Calabar, cooperated with colonial officials to protect Efik interests, attended the opening of Watt Market in 1901 and held the Ekpe grade of Murua Nkanda. He died on 1 July 1906.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia's Duke Town list names the 1901–1906 ruler 'Edem Effiom Edem'.

rulers.name: Ekpo Eyo Asibong
rulers.note: Succeeded Adam I and reigned briefly.
rulers.dispute: Also spelt 'Asibong IV'. Dates are from WorldStatesmen only.

rulers.name: Bassey Eyo Ephraim Adam
rulers.note: An electrical engineer and Etubom of the Etim Efiom house, crowned on 27 November 1982.
rulers.bio: Born in Calabar on Christmas Day 1904, he was educated at mission schools in Calabar, the Hope Waddell Training Institution and King's College, Lagos, and trained in engineering in Lagos and at Bournemouth in England. He worked as an electrical engineer and building contractor across Northern Nigeria, and in Jos he helped raise funds for the campaign for a Calabar-Ogoja-Rivers State. He became Etubom (head) of the Etim Efiom house in 1979. After Oku V died he was chosen over his cousin Etubom Cobham Eneyo Boco on 8 November 1982 and crowned on 27 November 1982. As Obong he toured Cross River State's local governments with other rulers to promote national campaigns on discipline and unity, and visited other states' councils of chiefs. He died on 14 December 1986.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia's Obong of Calabar list gives 1982–1987.

rulers.name: Otu Ekpenyong Effa
rulers.note: Crowned in November 1987; a short reign.

rulers.name: Boco Ene Mkpang Cobham
rulers.note: From Central Calabar, he reigned for about a decade from December 1989.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen dates his death to 2 January 1999; a 2023 ThisDay column places it in 2001.

rulers.name: Nta Elijah Henshaw
rulers.note: A professor from the Nsidung house of Central Calabar. His selection departed from the expected rotation, and Governor Donald Duke brokered a compromise that the stool would next pass to Western Calabar.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen records a first, week-long reign in August 1999 and a second from 31 August 2000 to 16 February 2008; Wikipedia gives 2001–2008 and the Duke Town list 2001–2004.

rulers.name: Bassey Ekpo Bassey
rulers.note: Proclaimed Obong by a rival faction in 2008 after Henshaw VI's death; WorldStatesmen lists him as a claimant 'in opposition'.
rulers.dispute: Not recognised by the state government; Abasi Otu V was the recognised Obong.

rulers.name: Ekpo Okon Abasi Otu
rulers.note: Selected in 2008 when the stool rotated to Western Calabar; his title has been tested in the courts ever since, but the Cross River State government recognises him.
rulers.bio: Ekpo Okon Abasi Otu, from Western Calabar and the Adiabo area, had been capped as an Etubom (head of a ruling house) by Obong Henshaw VI in 2004, which made him eligible for the stool. After Henshaw's death in 2008 the Etuboms selected him in preference to Anthony Ani, who was not a capped Etubom. Ani challenged the choice: the Calabar High Court voided the selection in 2012, the Court of Appeal held in 2013 that Ani was not qualified but ordered a fresh selection, and the Etuboms re-elected Otu in July 2013. On 13 January 2023 the Supreme Court declared the throne vacant and ordered a new election under the 2002 Palace Constitution; an Etubom conclave re-elected Otu days later, while the Etuboms Traditional Council proclaimed Ani instead. In November 2023 the Cross River State government declared Otu V the valid Obong. He is also Chancellor of the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta, and continues to carry out the Obong's public functions in Calabar.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen counts three separate reigns (from 2008, 2012 and July 2013) with regencies between court rulings. His legitimacy is still contested by the faction backing Anthony Ani.

thrones.title: Amanyanabo of Bonny
thrones.established: Pre-colonial (founding kings remembered in Ibani tradition; dated list begins 1759)
thrones.about: The Amanyanabo ('owner of the town') is the paramount ruler of Grand Bonny, the Ibani (Eastern Ijaw) city-state on Bonny Island at the mouth of the Bonny River. Bonny was one of the great Atlantic trading ports of the Niger Delta. Since the 18th century its kings have come from the Pepple (Perekule) dynasty.

authority.text: The Amanyanabo is a traditional ruler whose role today is largely ceremonial and civic; he holds no formal priestly title. In the past the kingdom's religious life centred on the monitor lizard, regarded as sacred and protected; King George Pepple I, backed by his chiefs, ended that status in 1867, and Bonny later became predominantly Christian.

sections.history:
Ibani tradition says Bonny was founded by migrants from the Ijaw heartland in present-day Bayelsa State, who settled first at Orupiri and then on the island, which they named Okoloama ('curlew town'). Four founding fathers, Ndoli, Opuamakuba, Alagbariya (honoured as Bonny's founder) and Asimini, are remembered as the first kings, and their line ruled until Awusa ('King Halliday'), the twelfth monarch.

Around 1760 Perekule ('Captain Pepple') was crowned by Chief Adapa Alagbariya and founded the Pepple dynasty, creating a new class of chiefs. Bonny grew into a leading port of the Atlantic slave trade, protected by fleets of war canoes, and after Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 it switched to exporting palm oil, ivory and pepper.

The 19th century brought strife between the great canoe houses and increasing British intervention. The consul deported William Dappa Pepple I in 1854 and installed regents, before restoring him in 1861. In 1869 rivalry between the Manilla Pepple house led by Oko Jumbo and the Anne Pepple house led by Jaja, a former slave who had risen to head his house, ended in war, and Jaja founded Opobo. Bonny then pushed into rivers controlled by Kalabari, leading to clashes that British consuls ended with treaties in 1873 and 1882.

A protectorate treaty in 1886 placed Bonny under British protection. After George Pepple I died in 1888 the kingdom was ruled mostly by regents until 1957, apart from Secondus George Pepple II (1932–1937). Eugene William Dappa Pepple II reigned from 1957 to 1970 and Opuada Pepple from 1978 to 1993; the present Amanyanabo, Edward Asimini William Dappa Pepple III, has reigned since 1996.
sections.selection: The Amanyanabo comes from the Perekule (Pepple) royal house, and in recent generations kings have come from its George Pepple lineage. The choice is made within the royal house and accepted by the Chiefs' Council of the major and minor houses before installation; long regencies have filled the throne when no candidate was agreed. The sources consulted do not describe the detailed procedure.
sections.council: Bonny is organised as a commonwealth of chieftaincy houses: 35 houses in all, of which 14 are major houses (five of them Duawari, or original royal houses) and 20 are minor houses, plus the George Pepple lineage of the royal house. Each high chief rules his own house, and together they form the Chiefs' Council that serves the Amanyanabo; it is led by the high chief of the Wilcox Major House.
sections.palace: The Amanyanabo's palace is in Bonny town. Bonny's ceremonial life draws on its maritime past, including war canoes and canoe-house chiefs, though the sources consulted give little detail on regalia or specific royal festivals.
sections.today: The Amanyanabo is a member of the Rivers State traditional institution and a voice for Bonny in dealings with government and the oil and gas industry, which dominates the island through the Nigeria LNG plant and oil terminal. In 2022 the kingdom marked the 25th anniversary of the present king's reign.

rulers.name: Awusa ("King Halliday")
rulers.note: Remembered as the twelfth and last king from the founders' line. Tradition says Chief Adapa Alagbariya crowned him.

rulers.name: Perekule I ("Captain Pepple")
rulers.note: Founder of the Pepple dynasty. He created a new class of chiefs, beginning with Chief Allison.

rulers.name: Fubara I Agbaa ("Manilla Pepple")
rulers.note: Ruled in the late 18th century, when Bonny was a leading Atlantic trading port.

rulers.name: Opubo ("Annie Pepple the Great")
rulers.note: Long reign during which Bonny's trading houses and war-canoe power grew.

rulers.name: Adumtaye-Bereibibo Adapa Bristol-Alagbariya
rulers.note: Short reign before William Dappa Pepple's accession.

rulers.name: William Dappa Pepple I (Dappa Perekule), first reign
rulers.note: Formally installed in 1837. His reign saw rising rivalry between Bonny's great houses and growing British consular pressure. A stroke in 1852 weakened him, and the consul exiled him in 1854.
rulers.bio: William Dappa Pepple I came to the throne in 1830 and was formally installed again in January 1837. His reign saw Bonny prosper on the palm-oil trade after the end of legal British slave trading, but also growing rivalry between the great trading houses, especially the Manilla Pepple and Anne Pepple houses. A stroke in 1852 left him weak, his opponents gained ground, and in January 1854 the British consul deported him. He spent several years in exile in England before British officials and the governor general Omoni Jack Brown helped restore him in August 1861. He reigned until his death on 30 September 1866 and was succeeded by his son George.

rulers.name: Dapu Fubara II Pepple ("King Dappo")
rulers.note: Installed in place of the deported king. He died after about 18 months.

rulers.name: Regency council (Anne Pepple, Ada Allison, Captain Hart, Manilla Pepple)
rulers.ended: Ended when the exiled king was restored, 18 Aug 1861
rulers.note: Appointed by the acting British Consul on 11 Sep 1855 and directed to consult leading chiefs, including Oko Jumbo.

rulers.name: William Dappa Pepple I, second reign
rulers.note: Restored after exile in England. He reigned until his death.

rulers.name: George Oruigbiji Pepple I
rulers.parent: Son of William Dappa Pepple I
rulers.note: His reign saw a bitter house rivalry that led Jaja to break away and found Opobo in 1869. In 1867 he ended the monitor lizard's sacred status. He was deposed on 14 Dec 1883 and restored under the 1886 protectorate treaty.
rulers.bio: Born in 1849 and educated in England, George Oruigbiji Pepple succeeded his father William Dappa Pepple I in 1866. In April 1867, with the support of Oko Jumbo and other chiefs, he declared that the monitor lizard, long the kingdom's sacred animal, was no longer protected. The rivalry between the Manilla Pepple house under Oko Jumbo and the Anne Pepple house under Jaja broke into war in 1869, and Jaja left to found the rival port of Opobo, taking much of Bonny's palm-oil trade. George was deposed in December 1883 amid the chiefs' quarrels; after Oko Jumbo's power collapsed, a protectorate treaty with Britain in 1886 created a ruling council and restored him. He died in October 1888, after which Bonny was ruled mainly by regents for decades.
rulers.dispute: Sources differ on when he was restored: February 1886 (narrative) or 22 Jan 1887 (table).

rulers.name: Waribo (Regent)
rulers.note: First of several regencies after George Pepple's death. For some of this period a Chiefs Council governed.

rulers.name: Ate (Regent)
rulers.note: Long regency in the early colonial period.
rulers.dispute: The source lists no ruler for 1923–1932.

rulers.name: Secondus George Pepple II
rulers.note: Installed on 14 Feb 1932. His reign brought back a crowned king after decades of regency.
rulers.dispute: The source also gives his death as 1939, and its regency entries for Claude Sodienye around 1932 are inconsistent.

rulers.name: Claude Sodienye (Regent)
rulers.note: Regency through the late colonial period.

rulers.name: Francis D. Banigo (Regent)
rulers.note: Regent until a king was installed in December 1957.

rulers.name: Eugene William Dappa Pepple II
rulers.note: Installed on 27 Dec 1957, shortly before Nigerian independence. A regency followed his reign (1970–1978).

rulers.name: Opuada Pepple
rulers.note: Reigned as the oil and gas industry grew on Bonny Island. Osobonye Rogers Longjohn served as regent from 1993 to 1996.

rulers.name: Edward Asimini William Dappa Pepple III (Perekule XI)
rulers.note: Amanyanabo of Grand Bonny since 1996, from the Perekule (Pepple) royal house. A 2022 book launch marked his 25 years on the throne, during which Bonny Island became a centre of Nigeria's liquefied natural gas industry.
rulers.dispute: The 25th anniversary in 2022 suggests an accession around 1996–97.

thrones.title: Amanyanabo of Kalabari
thrones.established: c. 1550 (traditional reckoning)
thrones.about: The Amanyanabo of Kalabari is the paramount ruler of the Kalabari, an Eastern Ijaw people of the Niger Delta whose trading state was known to Europeans as New Calabar. After civil strife in the 1880s the royal Amachree line moved inland to Buguma. Since the death of Amachree XI, announced in 2023, a regent has led the kingdom.

authority.text: The Amanyanabo is a traditional ruler without a formal priestly title. Kalabari tradition honours Owamekaso, regarded as the mother of the clan's deities and a goddess opposed to war, and the kingship is linked to the community's ancestral and festival life, but the sources consulted do not assign the king a specific priestly office.

sections.history:
The Kalabari trace their kingdom to settlers who founded Elem Kalabari on a mangrove island near the mouth of the New Calabar River. One tradition links them to Calabar further east, but this is thought to be a later invention; another credits Ijaw settlers from Amafo, joined by others. The early king list begins with an eponymous founder, Kalabari, placed around 1550.

Kalabari became a major port of the Atlantic slave trade, buying captives mainly from Igbo country upriver, and later traded palm oil and ivory for cloth, metal goods, guns and salt. Tradition credits King Owerri Daba with opening the overseas slave trade. Amakiri (Amachree) I, who reigned in the late 18th century, founded the Amachree dynasty, under which the great trading houses grew.

The 19th century brought wars with neighbouring Nembe, Bonny and Okrika over trade routes; Nembe inflicted a heavy defeat in 1863, and Kalabari later allied with Jaja's Opobo against Bonny. Treaties brokered by British consuls in 1873 and 1882 failed to keep the peace. In 1881–1884 rival royal factions split the state: the Barboy (Will Braide) group moved to Bakana, and the Amachree faction abandoned Elem Kalabari for Abonnema and Buguma.

Kalabari passed under British protection and then into independent Nigeria. Kings since 1900 have taken the regnal name Amachree with a number, and members of the Princewill family have held the throne for much of the 20th and 21st centuries. Amachree XI reigned from 2002; after his death was announced in 2023, Chief C.I.T. (Charles) Numbere became regent.
sections.selection: Kings come from the Amachree royal dynasty, now largely represented by the Princewill and Keini branches, and are chosen within the royal family and accepted by the Kalabari council of chiefs before installation. Interregna have sometimes lasted years while candidates were agreed, as in 1998–2002 and again since 2023. The detailed procedure is not described in the sources consulted.
sections.council: The Amanyanabo heads the Kalabari royal court together with a Council of Chiefs, most of them royal princes and heads of the great houses and groups of houses (such as Da Ogo). Chieftaincy installations proceed in stages before family, compound and kingdom-wide gatherings, the highest being the Se Diye, at which a candidate is affirmed before chiefs from across the kingdom.
sections.palace: The royal seat is at Buguma, where memorial halls named after past kings host state ceremonies. Kalabari ceremonies combine chiefly regalia with the kingdom's maritime heritage: boat regattas with decorated canoes, drumming and dance close major installations.
sections.today: The Buguma throne has been vacant since the death of Amachree XI, with Chief Charles Numbere serving as regent and presiding over kingdom ceremonies as recently as February 2026. Separately, the former militant leader Mujahid Dokubo-Asari has been installed with the style 'Amanyanabo of Elem Kalabari' at the ancestral island town; the sources do not explain how this stool relates to the Buguma throne. Kalabari communities across Asari-Toru, Akuku-Toru and Degema local government areas have held joint unity festivals at Elem Kalabari since 2024–2025.

rulers.bio: Theophilus J.T. Princewill, born in 1930, was a university professor and, before becoming king, head of the Da Ogo group of houses in Buguma, a seat later held by his son. He was chosen to end a four-year interregnum after Amachree X died in 1998 and reigned as Amachree XI from 2002. He led the kingdom for two decades as its senior traditional ruler in Rivers State. His death was announced in June 2023, the Rivers State governor was formally notified in November 2023, and he was buried at Buguma on 30 November 2023. His son, the politician Tonye Princewill, was installed as Da Abbiye-Ogo VI, head of the Da Ogo group of houses, in September 2025.

thrones.title: Orodje of Okpe
thrones.established: c. 1770 (first Orodje, Esezi I)
thrones.about: The Orodje (also styled Ovie) is the king of the Okpe, an Urhobo-speaking kingdom in Delta State with its seat at Orerokpe. The kingship began with Esezi I around 1770 but was vacant for long periods; it is rotated among four ruling houses. The present Orodje, Orhue I, a retired army general, was crowned in 2006.

authority.text: The Orodje is a traditional monarch with customary authority over Okpe land, including the town of Sapele, which Okpe people founded. The sources consulted do not describe a formal priestly title attached to the office, and it holds no Christian or Islamic role.

sections.history:
The Okpe are one of the kingdoms of the Urhobo cultural area in the western Niger Delta. Okpe tradition dates the monarchy to about 1770, when Esezi I became the first Orodje; his reign was short, and no further Orodje is recorded until the 20th century.

The monarchy was revived in the 20th century with Esezi II, who reigned from about 1945 to 1966 and is remembered as a pioneer advocate of democracy, attending a 1957 constitutional conference in London. Okpe settlers had earlier founded the trading town of Sapele on the Benin River, and the Orodje's land rights there remain a source of local pride.

After another gap, Orhoro I, a former police officer and company director, reigned from about 1972 until 2004. His successor, Major General Felix Mujakperuo (retd), was crowned Orhue I on 29 July 2006.
sections.selection: Kingship usually rotates among the four ruling houses of the Okpe kingdom. The sources consulted do not give the detailed procedure, the names of the four houses or the role of the state government.
sections.council: The Orodje rules with a council of Okpe chiefs drawn from the kingdom's communities; the sources consulted do not list its titles.
sections.palace: The royal seat is at Orerokpe, headquarters of Okpe local government area. The sources consulted give no detail on regalia or royal festivals.
sections.today: The Orodje is a member of the Delta State traditional institution and the custodian of Okpe customs and land, including Sapele. Orhue I has reigned since 2006.

images.caption: The Orodje of Okpe

rulers.note: Remembered as the first Orodje of Okpe.
rulers.dispute: No ruler is recorded between c. 1779 and c. 1945; the source does not explain the gap.

rulers.note: Restored the kingship in the 20th century. A campaigner for democracy, he attended a 1957 constitutional conference in London.
A former Nigeria Police officer who later became a company director before his reign.
rulers.dispute: The source gives no dates for 1966–1972.

rulers.name: Felix Mujakperuo
rulers.note: A retired major general of the Nigerian Army, crowned on 29 July 2006.

thrones.title: Obi of Aboh
thrones.established: Pre-colonial (founded by Obi Essumei Ukwu; date not recorded)
thrones.about: The Obi of Aboh is the king of Aboh, an Ukwuani (Ndokwa) kingdom near the head of the Niger Delta in Delta State. In the 19th century Aboh controlled traffic on the lower Niger and was the leading palm-oil market of the river. The Obi is an elective monarch who must be anointed by the kingdom's head priest.

authority.text: The Obiship is bound up with traditional religion (Odinala). No Obi can reign until the Oduah, the kingdom's head priest, whose office is older than the kingship, has anointed him with white chalk (ido nzu) and placed the cap on his head (ikpume okpu). The Obi holds the ofo nze staff of office, linked to Nri-derived ritual institutions, and presides at religious ceremonies with his titled chiefs.

sections.history:
Aboh was founded by Obi Essumei Ukwu. Oral tradition links some of its founders to a migration from the Benin Kingdom during a civil war there, a story similar to Onitsha's; other institutions, such as the ozo and ofo staffs and the ndichie titles, connect it with Nri. Its centralised kingship was unusual in the Niger Delta and may reflect Benin influence.

Sitting at the apex of the Delta, Aboh became a hub linking trade from Benin, Warri, Brass, Bonny and Calabar with the Niger, and was called 'the guard of the Niger'. It exported enslaved people and later palm oil, and imported cloth, beads, salt, guns and gunpowder; the Lander brothers, who passed in 1830, wrongly thought its king ruled all Igbo country. Under Obi Ossai, who died in 1844, the kingdom reached its height and could put hundreds of war canoes on the river; the British Niger expedition of 1841 passed through in his reign.

After Ossai's death his sons Aje and Chukwuma and Olisa of the Umuojugbali house disputed the throne, and an 18-year interregnum followed in which rival claimants ruled their own quarters and tributary towns broke away. Olisa was crowned in 1862. As British firms set up trading stations at Onitsha and Lokoja, Aboh lost its middleman role, and after clashes with British warships it was absorbed into the Southern Nigeria Protectorate.
sections.selection: The kingship is elective among royal lineages. In the 19th century about sixty electors decided between candidates, who spent heavily to win support, and a ruling Obi's own choice of heir could be overridden by the elders. The chosen candidate is anointed and crowned by the Oduah before he can reign.
sections.council: The Obi governs through the Izu Olinzele, the society of titled men, with the Obi and the Oduah (elder statesman and head priest) at its head. Below them come the Umudei, the Ndichie Ukwu (senior chiefs) and the Ndichie Nta (junior chiefs), each with fixed seating and ritual places; when an Oduah dies, the oldest man of the Umudei succeeds. Compound elders (okpala) manage local affairs.
sections.palace: The Obi's seat is at Aboh, headquarters of Ndokwa East local government area. Royal funerals follow strict ceremony: the body is carried by sixteen citizens, eight Ndichie and eight Umudei. The Obi's insignia include the ofo nze staff.
sections.today: Aboh remains the centre of the Aboh kingdom within Ndokwa land, and the Obi is a member of the Delta State traditional institution. The sources consulted do not give the present holder or recent succession.

images.caption: Obi Ossai of Aboh and his wives, 1848 (engraving)

rulers.note: Founder of the Aboh kingdom in tradition.
Ancestor of the Umuojugbali royal house; his dates are not recorded in the sources.
Aboh's most powerful 19th-century king, able to raise up to 300 war canoes. He joined the Attah of Igala and the Nupe in an attack on Brass after the killing of a European trader.
rulers.dispute: His accession date is not given in the sources.

rulers.name: Aje and Chukwuma (rival claimants)
rulers.note: Ossai's sons Aje and Chukwuma and Olisa of the Umuojugbali house contested the throne; Aje, favoured by the elders, was never crowned and died in 1862.
Crowned in 1862, ending the interregnum. A descendant of Obi Ojugbali I.

thrones.title: Dein of Agbor
thrones.established: Pre-colonial (date not recorded in the sources consulted)
thrones.about: The Dein is the king of Agbor, the largest town of the Ika people in Delta State. Agbor was historically an autonomous kingdom on the borderland between Benin and the Igbo-speaking west of the Niger. The present Dein, Keagborekuzi I, was crowned in 1979 as a toddler and became famous as the world's youngest king.

authority.text: The Dein is a traditional monarch and custodian of Agbor customs. The sources consulted do not describe a formal priestly title attached to the office, and it holds no Christian or Islamic role.

sections.history:
Agbor is the principal town of the Ika, an Igboid-speaking people of the Anioma area west of the Niger. Historically Agbor, Owa, Abavo, Umunede and other towns were independent kingdoms that did not see themselves as a single 'Ika' people. The area lies at a crossroads of Igbo, Benin and Esan influence; a popular account treats it as former Benin territory, while a 2022 study argues that outside influences were absorbed into an older local culture.

The British made Agbor the headquarters of the Agbor District in 1901. The name Ika was adopted officially in 1945, when the Agbor District Council became the Ika District Council, followed by the Ika Federal Native Authority in 1952.

Obi Ikenchukwu I died on 29 April 1979, and his infant son was crowned the same year as Dein Keagborekuzi I. A regent governed while the young king lived and studied in the United Kingdom, and he returned to take up his duties in 2001.
sections.selection: The current Dein succeeded his father, and a regent governed while he was a minor. The detailed rules of succession are not given in the sources consulted.
sections.council: The Dein rules with councils of titled elders, while age grades (otu ogbo) and community assemblies handle much local regulation and dispute settlement across Ika communities. The sources consulted do not list Agbor's chieftaincy titles.
sections.palace: The palace is in Agbor, headquarters of Ika South local government area. The sources consulted give little detail on regalia; the Ogwa Ika festival is a major annual celebration of Ika culture.
sections.today: Dein Keagborekuzi I is regarded as the highest-ranking traditional ruler in Delta State. He served as Chancellor of the University of Ilorin from 2006 to 2015 and has joined other Delta monarchs on security and anti-trafficking initiatives.

rulers.note: Dein of Agbor until his death in 1979.
rulers.dispute: His accession date is not given in the sources.

rulers.name: Benjamin Ikenchukwu Keagborekuzi
rulers.note: Crowned in 1979 at about 22 months old; a regent ruled until 2001.
rulers.bio: Born in Agbor on 29 June 1977, he was not yet two when his father, Dein Ikenchukwu I, died in April 1979, and he was crowned the same year. The 1980 Guinness Book of World Records listed him as the world's youngest crowned monarch. He was taken to the United Kingdom in 1981 and lived there for about twenty years while a regent governed Agbor, returning to take up his full duties in 2001. He served as Chancellor of the University of Ilorin from 2006 to 2015 and was made Commander of the Order of the Niger. As Dein he has mediated local disputes and in 2020 joined other Delta State rulers in restricting herders' activities after attacks and pledged cooperation with the anti-trafficking agency NAPTIP.
rulers.dispute: Sources give his birth name in slightly different forms (Benjamin Keagborekuzi Ikenchukwu, or with the surname Gbenoba).

thrones.title: Eze Nri
thrones.established: c. 10th century (traditional reconstruction)
thrones.about: The Eze Nri is the priest-king of Nri, a town in Anambra State that was for centuries the ritual centre of much of Igboland. Nri's influence rested on religion, purification and title-giving rather than armies, carried by travelling ritual specialists. The office survived colonial rule as a non-sovereign title; the throne has been in interregnum since the death of Ènweleána II in 2017.

authority.text: The Eze Nri is a sacred king in Igbo traditional religion (Odinala). His authority derives from Chukwu, the culture hero Eri, the ancestors and the earth deity Ala; he must keep strict ritual purity and lives under special restrictions. Nri specialists cleansed abominations against the earth (nso ani), took part in conferring ozo titles and ofo staffs, and tradition credits the Eze Nri with proclaiming the agricultural year. He holds no Christian or Islamic office.

sections.history:
Nri tradition traces its kingship to Eri, a sky-born founder sent by Chukwu, and his son Nri, who settled at Agukwu. Aguleri, Enugwu-Ukwu and Nri all see themselves as children of Eri, though their accounts differ. The anthropologist M. A. Onwuejeogwu reconstructed a dynasty beginning around the 10th century; historians treat his dates as estimates. The nearby Igbo-Ukwu bronzes show a rich, specialised society from the 9th century onward, but archaeology has not proved that they belonged to the Nri kings.

Nri was never a conventional territorial state. Its power travelled with ritual specialists (ndi Nri), some marked with ichi facial scarification, who purified people and land, settled disputes and installed title-holders in towns that chose to use their services. Onwuejeogwu placed Nri's widest influence between the 16th and late 17th centuries.

From the late 17th century the rise of the Aro trading network, the Atlantic trade and pressure from Benin, Igala and Agbor gradually weakened Nri's sphere, though it kept great prestige. British officials reached the area in the 1900s; Eze Nri Òbalíke was made to appear at the court in Awka, and later accounts say that in 1911 he was forced to annul the taboos binding other communities to Nri.

The title continued as a non-sovereign office. Interest in Nri revived after Thurstan Shaw's excavations at Igbo-Ukwu (1959–1964) and the civil war; an Odinani museum was founded at Nri in the 1970s. Ènweleána II reigned from 1988 until his death in December 2017.
sections.selection: An Eze Nri is not chosen by simple inheritance. After a king's death there is a long interregnum while the royal lineages, senior title-holders and diviners wait for signs identifying the next ruler; the candidate must show through visions confirmed by diviners that he is chosen by Chukwu, Eri and the ancestors, and he may not have a living father. He travels to Aguleri to fetch clay from the Anambra River for the shrine pot (odudu), undergoes seclusion and a ritual burial and rebirth, and is then acclaimed as Eze Nri or Igwe. The title-holders (Nze and Nzemabua) choose him, and the community must accept the choice.
sections.council: The Eze Nri shares authority with lineage heads, ozo title-holders (Nze and Nzemabua) and councils, while each village keeps its own assembly, age grades and priests. The ndi Nri ritual specialists acted as his agents in other communities.
sections.palace: The royal seat is at Agukwu, Nri, in Anaocha local government area. Key symbols of the office include ofo staffs and the shrine of Nri Menri; the Odinani Museum at Nri preserves heritage objects.
sections.today: Since December 2017 the throne has been in interregnum, with Prince Ikenna Onyesoh acting as regent; reports from 2019 describe disputes between the palace and kingmakers. The Eze Nri is recognised as a traditional and religious office in Anambra State and as a guardian of Igbo heritage.

rulers.name: Ìfikuánim
rulers.note: Oral tradition names Ìfikuánim as the first Eze Nri, after the founding by the culture hero Eri.
rulers.dispute: The dates come from Onwuejeogwu's 1981 reconstruction and are not historical records; other scholars place the dynasty's start later (e.g. c. 1225).
