thrones.title: Ooni of Ife
thrones.established: Ancient; historians place the dynasty's origins between the 7th and 9th centuries CE, and tradition traces it to Oduduwa
thrones.about: The Ooni of Ife is the paramount ruler of Ile-Ife, which the Yoruba regard as the place where their world and their kingship began; he carries the titles Arole Oduduwa (heir of Oduduwa) and Olofin Adimula. The office is both a civil kingship and the senior sacred kingship of the Yoruba, and its holder is often treated as the first among Yoruba obas. Since the 20th century the throne has rotated among four ruling houses: Lafogido, Osinkola, Ogboru and Giesi. Rulers before the late 18th century have no reliable dates and their order is disputed; the main list numbers no ruler 31, and secondary claimants listed in that source are left out here.

authority.text: The Ooni is a sacred king in Yoruba traditional religion as well as a traditional ruler. Ife tradition treats him as the living heir of Oduduwa and as the chief custodian of the shrines, priesthoods and festivals of Ile-Ife, the city regarded as the spiritual home of the Yoruba; some Ife sources even describe him as the 401st orisa. He presides over the cycle of Ife festivals, above all Olojo, during which he appears publicly wearing the sacred Are crown, and he works with the Isoro (priestly) chiefs who serve the many orisa cults of the town. The official palace site describes him as the spiritual and cultural head of Yoruba people worldwide; he holds no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Ile-Ife was settled long before the kingship remembered today. Ife tradition tells of an older order of thirteen communities led by Obatala that was displaced by Oduduwa's group, after which the two were reconciled into a single Ife state – a rivalry still re-enacted in the Itapa festival. Historians who read Oduduwa as a historical figure place the start of this kingship around the late first millennium CE, while in Yoruba cosmology Oduduwa is the divinity who came down from heaven to create dry land at Ife. Traditions say that princes who left Ife founded many later Yoruba and related kingdoms, Oranmiyan being remembered as the last of them.

Between about 1000 and 1400 CE Ife was a large, wealthy city whose craftsmen produced the naturalistic brass, copper, stone and terracotta heads for which it is now world-famous, and whose glass workshops at Igbo Olokun made beads traded far across West Africa. Much of this art is associated with the reign of Obalufon Alayemore (often called Obalufon II), who was driven out by Oranmiyan and later restored, and who was afterwards worshipped as the orisa of brass-casting, weaving and regalia. The heroine Moremi Ajasoro, remembered in the Edi festival for helping Ife defeat raiders from Ugbo, belongs to the same remembered era.

From the 15th century political power in the Yoruba region shifted towards Oyo and Benin, but Ife kept its ritual pre-eminence: kings elsewhere looked to Ife for the legitimacy of their crowns. The order and dates of the many Oonis between Oranmiyan and the late 18th century are uncertain, and Ife tradition is unclear even about basic relationships, such as Lajamisan's descent from Oranmiyan.

The 19th-century Yoruba wars hit Ife hard. The town was sacked in 1849 and again in 1882, partly in conflicts linked to Modakeke, a settlement of Oyo refugees on Ife land, and at least one Ooni (Derin Ologbenla) died in exile at Okeigbo without being crowned in Ife. Only after the Ekitiparapo (Kiriji) war ended did Adelekan Olubuse I re-establish the court in Ife itself.

Under British rule and after independence the office gained national prominence. Adesoji Aderemi (1930–1980) was also Governor of the Western Region and helped bring the University of Ife to the town; Okunade Sijuwade (1980–2015) mediated in many disputes, while relations with Modakeke and rivalry with the Alaafin over seniority continued. The present Ooni, Adeyeye Enitan Ogunwusi (Ojaja II), was crowned in December 2015.
sections.selection: Before the 20th century succession was fluid. Rules agreed in a 1957 chieftaincy declaration, restated in a 1980 declaration under the Osun State Chiefs Law, recognise four ruling houses – Osinkola, Ogboru, Giesi and Lafogido – which take turns. When the throne falls vacant the house whose turn it is presents candidates, the Ife kingmakers choose among them after traditional consultations, and the Osun State government approves the choice and presents the staff of office. In 2015 the turn passed to Giesi; members of other houses challenged parts of the rotation in court.
sections.council: The Ooni governs with a council of titled chiefs. The senior palace and town chiefs (often grouped as the Ihare) act as kingmakers and advisers, while the Isoro chiefs are the priests of the many orisa cults of Ife whose rites the Ooni oversees. Outside Ife, the Ooni chairs or co-chairs bodies of Yoruba obas and is a permanent member of the Osun State Council of Obas.
sections.palace: The palace (Afin Ooni) stands at Enuwa in the centre of Ile-Ife, Ife Central LGA; the old palace used enamelled bricks and porcelain tiles and the modern complex sits beside it. Royal regalia include beaded crowns and the sacred Are crown worn at Olojo. The Ife festival year includes Olojo (the festival of the 'first dawn', linked to Ogun), Edi (honouring Moremi), Itapa (Obatala) and Obameri. Traditionally the Ooni appeared in public only during Olojo; today the festival is a large public event drawing visitors from the diaspora (the 2026 edition ran from late September into early October).
sections.today: The Ooni has no formal government powers but is the most senior traditional ruler in Osun State and one of the most prominent in Nigeria. Ogunwusi has used the office for cultural diplomacy at home and abroad, chairs university councils and runs foundations, and received the national honour CFR in 2022. The long rivalry between the Ooni and the Alaafin of Oyo over pre-eminence among Yoruba obas, and the Ife–Modakeke relationship, remain recurring public issues; his marriages have also drawn press attention.

rulers.name: Oduduwa
rulers.note: Progenitor of the Yoruba and founder of the Ife kingship in tradition; Ife historians remember his reign as short.
rulers.bio: In Yoruba cosmology Oduduwa is the divinity sent from heaven who created the land at Ile-Ife; in Ife's historical tradition he leads a group from Oke Ora, east of Ife, that overcame the older communities led by Obatala and then made peace with them. He held the title Olofin of Ile-Ife, and every Ooni since has claimed to be his heir (Arole Oduduwa). Traditions say up to sixteen princes or groups left Ife to found other kingdoms, which historians read as remembered founders rather than a literal family tree. Scholars who treat him as a historical king place him around 800–1000 CE.
rulers.dispute: Some lists start numbering with Obatala, and some accounts name Oranfe as the first ruler of Ife.

rulers.name: Obatala
rulers.note: Took power after Oduduwa's short rule, in Ife tradition.
rulers.dispute: Obatala is chiefly known as the leader of the pre-Oduduwa communities and as an orisa; his place as a numbered ruler after Oduduwa follows the main king list.

rulers.name: Ogun
rulers.note: Tried to take the throne after Oduduwa but failed and was pushed out.
rulers.dispute: The source list gives him and Obalufon Ogbogbodirin the same number (2).

rulers.name: Obalufon Ogbogbodirin
rulers.note: Also called Osangangan Obamakin; remembered for a long reign and as father of Obalufon Alayemore.

rulers.name: Obalufon Alayemore
rulers.note: Often treated as the first Ooni in the modern sense; driven out by Oranmiyan and later restored. His reign is seen as the high point of classical Ife art.
rulers.bio: Obalufon Alayemore, often called Obalufon II, succeeded his father Obalufon Ogbogbodirin, probably in the 13th or 14th century. Oranmiyan pushed him off the throne, and he returned with local support after Oranmiyan's death or departure. Tradition credits him with commissioning brass images of royal ancestors and with being the first Ife ruler to wear a crown as a sign of authority; the life-size copper mask associated with him was long kept in the palace room used for coronations. He is also remembered for restoring Ife's control of trade routes and is credited with founding the Ogboni association. After his death he was deified as Obalufon, orisa of brass-casting, weaving and regalia. Some accounts say he died in a smallpox epidemic.

rulers.name: Oranmiyan
rulers.note: Came back to Ife and displaced Obalufon Alayemore; also remembered as founder of the Oyo kingship and as linked to the Benin dynasty.
rulers.bio: Oranmiyan is remembered as the last-born son, or in other versions the grandson, of Oduduwa. Traditions make him a warrior prince who left Ife on expeditions, spent time in the Edo country where his line is linked to the Benin dynasty, and founded the kingship of Oyo. On returning to Ife he took the throne from Obalufon Alayemore, who was restored after him. In Ife tradition the heroine Moremi Ajasoro was his wife. A tall granite monolith in Ife known as Opa Oranmiyan (Oranmiyan's staff) is associated with him.

rulers.dispute: Popularly called a son or grandson of Oranmiyan, but Ife tradition is unclear on his parentage.

rulers.name: Adelekan Olubuse I
rulers.note: Ogboru house; first Ooni to reign in Ife itself after the Ekitiparapo war ended. Grandfather of Okunade Sijuwade.
rulers.bio: Adelekan Olubuse I came from the Ogboru house and took the throne in 1894, after a period in which war had kept the Ooni's court away from Ife. He restored the monarchy in the town as peace returned at the end of the Ekitiparapo (Kiriji) war, and his reign coincided with the extension of British authority over the Yoruba interior. His grandson Okunade Sijuwade later reigned as Olubuse II.

rulers.name: Adekola
rulers.note: Lajodogun line; Ooni-elect for only about two months in mid-1910.

rulers.name: Ademiluyi Ajagun
rulers.note: Lafogido house; Modakeke people returned to Ife in 1921.

rulers.name: Adesoji Aderemi
rulers.note: Osinkola house; reigned 50 years and also served as Governor of the Western Region (1960–1962/63). The 1980 succession declaration was confirmed just before his death.
rulers.bio: Adesoji Aderemi was born in Ile-Ife on 15 November 1889 and became Ooni on 2 September 1930. During half a century on the throne he became a national figure: he sat in the regional institutions of colonial Nigeria, took part in the nationalist politics of the Western Region, and after independence served as the first Nigerian Governor of the Western Region from 1960 to about 1962. He pressed strongly for Ife to host the new regional university, now Obafemi Awolowo University. The rotation of the throne among four ruling houses was formalised late in his reign. He died in Ile-Ife on 3 July 1980.

image.caption: Ooni Adesoji Aderemi wielding the Ada at Olojo

rulers.name: Okunade Sijuwade (Olubuse II)
rulers.note: Ogboru house; crowned 6 December 1980. Mediated many disputes, including over LAUTECH and the Ife–Modakeke land question.
rulers.bio: Okunade Sijuwade was born in Ile-Ife on 1 January 1930 into the Ogboru house; his grandfather was Ooni Adelekan Olubuse I. After schooling in Abeokuta and Ile-Ife he studied business management in Northampton, England, then worked as a reporter, a manager at A.G. Leventis and sales director of National Motors, and built his own trading group, the Sijuwade Group. Crowned the 50th Ooni on 6 December 1980 as Olubuse II, he reigned for almost 35 years. His reign saw renewed Ife–Modakeke clashes, a long public rivalry with the Alaafin of Oyo over seniority, and mediation in disputes such as the 2010 quarrel between Oyo and Osun states over LAUTECH. He died in a London hospital in July 2015 and was buried at Ile Oodua, Ile-Ife.
rulers.dispute: His death was reported on 28 July 2015 but was officially announced by Ife chiefs only on 12 August 2015.

rulers.name: Adeyeye Enitan Ogunwusi (Ojaja II)
rulers.note: Giesi house; selected 26 October 2015 and crowned 7 December 2015 as the 51st Ooni. The reigning Ooni.
rulers.bio: Adeyeye Enitan Babatunde Ogunwusi was born in Ile-Ife on 17 October 1974 to Prince John Oluropo Ogunwusi and Princess Sidikat Wuraola Ogunwusi of the Giesi house. He was educated in Ibadan and Ile-Ife, qualified as an accountant at The Polytechnic, Ibadan, became a chartered accountant, and worked in business and real estate. The Ife kingmakers selected him on 26 October 2015 and he was crowned Ojaja II on 7 December 2015, aged 41. He has promoted Yoruba culture and the Olojo festival internationally, runs the House of Oduduwa Foundation, chairs university councils (including the University of Nigeria, Nsukka) and received the CFR in 2022. His several marriages have been widely reported in the press.

image.caption: Ooni Adeyeye Enitan Ogunwusi, Ojaja II

thrones.title: Alaafin of Oyo
thrones.established: c. 14th century (Oranyan, by tradition); refounded at present-day Oyo by Atiba around 1837
thrones.about: The Alaafin ('owner of the palace') ruled the Oyo Empire, the largest Yoruba state, from Oyo-Ile until its collapse in the 1830s; the dynasty then continued at the present town of Oyo, refounded by Atiba. All later Alaafins descend from Atiba. Dates before the 19th century are rough reconstructions, and unnamed regencies (1944–45, 1955–56) are left out. The palace lies in the Oke-Afin area of Oyo, which INEC records place in Atiba LGA (an earlier version of this entry said Oyo East).

authority.text: The Alaafin is a traditional ruler whose office also carries sacred, priestly duties in Yoruba traditional religion. He was regarded as the 'companion of the gods' (ekeji orisa); the cult of Sango – himself remembered as an early Alaafin – was closely tied to the palace, and Oyo tradition credits Alaafin Abipa with establishing the Egungun and Ifa cults at the capital. The annual Bere festival was the public acclamation of a reign, and the Alaafin's priests and palace officials (Ilari) still perform rites at the palace shrines. The office has no formal role in Islam or Christianity.

sections.history:
Oyo tradition names Oranyan (Oranmiyan), a prince of Ile-Ife, as founder, with his sons Ajaka and Sango as early rulers; Sango was later worshipped as the orisa of thunder. The first capital, Oyo-Ile (Old Oyo), lay in the savanna north of the forest, which suited cavalry. Around the early 16th century Nupe invaders drove the court into exile in Borgu and then to Igboho, where several Alaafins ruled until Abipa brought the capital back to Oyo-Ile around 1580.

In the 17th and 18th centuries Oyo became the dominant inland power of the region. Its cavalry forced Dahomey to pay tribute from about 1730 (finally subjugated in 1748), and the empire covered a large area of the present South-West and beyond, trading through the coast. The Alaafin governed through the Oyo Mesi, a council of seven chiefs led by the Basorun, who chose the king and could reject him by presenting an empty calabash or parrot's eggs, after which the Alaafin was expected to die. The Ogboni society balanced the Oyo Mesi, and the Aare Ona Kakanfo led the provincial army.

From 1754 the Basorun Gaa dominated the state and forced several Alaafins to their deaths until Abiodun overthrew him in 1774. Under Abiodun Oyo was prosperous, but the Egba broke away. His son Awole quarrelled with the Aare Ona Kakanfo Afonja, whose revolt at Ilorin from the 1790s and secession around 1817 started the empire's collapse; Ilorin joined the Sokoto Caliphate and sacked Oyo-Ile in the 1830s.

After the Eleduwe war (c. 1835) Oyo-Ile was abandoned. Atiba Atobatele, a son of Abiodun, re-established the kingdom at Ago d'Oyo – the present Oyo – around 1837 and shared power with the new military states of Ibadan and Ijaye, making Oluyole of Ibadan Basorun and Kurunmi of Ijaye Aare Ona Kakanfo. He also introduced succession by the crown prince.

In 1888 Adeyemi I signed a treaty with the British; Oyo was bombarded in 1895 and absorbed into the Lagos Protectorate. Under indirect rule the Alaafin was made the chief native authority over a wide area. Adeyemi II was deposed in the 1950s for siding with the NCNC party, and Lamidi Adeyemi III reigned for more than 51 years from 1970 to 2022. After a contested vacancy of nearly three years, Abimbola Owoade I was crowned in April 2025.
sections.selection: Historically the Oyo Mesi, led by the Basorun, chose the Alaafin from princes descended from Oranyan, after Ifa had been consulted; the Basorun's nomination was decisive. Atiba replaced this with succession by his son and heir, and all later Alaafins are his descendants, drawn from several royal houses (such as the Alowolodu and Agunloye lines). Today the ruling houses present candidates, the Oyo Mesi as kingmakers make the choice with Ifa consultation, and the Oyo State governor approves and presents the staff of office. The 2022–2025 selection was contested in court by some royal families and saw open disagreement between the Oyo Mesi and the state government.
sections.council: The Oyo Mesi – the Basorun, Agbaakin, Samu, Alapini, Laguna, Akinniku and Asipa – remain the senior chiefs and kingmakers. Palace officials (Ilari), the eunuch officials of the old empire (Ona Efa, Otun Efa, Osi Efa) and the Ogboni have ritual and advisory roles. The historic military title Aare Ona Kakanfo is still conferred by the Alaafin on prominent Yoruba figures (for example M.K.O. Abiola in 1988 and Gani Adams in 2017).
sections.palace: The palace (Afin Oyo) at Oke-Afin faces the old Akesan market; it is a large complex with many courtyards, shrines, carved posts and doors, said to be about two centuries old. After years of decay it was restored and Owoade moved into it in January 2026. Regalia include beaded crowns (Ajagbo is said to have first worn the Sesefun crown), and the palace hosts the Sango and Egungun festivals and the coronation rites. The ruins of Oyo-Ile lie in Old Oyo National Park, whose museum keeps artefacts of the empire.
sections.today: The Alaafin has no executive powers but is the most senior traditional ruler in Oyo State and one of the leading Yoruba monarchs, often styled 'Imperial Majesty'. Recent controversies include a 2011 law that ended the Alaafin's permanent chairmanship of the Oyo State Council of Obas, the long rivalry with the Ooni of Ife over pre-eminence, and the disputed 2022–2025 succession. Owoade has focused on restoring the old palace.

rulers.name: Oranyan (Oranmiyan)
rulers.note: Founder of Oyo after leaving Ile-Ife; tradition also links him to the founding of Benin.
rulers.bio: Oranyan (Oranmiyan) is remembered as a warrior prince of Ile-Ife, son or grandson of Oduduwa, who led expeditions out of Ife and founded the kingdom of Oyo at Oyo-Ile. Traditions also link him to the founding of the Benin dynasty and make him a ruler of Ife for a time. His sons Ajaka and Sango followed him on the Oyo throne. Historians treat him as a founding figure of the 13th–14th centuries rather than a precisely dated king.
rulers.dispute: Some accounts call him a son rather than grandson of Oduduwa.

rulers.name: Ajaka
rulers.note: Remembered as a mild ruler; removed in favour of his brother Sango.

rulers.name: Sango
rulers.note: Set on the throne by the Oyo Mesi and ruled about seven years; later venerated as the orisa of thunder.
rulers.bio: Sango is remembered as a son of Oranyan who displaced his gentler brother Ajaka and ruled for about seven years. Traditions describe him as a powerful, fiery king associated with fire and lightning; accounts of his end differ, but he was afterwards worshipped as Sango, orisa of thunder and lightning. The Sango cult became closely connected with the Oyo palace and spread wherever Oyo influence reached, and it remains one of the best-known Yoruba orisa traditions in Africa and the Americas.
rulers.dispute: Traditions differ on the length of his reign and the manner of his death.

rulers.name: Ajaka (restored)
rulers.note: Returned to the throne after Sango's death.

rulers.name: Aganju
rulers.parent: Probably a younger son of Ajaka
rulers.note: Very long reign beginning around the mid-14th century.

rulers.name: Kori
rulers.note: Took the throne as a child with his mother Iyayun as regent; reigned more than 50 years.

rulers.name: Oluaso
rulers.note: Reigned in the early 15th century.

rulers.name: Onigbogi
rulers.note: Nupe invaders drove him out of Oyo-Ile and he fled to Borgu.

rulers.name: Ofiran
rulers.note: Crowned in exile after a regency by his mother Adasobo; won back some territory from the Nupe.

rulers.name: Eguguojo
rulers.note: Made Igboho the royal capital during the exile.

rulers.name: Orompoto
rulers.note: A woman ruler who broke the father-to-son pattern; pushed the Nupe back around 1555.

rulers.name: Ajiboyede
rulers.note: Credited with holding the first Bere festival.

rulers.name: Abipa (Ogbolu)
rulers.note: Brought the capital back from Igboho to Oyo-Ile, rebuilt around 1580; credited with establishing the Egungun and Ifa cults at the capital.

rulers.name: Obalokun
rulers.note: A period of expansion; salt from European traders reached Oyo.

rulers.name: Oluodo
rulers.note: Drowned in the Niger while fighting the Nupe.

rulers.name: Ajagbo
rulers.note: Said to be the first to wear the Sesefun crown; created the Aare Ona Kakanfo military title.

rulers.name: Odarawu
rulers.note: The first Alaafin on record to be removed by the Oyo Mesi.

rulers.name: Kanran
rulers.note: Refused the order to take his own life and was killed in a mutiny of the army.

rulers.name: Jayin
rulers.note: Remembered as a tyrant and removed by the Oyo Mesi.

rulers.name: Ayibi
rulers.note: The Basorun acted as regent while he was a minor; later rejected by the Oyo Mesi.

rulers.name: Osiyago
rulers.note: Killed amid a dispute between two claimants.

rulers.name: Ojigi
rulers.note: Oyo armies forced Dahomey to pay tribute around 1730.

rulers.name: Gberu
rulers.note: Gave the Basorun title to Jambu, who later turned against him.

rulers.name: Amuniwaiye
rulers.note: Killed by a personal enemy shortly after taking office.

rulers.name: Labisi
rulers.ended: compelled to die by Basorun Gaa
rulers.note: Forced to die by Basorun Gaa before he could fully take office.

rulers.name: Awonbioju
rulers.ended: compelled to die by Basorun Gaa
rulers.note: Ruled about 130 days before Basorun Gaa forced his death.

rulers.name: Agboluaje
rulers.ended: compelled to die by Basorun Gaa
rulers.note: Basorun Gaa forced his death after he refused to wage war on Ifonyin.

rulers.name: Majeogbe
rulers.note: Reigned while Basorun Gaa dominated the state.

rulers.name: Abiodun
rulers.note: Overthrew Basorun Gaa in 1774 with the help of Oyabi; a long, prosperous reign, though the Egba broke away. Father of Atiba.
rulers.bio: Abiodun came to the throne in 1774 at a time when the Basorun Gaa had made the Alaafin powerless and forced several of his predecessors to die. With the help of Oyabi, the Aare Ona Kakanfo, he defeated and executed Gaa, restoring royal authority. His reign is remembered as a time of peace and wealth based on trade with the coast, but the Egba, under the leader remembered as Lisabi, threw off Oyo rule, and campaigns against Borgu and Nupe in the 1780s went badly. He died in 1789. His son Atiba later refounded Oyo, so all modern Alaafins descend from him.

rulers.name: Awole Arogangan
rulers.note: His conflict with Afonja, the Aare Ona Kakanfo, whose revolt at Ilorin began in the 1790s, started the collapse of the empire.

rulers.name: Adebo
rulers.note: Reigned about 130 days.

rulers.name: Maku
rulers.note: Reigned only about two months.

rulers.name: Interregnum (Basorun Asamu as regent)
rulers.note: The throne stood empty for about five years.

rulers.name: Majotu
rulers.note: Elderly when crowned; Ilorin broke away in 1817 and Dahomey threw off Oyo rule in 1823.

rulers.name: Amodo
rulers.note: Ilorin forces sacked the palace in 1833 after a long siege.

rulers.name: Oluewu
rulers.note: The Oyo Empire collapsed after the Eleduwe war, and Oyo-Ile was abandoned.

rulers.name: Atiba Atobatele
rulers.note: Re-founded Oyo further south (the present Oyo) around 1837 and made the succession pass to his heir; all later Alaafins descend from him.
rulers.bio: Atiba was a son of Alaafin Abiodun and Eni-olufan (Adegoolu), born at Gudugbu. In the chaos after his father's death he became a strongman at Ago (Ago Oja), raising a private army. After Oyo-Ile was abandoned following Alaafin Oluewu's death in the Eleduwe war, the Oyo chiefs invited him to rebuild the kingdom, and he made Ago – renamed Oyo – the new capital around 1837. He shared power with the rising military towns, recognising Oluyole of Ibadan as Basorun and Kurunmi of Ijaye as Aare Ona Kakanfo, and changed the succession so that his eldest son Adelu would succeed him rather than die with him. He died shortly after celebrating the Bere festival, around 1858–59.
rulers.dispute: The king list gives 1859 for his death; his Wikipedia biography gives c. 1858.

rulers.name: Adelu Agunloye
rulers.note: Chosen by his father as successor.

rulers.name: Adeyemi I Alowolodu
rulers.note: Last independent Alaafin; signed a treaty with the British in 1888, after which Oyo was bombarded (1895) and brought under colonial rule.
rulers.bio: Adeyemi I Alowolodu, a son of Atiba, became Alaafin in 1876, during the long 19th-century wars among the Yoruba states. He tried to reassert Oyo's old seniority while Ibadan and the Ekitiparapo fought the Kiriji war, and in 1888 he signed a treaty with the British of Lagos. Relations soured, and in 1895 a British force shelled Oyo, after which the kingdom was absorbed into the Lagos Protectorate. He died in 1905. His royal house, Alowolodu, later produced Adeyemi II and Lamidi Adeyemi III.

rulers.name: Siyanbola Oladigbolu I
rulers.note: Long reign under British indirect rule; a regency followed (1944–45).

rulers.name: Adeniran Adeyemi II
rulers.note: Deposed by the Western Region government in the 1950s after supporting the NCNC party, and exiled to Lagos, where he died in 1960.
rulers.dispute: Sources give 1954 or July 1955 for the deposition.

rulers.name: Bello Gbadegesin Oladigbolu II
rulers.note: Installed after Adeyemi II's deposition; reigned across the end of colonial rule and Nigeria's independence in 1960.

rulers.name: Lamidi Olayiwola Adeyemi III
rulers.note: Installed in November 1970 and died on 22 April 2022 after more than 51 years, the longest reign of any Alaafin in recorded history; a vacancy of almost three years followed.
rulers.bio: Lamidi Olayiwola Adeyemi was born in Oyo on 15 October 1938 into the Alowolodu royal house; his father Adeyemi II had been deposed and exiled in the 1950s, and his grandfather was Adeyemi I. He was a boxer in his youth. Crowned on 18 November 1970, he became one of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, serving as chancellor of Usmanu Danfodiyo University (1980–1992) and later of the University of Maiduguri, and conferring the Aare Ona Kakanfo title on M.K.O. Abiola (1988) and Gani Adams (2017). He was a vocal defender of the Alaafin's seniority among Yoruba obas. In 2011 a new state law ended his position as permanent chairman of the Oyo State Council of Obas. He died on 22 April 2022 in Ado-Ekiti, aged 83.

rulers.name: Abimbola Akeem Owoade I
rulers.note: Approved by the Oyo State governor on 10 January 2025, given his staff of office on 13 January and crowned on 5 April 2025; some royal families contested the selection. Moved into the restored old palace in January 2026.
rulers.bio: Abimbola Akeem Owoade was born on 17 July 1975 into the Owoade-Agunloye family of Agure compound, Oyo; he is a great-grandson of Alaafin Lawani Agogoja and a descendant of Atiba. A mechanical engineer, he studied at the Federal Polytechnic Ilaro and The Polytechnic, Ibadan, then at the universities of Sunderland and Northumbria in England, and worked in banking, project management and, latterly, as a project coordinator with Manitoba Hydro in Canada. After a vacancy of almost three years marked by court cases and disagreement between the kingmakers and the state government, Governor Seyi Makinde approved his selection on 10 January 2025. He received his staff of office on 13 January and was crowned on 5 April 2025. He launched a restoration of the old palace and moved into it in January 2026.
rulers.dispute: Numbering differs: he is usually called the 46th Alaafin, but the Wikipedia list numbers him differently.

thrones.title: Alake of Egbaland
thrones.established: 1854 at Abeokuta (Okukenu); earlier Alakes ruled at Igbo-Egba before the Egba migration around 1830
thrones.about: The Alake is the paramount ruler of the Egba people, with his seat at Ake in Abeokuta. The title is older than Abeokuta itself: Alakes ruled at Ake in the old Egba forest before the Egba were driven out in the 19th-century wars and founded Abeokuta around 1830. Kingmakers choose the Alake from the ruling houses of the Egba Ake section. Two regencies are included for continuity.

authority.text: The Alake is a traditional ruler without a formal religious office. Like other Yoruba obas he performs customary rites at his installation and presides over Egba festivals, and the Ogboni society has an important role in Egba kingship and custom, but the office is chiefly civil and cultural. It has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
The Egba were once a confederation of townships in the forest south of Oyo, with the Alake at Ake as senior ruler. They were under Oyo overlordship until a revolt in the late 18th century, remembered through the hero Lisabi. In the wars that followed the fall of Oyo in the early 19th century their towns were destroyed, and around 1830 refugees led by the warrior Sodeke settled at the rock shelter of Olumo, founding Abeokuta ('under the rock'). Each Egba section rebuilt its own quarter, so Abeokuta became a federation of townships.

The Alake title was revived at Abeokuta in 1854 with the installation of Okukenu. Abeokuta was a major centre of missionary activity, trade and literacy in the 19th century and resisted attacks from Dahomey (notably in 1851 and 1864). Rivalries among Egba sections and the Ogboni made the early Alakes' authority uncertain, and there were long vacancies.

In 1893 the Egba signed a treaty with the British Lagos Colony that recognised their independence, and in 1898 the Egba United Government was formed with Gbadebo I at its head. Egbaland kept nominal independence until 1914, when it was absorbed into Nigeria after the Ijemo disturbances.

Ladapo Ademola II (1920–1962) was a leading figure of colonial Nigeria, but in 1948–49 mass protests by the Abeokuta Women's Union, led by Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, against taxation of women forced him to leave the throne for a time. Later Alakes include Samuel Oyebade Lipede (1972–2005) and Adedotun Aremu Gbadebo III, who has reigned since 2005.
sections.selection: The Alake is chosen from the recognised ruling houses of the Egba Ake section. When the throne falls vacant, the houses present candidates and the Egba kingmakers vote; in 2005 Gbadebo III won 15 of the 23 votes against eight rivals. The Ogun State government then approves the choice and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The Alake heads the Egba Traditional Council, which brings together the obas of the other Egba sections (such as the Osile of Oke-Ona, the Agura of Gbagura and the Olowu of Owu) and other Egba obas, and is a senior member of the Ogun State Council of Obas. His own chiefs include the Ogboni, war chiefs (Ologun), trade chiefs (Parakoyi) and women chiefs.
sections.palace: The Ake palace (Afin Ake) in Abeokuta is the seat of the Alake; Olumo Rock nearby is the symbolic birthplace of the town. Key public occasions include coronation anniversaries and the Lisabi festival celebrating the Egba hero of independence from Oyo.
sections.today: The Alake has no executive power but is the most senior traditional ruler in the Abeokuta area and one of the leading obas of Ogun State. Gbadebo III, a retired army colonel, has been active in public affairs; in 2010 a dispute over titles with the Olu of Igbein went to court. The Ogun State governor congratulated him on his 20th coronation anniversary in November 2025.

rulers.name: Shomoye (regent)
rulers.note: Served as regent after the death of the warlord Sodeke, before the Alake title was revived at Abeokuta.

rulers.name: Okukenu (Sagbua)
rulers.note: First Alake of Egbaland at Abeokuta, installed in August 1854.
rulers.dispute: The source gives both 8 and 28 August 1854 as the installation date.

rulers.name: Shomoye (regent, second time)
rulers.note: Governed during the vacancy after Okukenu's death.
rulers.dispute: The source gives his second regency ending in either 1866 or 1868.

rulers.name: Ademola I
rulers.parent: Grandson of Jibodu through his mother
rulers.note: For years the Ogboni chiefs, who backed Oyekan, refused to accept him.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives his reign as 1878–1881, shifting the dates of the next two Alakes later; the dates here follow Wikipedia.

rulers.name: Oyekan
rulers.note: Already old when he became Alake.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives 1881–1885.

rulers.name: Oluwaji
rulers.parent: Grandson of Jibodu through his mother
rulers.note: From Itoku; a vacancy of about two years followed his death.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives 9 February 1885 – 27 January 1889.

rulers.name: Oshokalu
rulers.note: The 1893 trade treaty between Egbaland and the British Lagos Colony was signed during his reign.

rulers.name: Gbadebo I
rulers.note: The Egba United Government was formed in 1898; he made a state visit to England in 1904, and Egbaland was absorbed into Nigeria in 1914.
rulers.bio: Gbadebo I, a son of the first Alake Okukenu, became Alake in August 1898, the year the Egba United Government was created with British support to run the nominally independent Egba state. Working with educated Egba officials, his government set up a secretariat, courts and public works and taxed trade, and he made a state visit to England in 1904. Unrest in 1914 (the Ijemo affair) gave the British a reason to end Egba independence and absorb Egbaland into Nigeria. He died on 28 May 1920. His grandson Adedotun Aremu Gbadebo III is the present Alake.

rulers.name: Ladapo Ademola II
rulers.note: Reigned 42 years; protests led by Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti forced him off the throne for a time before he returned.
rulers.bio: Ladapo Ademola II, a son of Alake Ademola I, became Alake in September 1920 and reigned for 42 years. He was one of the most prominent traditional rulers of colonial Nigeria, working closely with the British administration under indirect rule. His support for unpopular taxes on women provoked a long campaign by the Abeokuta Women's Union led by Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, and mass protests forced him off the throne for a time at the end of the 1940s before he returned. He died on 27 December 1962.
rulers.dispute: Sources differ on the 1920 start date and on whether he left in 1948 or 1949.

rulers.name: Adesina Samuel Gbadebo II
rulers.note: Took office after a one-year vacancy.

rulers.name: Samuel Oyebade Lipede I
rulers.note: Reigned about 33 years until his death in February 2005.

rulers.name: Adedotun Aremu Gbadebo III
rulers.note: Chosen by the Egba kingmakers, 15 votes out of 23, and took office on 2 August 2005; he is the reigning Alake.
rulers.bio: Adedotun Aremu Gbadebo was born in Abeokuta on 14 September 1943 into the Laarun ruling house; he is a grandson of Gbadebo I and a great-grandson of the first Alake, Okukenu. After school in Abeokuta and Ibadan he graduated from the University of Ibadan in 1969 and joined the Nigerian Army, attending the Command and Staff College, Jaji, and serving as principal staff officer to Major-General Tunde Idiagbon at Supreme Headquarters in 1984–85. He retired as a colonel. After Alake Lipede died in February 2005, the Egba kingmakers chose him by 15 votes to his rivals' 8, and he took office on 2 August 2005. He marked 20 years on the throne in 2025.

thrones.title: Awujale of Ijebuland
thrones.established: c. 1450 (Obanta, per Oduwobi's revised chronology)
thrones.about: The Awujale is the paramount ruler of the Ijebu kingdom, with his seat at Ijebu-Ode. Under a 1957 declaration the throne rotates among four ruling houses: Gbelegbuwa, Anikinaiya, Fusengbuwa and Fidipote. The throne is VACANT: Oba Sikiru Adetona died on 13 July 2025 after a 65-year reign. It is the Fusengbuwa house's turn, but the Ogun State government suspended the selection in January 2026 over petitions and bribery allegations, and as of September 2026 the ruling house's suit to compel completion of the process was awaiting reassignment to a new judge. Dates before 1900 are reconstructed and approximate.

authority.text: The Awujale is a traditional ruler whose office is civil and cultural rather than a formal religious post. Ijebu kingship carries customary rites – the king-elect goes through seclusion and installation ceremonies with the Osugbo and palace chiefs, and the Awujale presides over the Ojude Oba festival and other state occasions – but he has no formal priestly title. The office has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Ijebu tradition names Obanta (also called Ogborogan) as founder, a grandson of Olu-Iwa through his daughter Gborowo, who came to the Ijebu-Ode area and established the kingship; the title Awujale is explained by a story of his wrestling victory over a chief who blocked his way. Historians place the founding around the 15th century, although older lists give different dates. Ijebu-Ode became the capital of a compact, wealthy kingdom between the coastal lagoons and the interior.

From the 16th to the 19th century the Ijebu controlled much of the trade between the interior and the lagoon ports of Lagos and the coast, and were known for tight control of their trade routes. The king list includes several women rulers (such as Ore-Yeye and Ore-Geje) and a long-reigning king, Fusengbuwa, who gave his name to one of the modern ruling houses.

In 1892, after the Ijebu closed their routes to Lagos traders, a British force invaded, defeated the Ijebu army at Imagbon and took Ijebu-Ode; the Osugbo meeting house was burned. Ijebu was then placed under the Lagos Protectorate. In the colonial period the Awujale served as the chief native authority; Adenuga was deposed in 1929 and exiled to Ilorin.

Sikiru Kayode Adetona (Ogbagba II), crowned in 1960, reigned 65 years and became Nigeria's longest-serving monarch. He survived a suspension and attempted deposition by the Ogun State government in 1981–84 and became a major figure in Ijebu development and national affairs. Since his death in July 2025 the throne has been vacant.
sections.selection: Under the 1957 Customary Law Declaration the throne rotates among the Gbelegbuwa, Anikinaiya, Fusengbuwa and Fidipote ruling houses. The house whose turn it is nominates candidates (Fusengbuwa put forward about 95 princes and princesses in January 2026), and the kingmakers choose among them. The Ogun State government must approve the choice before the Awujale-elect enters seclusion and is installed.
sections.council: The Awujale rules with the Ijebu traditional council, which includes the Osugbo (Ogboni) elders, palace chiefs, the Parakoyi (trade chiefs), war chiefs and the obas and baales of the towns of Ijebuland. The kingmakers in the current selection include senior Ijebu chiefs named as defendants in the 2026 suit.
sections.palace: The palace (Afin Awujale) stands in the centre of Ijebu-Ode. The best-known royal occasion is Ojude Oba, a colourful festival in which Ijebu age-grade groups (regberegbe) and families parade on horseback and on foot to pay homage to the Awujale.
sections.today: The Awujale has no executive power but is the most senior traditional ruler of the Ijebu and a permanent member of the Ogun State Council of Obas. The current vacancy is the main issue: the Fusengbuwa house has accused the state of stalling, the government cited petitions and bribery allegations, and the matter is before the Ogun State High Court.

rulers.parent: Grandson of Olu-Iwa through his daughter Gborowo

rulers.name: Obaruwa
rulers.note: Remembered as a warrior king, credited with founding the Ode and Makun dynasties in Remo.

rulers.name: Otutubiosun

rulers.name: Ajuwakale

rulers.name: Ore-Yeye
rulers.note: A woman ruler.

rulers.name: Mekun
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives Mekun 1692–1702, Gbodogi 1702–1710 and Ojigi 1710–1730, about 20 years earlier than Oduwobi's chronology.

rulers.name: Boyejo

rulers.name: Oniyewe

rulers.name: Ore-Geje
rulers.note: A woman ruler.

rulers.name: Sapenuwa Rubakoye
rulers.note: Tradition says he followed his sister on the throne.

rulers.name: Fusengbuwa

rulers.name: Anikilaya
rulers.note: Founder of the Anikinaiya ruling house; great-grandfather of Sikiru Adetona.

rulers.name: Tunwase

rulers.name: Adekoya
rulers.note: Very short reign.

rulers.name: Adenuga
rulers.note: Installed in 1925; deposed in 1929 after allegations of corruption over forestry fees and exiled to Ilorin.

rulers.name: Adesanya

rulers.name: Sikiru Kayode Adetona (Ogbagba II)
rulers.note: Became Awujale at about 25 and reigned 65 years, making him Nigeria's longest-serving monarch; died on 13 July 2025 aged 91.
rulers.bio: Sikiru Kayode Adetona was born on 10 May 1934 at Imupa, Ijebu-Ode, to Prince Rufai Adetona Adeleke of the Anikinaiya house. After Olu-Iwa College he worked in the Western Region's audit department and left to study accountancy in the United Kingdom. Chosen by the kingmakers from six nominees, he received his appointment letter in January 1960 and was crowned on 2 April 1960 as Ogbagba II. In 1981 the Ogun State government suspended him and a commission recommended his removal, but the December 1983 coup halted the process and a 1984 court ruling restored him. Over 65 years he became a strong voice in Ijebu affairs and national life. He died on 13 July 2025, aged 91.
rulers.dispute: Regnal numbering differs: in this list (after Oduwobi) he is the 53rd Awujale, while recent reports describe his successor as the 60th.

thrones.title: Olubadan of Ibadan
thrones.established: c. 1820–1829 as a war camp (rulers styled Baale or by military title); Olubadan title revived 1936
thrones.about: The Olubadan ('lord of Ibadan') is the paramount ruler of Ibadan, Nigeria's third-largest city. Unlike most Yoruba thrones it is not hereditary: the title passes in turn between two chieftaincy ladders, the civil Otun line and the military Balogun line, and any male Ibadan indigene can in principle reach it by climbing one of them. Early rulers were styled Baale or held war titles; dates before 1900 are approximate and early sources differ.

authority.text: The Olubadan is a civil traditional ruler. Ibadan was founded as a military republic of Oyo warriors, and the office grew out of its war-chief hierarchy rather than from a sacred royal lineage, so it carries no priestly role in Yoruba traditional religion beyond customary rites performed at installation and at city festivals. It has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Tradition remembers an older Ibadan founded by Lagelu, a warrior from Ile-Ife, which was destroyed and later re-established. The modern city began around 1820–1829 as a war camp of Ife, Ijebu and Oyo soldiers during the wars that followed the decline of the Oyo Empire, under leaders such as Maye Okunade. Oyo refugees soon dominated it, and Ibadan developed a unique system in which leadership went to the most successful warriors rather than a royal family.

In the 1830s, when Alaafin Atiba refounded Oyo, he made the Ibadan leader Oluyole Basorun, giving Ibadan formal charge of defending Yorubaland. Ibadan defeated Ilorin at Osogbo around 1840, crushed Ijaye in 1862 and built an empire over much of the Yoruba interior, until the Ekiti and Ijesa rose against it in the Ekitiparapo (Kiriji) war from 1877. The town was led successively by a Baale (civil head) and by military titleholders such as the Basorun, Balogun and Aare Ona Kakanfo.

An agreement in 1893 placed Ibadan under British protection, and in 1897 an Ibadan Town Council was set up; from 1901 the Baale presided over it. The title Olubadan was revived in 1936 for Okunola Abaasi, and from the 1950s holders have been styled Oba. Ibadan became the capital of the Western Region and later of Oyo State.

Since 2017 the structure of the Ibadan chieftaincy has been contested. Governor Abiola Ajimobi elevated several high chiefs and baales to beaded-crown obas in 2017, a move challenged in court by the Otun Olubadan Rashidi Ladoja; in 2023 Governor Seyi Makinde signed a new law making the 11 members of the Olubadan-in-Council obas and traditional heads of Ibadan's 11 LGAs. Ladoja himself became the 44th Olubadan in September 2025.
sections.selection: Succession follows two ladders of titles: the Otun (civil) line, headed by the Otun Olubadan, with 22 steps, and the Balogun (military) line, headed by the Balogun, with 23 steps. A chief must climb his line one rung at a time, often over decades, and when the Olubadan dies the throne normally goes to the head of the line whose turn it is, so the two lines alternate. The Olubadan-in-Council confirms the candidate and the Oyo State governor approves him and presents the staff of office. Because heirs are usually elderly, many Olubadans have reigned only briefly.
sections.council: The Olubadan-in-Council is made up of the senior chiefs at the top of both ladders – the Otun Olubadan, Osi Olubadan, Ashipa Olubadan and others in the civil line, and the Balogun, Otun Balogun, Osi Balogun and others in the military line. Since 2023 these 11 high chiefs are also beaded-crown obas heading the 11 Ibadan LGAs. Below them are the mogajis (heads of compounds) and baales of the villages, and the Iyalode leads the women chiefs.
sections.palace: Because the title is not hereditary, Olubadans traditionally reigned from their own family compounds. A new official palace on a six-acre site at Oke Aremo was opened in July 2024. Installations and major ceremonies take place at Mapo Hall, the colonial-era city hall on Mapo hill. Ibadan's best-known festival tied to the city's origins is the Okebadan festival honouring the hill of Ibadan.
sections.today: The Olubadan has no executive power but is the senior traditional ruler of Ibadan and a leading member of the Oyo State Council of Obas. The main controversies concern the 2017 and 2023 elevation of high chiefs to obas, which critics said threatened the two-line succession, and the many legal disputes that followed.

rulers.name: Lagelu
rulers.note: Legendary founder of the first Ibadan settlement, remembered as a warrior from Ile-Ife; the Olubadan's lineage of authority is traced symbolically to him.
rulers.dispute: The Guardian list counts Lagelu as the first ruler and dates him to 1820, but tradition places the first Ibadan (Eba Odan) centuries earlier; the modern city was refounded as a war camp around 1820–1829.

rulers.name: Maye Okunade
rulers.note: Ife warrior who led the war camp that became modern Ibadan; usually counted as the first Baale.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives c. 1820–c. 1830; the Guardian list gives 1820–1826.

rulers.name: Oluyedun (Labosinde)
rulers.note: Baale; the Guardian list names him Oluyedun Labosinde.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives c. 1830–c. 1835.

rulers.name: Lakanle (Agbeni)
rulers.note: Baale.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives c. 1835–c. 1836.

rulers.name: Oluyole (Oja'ba)
rulers.note: Basorun; recognised by Alaafin Atiba as Basorun of the new Oyo kingdom, he built Ibadan into the leading military power of Yorubaland.
rulers.bio: Oluyole was a grandson of Alaafin Abiodun through his mother and one of the Oyo warriors who settled at the Ibadan war camp. In the reorganisation after the fall of Oyo-Ile, Alaafin Atiba made him Basorun, the highest Oyo title below the king, giving Ibadan formal responsibility for defending the Yoruba heartland against Ilorin. He ruled Ibadan from about 1836 to 1850, turning the camp into a town with a strong military organisation and wide control over surrounding districts. His residence area, Oja'ba (Oja Oba), remains a historic centre of the city.
rulers.dispute: The Guardian list gives 1835–1850.

rulers.name: Oderinlo (Opeagbe)
rulers.note: Baale.

rulers.name: Oyesile Olugbode
rulers.note: Baale; long reign during the expansion of Ibadan's power.

rulers.name: Ibikunle
rulers.note: Baale; Ibikunle is also remembered as a leading Ibadan war chief.

rulers.name: Ogunmola
rulers.note: Basorun; leading general of Ibadan in the Ijaye war.

rulers.name: Beyioku Akere I
rulers.note: Balogun.
rulers.dispute: The Guardian list gives 1867–1870.

rulers.name: Orowusi
rulers.note: Baale.

rulers.name: Iyanda Latoosa
rulers.note: Aare Ona Kakanfo; led Ibadan in the long Ekitiparapo (Kiriji) war and died in 1885 while the war was still unresolved.
rulers.bio: Latoosa (also Latosa) rose through Ibadan's military chieftaincies to become ruler of the town in October 1871 with the title Aare Ona Kakanfo, the supreme Yoruba war title. His reign was dominated by the Ekitiparapo or Kiriji war, in which the Ekiti, Ijesa and allies rose against Ibadan's domination from 1877, while Ibadan also faced the Egba, Ijebu and Ilorin. The war became a long stalemate in the hills near Igbajo. He died on 11 August 1885 while Ibadan's forces were still in the field; peace was negotiated with British mediation the following year.
rulers.dispute: The Guardian list gives his name as Oadoke Latoosa.

rulers.name: Ajayi Osungbekun
rulers.note: Balogun.

rulers.name: Fijabi I
rulers.note: Baale; British authority over Ibadan was formalised by an 1893 agreement during his reign.

rulers.name: Osuntoki Olosun
rulers.note: Baale.

rulers.name: Fajinmi
rulers.note: Basorun; the Ibadan Town Council was created in 1897.

rulers.name: Mosaderin
rulers.note: Baale.

rulers.name: Dada Opadare
rulers.note: Baale.

rulers.name: Sunmonu Apampa
rulers.note: Basorun.

rulers.name: Akintayo Awanibaku Elenpe
rulers.note: Baale.

rulers.name: Irefin
rulers.note: Baale.

rulers.name: Shittu
rulers.note: Baale.

rulers.name: Oyewole Aiyejenku (Foko)
rulers.note: The last ruler styled Baale.
rulers.dispute: The Guardian list gives 1925–1930.

rulers.name: Okunola Abaasi Alesinloye
rulers.note: The Olubadan title was revived for him in 1936; reigned through most of the late colonial period.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen ends his reign in October 1936; Wikipedia and the Guardian list give 1930–1946.

rulers.name: Fagbinrin Akere II
rulers.note: Reigned about five months (June–November 1946).

rulers.name: Oyetunde I
rulers.note: Reigned about a month at the end of 1946.
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen gives 26 November–30 December 1946; the Guardian list says about eight months.

rulers.name: Memudu Alli Iwo
rulers.note: Reigned about three months.

rulers.name: Igbintade Apete
rulers.note: A claimant, Bello Akinyo, was briefly named in 1955 but not recognised.

rulers.name: Isaac Babalola Akinyele
rulers.note: The first Olubadan styled 'Oba'; also a historian of Ibadan and later knighted.
rulers.bio: Isaac Babalola Akinyele rose through the Ibadan chieftaincy ranks and became Olubadan on 3 March 1955. He was also a writer, and his outline history of Ibadan is a standard local source on the city's founding. His reign covered the self-government period of the Western Region and Nigeria's independence in 1960, when Ibadan was the regional capital, and he was the first Olubadan formally styled Oba. He died on 30 May 1964.

rulers.name: Yesufu Kobiowu
rulers.note: Reigned about five months (July–December 1964).

rulers.name: Emmanuel Adegboyega Operinde I
rulers.dispute: WorldStatesmen lists him as Emmanuel Adegboyega Adeyemo.

rulers.name: Samuel Odulana Odugade I
rulers.note: A former teacher and politician; crowned at 93 and died in January 2016 aged over 100.
rulers.bio: Samuel Odulana was a teacher and later a politician before rising through the Ibadan chieftaincy ladder. He became Olubadan on 7 July 2007 at the age of 93, one of the oldest men ever crowned in Ibadan. His reign was largely ceremonial and peaceful. He died on 19 January 2016.

rulers.name: Saliu Akanmu Adetunji (Aje Ogunguniso I)
rulers.note: A former music promoter. In 2017 Governor Abiola Ajimobi elevated several high chiefs and baales to beaded-crown obas, provoking a court fight led by the Otun Olubadan, Rashidi Ladoja.

rulers.name: Moshood Olalekan Balogun (Alli Okunmade II)
rulers.note: A former senator; reigned from March 2022 until his death in March 2024. In 2023 the state law was changed to make the 11 high chiefs beaded-crown obas.

rulers.name: Owolabi Akinloye Olakulehin (Ige Olakulehin I)
rulers.note: Rose through the Balogun (military) line; reigned from April 2024 until his death on 7 July 2025.

rulers.name: Rashidi Adewolu Ladoja
rulers.note: Former Governor of Oyo State and Otun Olubadan; approved on 21 August 2025 and crowned at Mapo Hall on 26 September 2025. The reigning Olubadan.
rulers.bio: Rashidi Adewolu Ladoja was born on 25 September 1944 at Gambari near Ibadan. He studied chemical engineering at the University of Liège in Belgium, worked for about 13 years at Total Nigeria and then built businesses in shipping, manufacturing and banking. He was a senator in 1992–93 and Governor of Oyo State from 2003 to 2007; he was impeached in January 2006 but restored that December after the courts declared the impeachment illegal. As Otun Olubadan, head of the civil line, he opposed the elevation of high chiefs to beaded-crown obas in 2017 and 2023, accepting a ceremonial crown only in August 2024. After Olakulehin's death he was named Olubadan-designate, approved by Governor Seyi Makinde on 21 August 2025 and crowned on 26 September 2025, a day after his 81st birthday.

thrones.title: Ewi of Ado-Ekiti
thrones.established: Ancient; founded by Ewi Awamaro from Ile-Ife in tradition (no reliable date)
thrones.about: The Ewi is the paramount ruler of Ado-Ekiti, the capital of Ekiti State, and one of the senior obas of Ekiti, which has 16 historic kingdoms. Tradition traces the dynasty to Awamaro, a prince from Ile-Ife. Only the rulers since the late 19th century can be dated, and sources differ on some of their dates.

authority.text: The Ewi is a traditional ruler whose office is chiefly civil and cultural. Like other Ekiti obas he performs customary rites and presides over the town's festivals, such as the Udiroko new-year festival, but he holds no formal priestly title in Yoruba traditional religion. The office has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Ado tradition says Ewi Awamaro, son of Biritikolu, left Ile-Ife with his father and his uncle Oranmiyan and, after several stops, settled at Ulesun, the site of the present town, where he overcame the earlier ruler, the Elesun. The kingdom grew into one of the larger Ekiti states, with subordinate towns around it.

In the 19th century Ekiti was a battleground for Ibadan, Ilorin and others. The Ekiti kingdoms, with the Ijesa, formed the Ekitiparapo alliance and fought Ibadan in the long Kiriji war (1877–1886), which ended with British-mediated peace. British rule followed in the 1890s, and the Ewi became a member of the Ekiti native authority and its council of obas (Pelupelu).

Daniel Aladesanmi II (1937–1983) was a prominent figure in the Western Region. In 1996 Ekiti State was created from Ondo State with Ado-Ekiti as its capital, a change the current Ewi had campaigned for.
sections.selection: The Ewi is chosen from the royal houses of Ado-Ekiti by the town's kingmakers, after traditional consultations, and approved by the Ekiti State government, which issues the staff of office. A regency may govern during a vacancy, as in 1988–1990.
sections.council: The Ewi rules with his council of high chiefs (Ijoye) and the heads of the town's quarters, and with the obas and baales of subordinate towns. He is a senior member of the Ekiti State Council of Traditional Rulers, which groups obas into classes (A+, A, B and C).
sections.palace: The Ewi's palace stands in the centre of Ado-Ekiti and has been extended in recent decades. The best-known royal festival is Udiroko, which marks the traditional new year and the Ewi's public appearance before his people.
sections.today: The Ewi has no executive powers but is the traditional head of the state capital and a prominent member of the Ekiti State Council of Traditional Rulers. His long reign has been marked by Ado-Ekiti's growth since it became a state capital in 1996.

rulers.name: Awamaro
rulers.note: Founder of the Ewi kingship at Ado in tradition; son of Biritikolu, he left Ile-Ife and settled at Ulesun, the site of Ado-Ekiti.
rulers.bio: Ado tradition says that Awamaro, son of Biritikolu, left Ile-Ife with his father and his uncle Oranmiyan. After stopping at Oba-Ile, Idoani and Agbado – where the elders who stayed behind named their town Agba Ado – he settled at Ulesun, the site of present Ado-Ekiti, and overcame the local ruler there. He is regarded as the first Ewi, and later Ewis claim descent from him. No dates can be given for him.

rulers.name: Atewogboye (Ali Atewogboye)
rulers.note: The Ewi before Aladesanmi I; reigned in the era of the Ekitiparapo war.

rulers.name: Ajimudaoro Aladesanmi I
rulers.note: Founder of the Aladesanmi house; reigned as British rule reached Ekiti.
rulers.dispute: Start dates differ: 1886 (Wikipedia), 1892 (his son's biography) and c. 1902 (WorldStatesmen, perhaps reflecting colonial recognition).

rulers.name: Daniel Akomolafe Anirare Aladesanmi II
rulers.note: Reigned 45 years; a leading Ekiti figure in late colonial and early independent Nigeria.
rulers.bio: Daniel Aladesanmi was born about 1902, a son of Ewi Aladesanmi I. He trained at St Andrew's College, Oyo, where he led the Ekiti Parapo students' society, and worked as a railway officer before becoming Ewi on 18 June 1937. He presided over the Ekiti council of obas (Pelupelu) from 1938, survived protests against his rule in 1940, and promoted local development such as a 1950 weaving centre. He attended the 1948 and 1959 constitutional conferences in London, became deputy president of the Western House of Chiefs in 1960, was made OBE in 1962 and was the first recipient of the CFR in 1978. He was chancellor of the University of Maiduguri from 1979 and died in Ado-Ekiti on 7 January 1983.

rulers.name: Samuel Adeyemi George-Adelabu I
rulers.note: A regency followed (1988–1990).

rulers.name: Rufus Adeyemo Adejugbe Aladesanmi III
rulers.note: The reigning Ewi; marked his 80th birthday and 35 years on the throne in 2025.
rulers.bio: Rufus Adeyemo Adejugbe Aladesanmi was born in 1945 into the Aladesanmi royal family and became Ewi in 1990, succeeding George-Adelabu I after a two-year regency. He was among the Ekiti leaders who campaigned for the creation of Ekiti State, achieved in 1996 with Ado-Ekiti as its capital, which turned his town into a state seat of government. He received the national honour CON in 2000 and has served as chancellor of the University of Jos and of Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University. In 2025 the governor and the President congratulated him on his 80th birthday and 35th coronation anniversary.

thrones.title: Owa Obokun of Ijesaland
thrones.established: Ancient; tradition traces it to Owa Ajibogun, son of Oduduwa; Ilesa founded by Owaluse
thrones.about: The Owa Obokun Adimula is the paramount ruler of the Ijesa people, with his seat at Ilesa. Tradition traces the title to Owa Ajibogun, a son of Oduduwa who fetched sea water (obokun) to heal his father's eyes. The throne rotates among ruling houses descended from earlier Owas. Dates before the 19th century are traditional estimates and the order of rulers differs between lists.

authority.text: The Owa Obokun is a traditional ruler whose office is chiefly civil and cultural. He performs customary rites at installation and presides over Ijesa festivals and the shrines associated with the kingship, but holds no formal priestly title in Yoruba traditional religion. The office has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Ijesa tradition says the first Owa, Ajibogun, was the son of Oduduwa who volunteered to fetch sea water when Ifa prescribed it to cure his father's blindness; he was rewarded with a sword and the right to found a kingdom. His grandson (in most versions) Owaluse founded Ilesa as the capital. Ijesa traditions also make the Akure royal house descend from the Owas through a princess.

The kingdom became one of the major forest states of eastern Yorubaland. Its king list includes several women rulers (the Yeye) and celebrated kings such as Atakunmosa, whose name is borne today by Ilesa's main market and two of its LGAs.

In the 19th century the Ijesa lost land in wars with Ibadan, and in 1877 they joined the Ekiti in the Ekitiparapo alliance, whose army, led by the Ijesa general Ogedengbe, fought Ibadan to a stalemate in the Kiriji war until peace in 1886. British rule followed.

In the 20th century the Owa became a member of the colonial native authority and later of the councils of obas of the Western Region, Oyo State and, since 1991, Osun State. Gabriel Aromolaran II reigned for 42 years (1982–2024). His successor, Clement Adesuyi Haastrup, was chosen in December 2024 amid controversy.
sections.selection: The Owa is chosen from the recognised ruling houses, such as the Bilaro and Biladu lines, according to their turn. Members of the house nominate candidates, the Ijesa kingmakers – a body of 13 senior chiefs – vote, and the Osun State government approves the choice and presents the staff of office. The 2024 selection was criticised because only a few kingmakers voted and because of a pending court case.
sections.council: The Owa rules with his high chiefs (led by titles such as the Obanla and Risawe), whose senior members form the body of kingmakers, and with the obas and baales of the towns of Ijesaland. He is a permanent member of the Osun State Council of Obas.
sections.palace: The Owa's palace (Afin Owa) is in the centre of Ilesa beside the Atakumosa market. Royal occasions include the coronation and the Iwude festival, in which the Owa appears in state before his people.
sections.today: The Owa Obokun has no executive powers but is the senior traditional ruler of Ijesaland and one of the most senior obas in Osun State. The 2024–25 selection of an elderly former deputy governor, and challenges to the procedure, have been the main recent controversies.

rulers.name: Ajibogun
rulers.note: Founder of the Ijesa kingship in tradition: Owa Ajibogun (also called Obokun) fetched sea water to cure the blindness of his father Oduduwa, giving the title Owa Obokun ('the Owa who fetched the sea').
rulers.dispute: Tradition makes him a son of Oduduwa; the Ijesha article also calls him a great-grandson. The date 1100 is a later estimate.

rulers.name: Owaluse
rulers.note: Credited with founding Ilesa ('a homeland we chose') as the capital.
rulers.dispute: The Ijesha article places the founding of Ilesa around 1250 yet dates Owaluse's reign to 1522–1526; both are traditional estimates.

rulers.name: Atakunmosa
rulers.note: One of the best-remembered Owas; the Atakumosa market and LGAs of Ilesa bear his name.

rulers.name: Yeyeladegba
rulers.note: A woman ruler (Yeye).

rulers.name: Yeyegunrogbo
rulers.note: A woman ruler (Yeye).

rulers.name: Yeyewaji
rulers.note: A woman ruler (Yeye).

rulers.name: Yeyeori
rulers.note: A woman ruler (Yeye).

rulers.name: Ofokutu
rulers.dispute: Also dated 1839–1853; Ariyasunle acted as regent in 1839 and 1853.

rulers.name: Oweweniye
rulers.note: Reigned in two spells (1871–1873 and 1873–1874) after a vacancy in 1870–71; the era of the Ekitiparapo alliance against Ibadan.

rulers.name: Adimula Agunloye-bi-Oyinbo
rulers.note: Reigned during the Ekitiparapo (Kiriji) war, in which the Ijesa led the alliance against Ibadan.

rulers.name: Ajimoko I
rulers.note: Reigned April 1896 – September 1901, as British rule was established.

rulers.name: Oduyomade Aromolaran I
rulers.note: Reigned June 1920 – 31 July 1942; a regent (Ajimoko Haastrup) briefly followed.

rulers.name: Ajimoko II (Fidipote)
rulers.note: Reigned 10 September 1942 – 18 October 1956; J. E. Awodiya acted as regent 1956–57.

rulers.name: Biladu III (Fiwajoye)
rulers.note: Reigned until July 1963; Ogunmokun acted as regent 1963–66.

rulers.name: Gabriel Adekunle Aromolaran II
rulers.note: Economist and publisher; installed 15 May 1982 and reigned 42 years.
rulers.bio: Gabriel Adekunle Aromolaran was born in Ilesa on 13 October 1937. He studied economics at University College Ibadan, later earned a PhD in development economics from the University of Ibadan, and rose to deputy permanent secretary in the Western Region civil service before founding Aromolaran Publishing Company in Ibadan in 1971. He became Owa Obokun on 15 May 1982. He wrote books on kingship and textbooks on government and economics, and served as chancellor of the Federal University of Technology, Yola (2002–2014). He died at the Obafemi Awolowo University Teaching Hospital, Ile-Ife, on 11 September 2024, aged about 86–87.
rulers.dispute: He is usually called the 40th Owa Obokun; the Ijesha article's list numbers rulers differently.

rulers.name: Clement Adesuyi Haastrup (Ajimoko III)
rulers.note: Former Deputy Governor of Osun State, from the Bilaro Oluodo ruling house; selected in December 2024 and given his staff of office in May 2025. The reigning Owa.
rulers.bio: Clement Adesuyi Haastrup belongs to the Haastrup family of Ilesa and the Bilaro Oluodo ruling house, and was formerly Deputy Governor of Osun State. After Owa Aromolaran's death he was chosen from ten candidates at a kingmakers' meeting in Ilesa in December 2024, at about 76 – reportedly the oldest person ever selected Owa. Critics alleged that the process was rushed, that few kingmakers took part and that a court injunction was ignored. He took the title Ajimoko III and received his staff of office in May 2025.
rulers.dispute: His middle name is spelled Adesuyi in most reports and Adewuyi in some. He is described as the 41st Owa Obokun by NAN, but as the 49th in the Ijesha article's numbering. Selection dated 27 December 2024 in the Wikipedia list; the Guardian implies an announcement around 20 December.

thrones.title: Deji of Akure
thrones.established: Ancient; present dynasty founded by Omoremilekun Asodeboyede from Ile-Ife (no reliable date); dated king list from 1678
thrones.about: The Deji is the paramount ruler of Akure, capital of Ondo State. The dynasty traces itself to Omoremilekun Asodeboyede, a descendant of Oduduwa, and its emblem is the leopard. Today the throne passes between two branches of the royal house, the Osupa and Ojijigogun families, both descended from Deji Arakale. Dates before 1897 come from WorldStatesmen's reconstruction and are approximate; several women served as rulers or regents.

authority.text: The Deji is a traditional ruler whose office is chiefly civil and cultural. He performs customary rites at installation and presides over Akure festivals such as Aheregbe and Oyemekun, but has no formal priestly title in Yoruba traditional religion. The office has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Akure tradition credits a figure called the Alakure with the first settlement, but the present dynasty is traced to Omoremilekun Asodeboyede, who left Ile-Ife after a test set by Oduduwa and conquered the Alakure. His name Ekun ('leopard') gave Akure its totem.

Akure lay on the frontier between the Yoruba and Benin worlds. A pre-colonial war with Benin is remembered as having drawn Akure and neighbouring Isinkan and Isolo closer together, and Benin influence is visible in some court customs. The dated king list begins in 1678 and includes women rulers such as Eyemoin (1705–1735).

Afunbiowo Adesida I, who came to the throne in 1897 as British rule arrived, reigned for 60 years and made Akure an important administrative town. Many later Dejis were his descendants. When Ondo State was created in 1976, Akure became its capital.

The 2000s were turbulent: a Deji elected in 2003 was disowned, and his successor was deposed by the state government in 2010 for publicly assaulting his wife. Adebiyi Adesida Afunbiowo II reigned briefly (2010–2013), and after a regency Aladetoyinbo Aladelusi (Odundun II) was installed in 2015.
sections.selection: The Deji is chosen from the royal house of Asodeboyede, whose two branches – the Osupa/Odundun and the Ojijigogun families – take turns. The family whose turn it is nominates candidates and the Akure kingmakers vote; the Ondo State government approves the choice. In 2015 the kingmakers chose from 13 candidates of the Osupa family. Princesses have often served as regents during vacancies.
sections.council: The Deji rules with six high chiefs known as the Iwarefa, other titled chiefs and the heads of quarters, and with the obas and baales of the towns around Akure. He is a senior member of the Ondo State Council of Obas.
sections.palace: The Deji's palace stands at the centre of Akure; parts of it are claimed to date back many centuries and it was declared a national monument in 1990. A new, larger palace is being built south of the old grounds. The leopard is the royal emblem.
sections.today: The Deji has no executive powers but is the senior traditional ruler of the Ondo State capital and an influential voice in state affairs. The 2010 deposition remains the best-known recent controversy.

images.caption: The old palace of the Deji, Akure

rulers.name: Omoremilekun Asodeboyede
rulers.note: Founder of the present Akure dynasty in tradition: a descendant of Oduduwa who left Ile-Ife and overcame the earlier ruler, the Alakure. His regnal name Ekun ('leopard') gave Akure its totem.
rulers.dispute: Ijesa tradition also links the Akure royal house to the Owa Obokun through a princess.

rulers.name: Eyemoin
rulers.note: A woman ruler.

rulers.name: Arakale
rulers.note: Long reign; both modern ruling families (Osupa and Ojijigogun) descend from his children.

rulers.name: Osupa I Adelabu
rulers.note: Ancestor of the Osupa ruling family.

rulers.name: Eye Aro Amarop
rulers.note: A woman ruler.

rulers.name: Ojijigogun
rulers.note: Ancestor of the Ojijigogun ruling family.

rulers.name: Afunbiowo Adesida I
rulers.note: Reigned 60 years from 22 June 1897; regarded as the most influential Deji of modern times, and ancestor of several later Dejis. His daughter Adetinu acted as regent in 1957.
rulers.bio: Afunbiowo Adesida I became Deji on 22 June 1897, just as British rule was being established over the Ondo and Ekiti country, and reigned for six decades. He worked within the colonial native-authority system and made Akure a regional administrative centre, laying foundations for its later role as capital of Ondo State. He is remembered as the most influential Deji of recent history, and several of his successors were his direct descendants. He died in 1957.

rulers.name: Gbeje Ademuagun Adesida II
rulers.note: A regency by Adebusola Odutan Adesida followed (1973–75).

rulers.name: Gabriel Adelegan Adesida III
rulers.note: Akure became capital of the new Ondo State in 1976.

rulers.name: Alaiyeluwa Ataiyesi Adesida IV
rulers.note: Reigned until October 1999; Adeyinka Adesida acted as regent afterwards.

rulers.name: Adegbola Adelabu II (Ileri Oluwa I)
rulers.note: Elected in 2003 but disowned in 2005 before being fully established.

rulers.name: Oluwadare Adepoju Adesida (Osupa II)
rulers.note: Installed 26 November 2005; deposed by the Ondo State government on 10 June 2010 for gross misconduct after publicly assaulting his estranged wife.
rulers.dispute: Named Oluwadare Adesida Adepoju Osupa II by WorldStatesmen and Oluwadamilare Adesina Osupa III by other sources.

rulers.name: Adebiyi Adegboye Adesida (Afunbiowo II)
rulers.note: Chosen 13 August 2010; died 30 November 2013. His daughter Adetutu Adesida-Ojei acted as regent until 2015.

rulers.name: Aladetoyinbo Ogunlade Aladelusi (Odundun II)
rulers.note: Architect; selected 17 June 2015 from the Osupa royal family and given his staff of office on 17 July 2015 as the 47th Deji. The reigning Deji.
rulers.bio: Aladetoyinbo Ogunlade Aladelusi was born on 28 December 1956 at Ayede-Ogbese, Akure, son of Prince Ogunlade Aladelusi, the Alayere of Ayede-Ogbese. After schooling in Akure he studied architecture at Florida State University and took a master's degree at Morgan State University in the United States, and practised as an architect and property developer, becoming a founding member of the Architects Registration Council of Nigeria. On 17 June 2015 he was chosen from 13 candidates of the Osupa royal family and received his staff of office on 17 July 2015. His reign, styled an 'epoch of peace', followed a turbulent decade on the throne. He was awarded the CFR in 2022.

thrones.title: Olowo of Owo
thrones.established: 11th century by Owo tradition (Ojugbelu Arere, said to have reigned 1019–1070)
thrones.about: The Olowo is the paramount ruler of Owo, an ancient Yoruba kingdom in Ondo State famous for its ivory carving, its 15th-century terracotta sculptures and the Igogo festival. The dynasty traces itself to Ojugbelu Arere, a descendant of Oduduwa. Early dates are traditional reckonings and the published list has gaps and a repeated entry; corrections are noted below.

authority.text: The Olowo is a traditional ruler whose office also carries ritual duties in Yoruba traditional religion. His installation involves the Iloro chiefs and the Ifa priest of Owo, Ifa is consulted to confirm the eligible princes, and during the Igogo festival the Olowo performs rites in honour of the heroine Oronsen and dresses in women's attire and coral beads as part of the ceremony. The office has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Owo tradition says the kingdom was founded by Ojugbelu Arere, a descendant of Oduduwa who came from the Ife region, and that the town's name, meaning 'respect', comes from his conduct. The king list places him in the 11th century, though these early dates are traditional reckonings. From about 1400 to 1600 Owo was a powerful city-state.

Owo lay between the Yoruba kingdoms and Benin. It kept practical independence from Benin while sometimes paying tribute, and influence flowed both ways: Benin kings imported Owo art and recruited its ivory carvers in the 17th and 18th centuries. Excavations by Ekpo Eyo in 1969–71 uncovered 15th-century terracotta sculptures that link Owo's art to both Ife and Benin traditions. The Aghofen palace, credited to Olowo Rerengejen in the 14th century, became one of the largest palace complexes in Africa.

British rule reached Owo in 1893. The town joined the Western Region in 1947, Western State in 1967 and Ondo State in 1976. In the 1960s the Olowo Sir Olateru Olagbegi II was removed after taking sides in Western Region politics; he returned in 1993, and his son and then a son of his rival succeeded him.

Owo made international news in June 2022 when gunmen attacked a church and killed at least 50 worshippers.
sections.selection: Eligible princes must descend from Olowo Elewuokun, as confirmed through Ifa consultation. The kingmakers, known as the Omolowo, choose the Olowo, and the Iloro chiefs, led by the Akowa, conduct the installation rites. The Ondo State government approves the choice and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The Olowo rules with several councils of chiefs, including the Iloro chiefs (led by the Akowa and including the Ighare and Ugbama), the advising chiefs such as the Edibo Ologho, Sashere, Ojumu, Elerewe and Ajana, and the Ifa priest of Owo. He is a senior member of the Ondo State Council of Obas.
sections.palace: The Aghofen palace in the centre of Owo is said to have had up to 100 courtyards and is a federal national monument; it is often described as the largest palace in Africa. The Owo Museum (founded 1968) holds archaeological finds from the town. The royal festival year is crowned by Igogo, held around September, which honours the heroine Oronsen and features dancing and processions.
sections.today: The Olowo has no executive powers but is the senior traditional ruler of Owo and a leading member of the Ondo State Council of Obas. The 2022 church attack and its aftermath have been a major public concern during the current reign.
