rulers.name: Ojugbelu Arere
rulers.note: First Olowo; described as a direct descendant of Oduduwa. The name Owo ('respect') is linked to a story about his conduct.
rulers.dispute: Dates for the early Olowos are traditional reckonings given by the list and cannot be verified.

rulers.name: Rerengejen
rulers.note: Credited with building the Aghofen palace in the 14th century.

rulers.name: Elewuokun
rulers.note: Long reign; all later Olowos descend from him, according to Owo tradition.

rulers.name: Aghagunghaye
rulers.note: The list records his reign together with his sons.

rulers.name: Aralepo Olubila
rulers.note: Very short reign.

rulers.name: Atanneye I
rulers.note: British rule reached Owo in 1893.

rulers.name: Olateru Olagbegi I
rulers.dispute: The list gives no ruler for 1902–1913.

rulers.name: Olateru Olagbegi II
rulers.note: Removed after siding with S. L. Akintola against Obafemi Awolowo in Western Region politics; went into exile and was restored in 1993.
rulers.bio: Sir Olateru Olagbegi II, born in 1910, became Olowo in 1941 and was one of the leading obas of the Western Region, holding office in its House of Chiefs. In the political crisis of the 1960s he sided with Premier S. L. Akintola against Obafemi Awolowo's faction, and after the fall of the First Republic he was removed from the throne and lived in exile for about 25 years. He was restored as Olowo in 1993 and reigned until his death in 1998. His son Folagbade succeeded him.
rulers.dispute: Sources give 1966 or 1968 for his removal.

rulers.name: Adekola Ogunoye II
rulers.note: Installed after Olagbegi II's removal; left the throne when Olagbegi II was restored. Father of Ogunoye III.
rulers.dispute: His son's biography gives his reign as 1968–1992.

rulers.name: Olateru Olagbegi II (restored)
rulers.note: Second reign after his restoration.
rulers.dispute: The Olowo list gives 1993–1999; he died in 1998.

rulers.name: Folagbade Olateru Olagbegi III
rulers.note: Senior Advocate of Nigeria and former Director-General of the Nigerian Law School.
rulers.bio: Victor Folagbade Olateru-Olagbegi was born in Owo on 26 June 1941, a son of Olowo Olateru Olagbegi II. He was educated at Imade College, Owo, and in England, where he studied law in London, and was called to the Nigerian bar in 1969. He joined the Nigerian Law School as a lecturer in 1975 and rose to be its Director-General, retiring in 1999 as a reader and a Senior Advocate of Nigeria. He succeeded his father as Olowo in 1999 and received his staff of office in December 2003. He died on 16 April 2019, aged 77.

rulers.name: Ajibade Gbadegesin Ogunoye III
rulers.note: Lawyer and former permanent secretary in the Ondo State civil service; crowned 14 December 2019. The reigning Olowo.
rulers.bio: Ajibade Gbadegesin Ogunoye was born in Owo on 6 July 1966, a son of Olowo Adekola Ogunoye II and Olori Adenike Ogunoye. He trained as a lawyer and was called to the Nigerian bar, then worked in the Ondo State public service, rising to director of finance and permanent secretary. He emerged as Olowo-elect in July 2019 after the death of Olagbegi III and was crowned on 14 December 2019, when Governor Rotimi Akeredolu presented his staff of office. He has promoted the Igogo festival as a cultural and tourist event. In June 2022 his town suffered a deadly attack on a church in which at least 50 worshippers were killed.

rulers.dispute: Wikipedia calls him the 32nd Olowo; the numbering here follows the list without repeating Olagbegi II.

thrones.title: Oba of Lagos
thrones.established: c. 1600–1630 (Ashipa, under Benin authority); first crowned king Ado
thrones.about: The Oba of Lagos is the traditional ruler of Lagos, Nigeria's largest city, with his palace at Iga Idunganran on Lagos Island. The line begins with Ashipa, an Awori war captain authorised by the Oba of Benin, and Lagos paid tribute to Benin until about 1830. Earlier rulers were styled Ologun or Eleko. Dates before the 19th century are approximate; restored reigns are listed separately.

authority.text: The Oba of Lagos is a traditional ruler whose office is civil and ceremonial; it has no formal priestly title in Yoruba traditional religion. The Eyo masquerade, which honours deceased obas and chiefs and pays homage to the reigning Oba, and other customary rites are closely tied to the throne and the palace. The office has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Lagos Island was settled by Awori Yoruba before Benin extended its power along the lagoon in the 16th century. Ashipa, an Awori war captain of the Oba of Benin, was given authority over Lagos, along with a sword and royal drum, and Benin sent officials led by Eletu Odibo, who became the first of the Akarigbere white-cap chiefs. Ado, Ashipa's successor, is counted as the first king, and Benin long claimed the right to confirm each new Oba.

In the 18th and early 19th centuries Lagos grew into a leading Atlantic slave-trading port, and rivalry between branches of the royal family was intense. Tribute to Benin stopped around 1830. Kosoko seized the throne from his uncle Akitoye in 1845; Britain, then suppressing the slave trade, bombarded Lagos in December 1851 and restored Akitoye.

In 1861 Akitoye's son Dosunmu signed the Treaty of Cession, making Lagos a British colony. The Oba (styled Eleko in colonial times) remained head of the indigenous community. Eshugbayi Eleko's deportation in 1925 and his restoration in 1931 after a Privy Council appeal became a landmark in Lagos nationalist politics, and Adeniji Adele's accession in 1949 was likewise contested in court.

After independence Lagos served as federal capital until 1991. Adeyinka Oyekan II reigned from 1965 to 2003, and Rilwan Akiolu, a retired police officer, has reigned since 2003.
sections.selection: The Oba is chosen from the royal descendants of Ologun Kutere and related branches (such as the Akitoye, Dosunmu, Oyekan and Adele lines; the Akinsemoyin family also claims eligibility). The Akarigbere kingmakers, led by the Eletu Odibo, select the candidate after consultations, and the Lagos State government confirms the choice.
sections.council: The Oba's chiefs are the 'white-cap' (Idejo and Akarigbere) chiefs and other titled ranks. The Idejo chiefs, such as the Oniru, Elegushi, Ojora and Aromire, are hereditary landowning chiefs of Lagos, several of whom are now obas in their own right; the Akarigbere chiefs, of Benin origin, are kingmakers and palace counsellors.
sections.palace: Iga Idunganran on Lagos Island has been the royal residence since about the 17th century and is a tourist site. The Eyo festival – white-clad masqueraders who parade from Idumota to the palace – is held to honour deceased obas and chiefs or for special occasions; one tradition dates the first Lagos procession to 1854, in memory of Akitoye.
sections.today: The Oba of Lagos has no executive powers but is the most prominent traditional ruler in Lagos State and chairs its Council of Obas and Chiefs. Akiolu's political statements, the 2020 palace invasion and the Akinsemoyin family's legal challenge have been the main recent controversies.

rulers.name: Ashipa
rulers.note: An Awori war captain of the Oba of Benin, given authority over Lagos with a sword and royal drum; never crowned, but all later Obas trace their line to him.

rulers.name: Ado
rulers.note: Counted as the first King of Lagos; the Iga Idunganran palace site dates from about his time.

rulers.name: Akinsemoyin
rulers.note: Ancestor of the Akinsemoyin royal family, which still contests the succession.

rulers.name: Ologun Kutere
rulers.note: Ancestor of most later Obas of Lagos.

rulers.name: Adele Ajosun
rulers.note: First reign; returned to the throne in 1832.

rulers.name: Adele Ajosun (restored)
rulers.note: Second reign. Lagos stopped paying regular tribute to Benin around 1830.

rulers.name: Akitoye
rulers.note: Driven out by his nephew Kosoko; went into exile at Badagry and sought British support.

rulers.name: Kosoko
rulers.note: Removed when British naval forces bombarded Lagos in December 1851 ('Ogun Ahoyaya'); the last Oba to send gifts to Benin.
rulers.bio: Kosoko, a prince of the Ologun Kutere line, seized the throne from his uncle Akitoye in 1845. Lagos was then a major Atlantic slave-trading port, and Kosoko was closely allied with the slave traders. Britain, now campaigning against the trade, backed Akitoye and attacked Lagos; after fighting on 26–28 December 1851 Kosoko's forces were defeated and he fled to Epe on the lagoon. He later made terms with the British and returned to Lagos, where he died in 1872.

rulers.name: Akitoye (restored)
rulers.note: Restored by the British; signed an 1852 treaty against the slave trade and ended allegiance to Benin.

rulers.name: Dosunmu (Docemo)
rulers.note: Signed the Lagos Treaty of Cession in August 1861, making Lagos a British colony; kept his title and a pension.
rulers.bio: Dosunmu succeeded his father Akitoye in 1853, when the British consul already exercised strong influence in Lagos. In August 1861, under pressure from a British naval force, he signed the treaty that ceded Lagos to the British Crown, after which the Oba kept his title and a pension but lost sovereignty. He reigned for another two decades as a ceremonial and customary authority over Lagos Island and died in 1885. His descendants form one of the main branches of the royal family.

rulers.name: Eshugbayi Eleko
rulers.note: Suspended in 1919 and deposed and deported to Oyo in August 1925 after clashing with the colonial government (the 'Eleko affair'); restored in 1931.
rulers.bio: Eshugbayi Eleko, a son of Dosunmu, was recognised as Oba (then styled Eleko) by Governor MacGregor in 1901. He was drawn into Lagos politics through the nationalist Herbert Macaulay, and in 1919 the colonial government withdrew recognition after he approved Muslim chieftaincy appointments it opposed. After further disputes the government deposed him and deported him to Oyo in August 1925. His lawyers took the case to the Privy Council, and in 1931 Governor Donald Cameron settled the matter and allowed him to return. He died on 24 October 1932 and was buried at Iga Idunganran.

rulers.name: Ibikunle Akitoye
rulers.note: Installed by the colonial government during Eleko's exile.

rulers.name: Sanusi Olusi
rulers.note: Gave up Iga Idunganran when Eleko was restored.

rulers.name: Eshugbayi Eleko (restored)
rulers.note: Second reign after his return from exile.
rulers.dispute: Wikipedia's list dates the second reign to 1932 only.

rulers.name: Adeniji Adele II
rulers.note: Former surveyor and civil servant; his accession was contested in court until the Privy Council upheld it in 1957.
rulers.bio: Musendiku Buraimoh Adeniji Adele was born in Lagos on 13 November 1893, a grandson of Oba Adele Ajosun. He trained as a surveyor, served with the Cameroon Expeditionary Force in the First World War, accompanied Chief Amodu Tijani Oluwa to London for the famous Oluwa land case in 1920, and later rose to chief clerk in the colonial treasury. He became Oba on 1 October 1949 with the support of the Nigerian Youth Movement and Awolowo's Egbe Omo Oduduwa, while the NNDP and NCNC challenged his eligibility; the Privy Council upheld his title in 1957. He was made CBE in 1956 and KBE in 1962, and died on 12 July 1964.

rulers.name: Adeyinka Oyekan II
rulers.note: Reigned almost four decades through military and civilian governments, and through the move of the federal capital from Lagos to Abuja (1991).

rulers.name: Rilwan Akiolu I
rulers.note: Retired Assistant Inspector-General of Police; chosen 23 May 2003 and crowned 9 August 2003. The reigning Oba.
rulers.bio: Rilwan Babatunde Osuolale Aremu Akiolu was born in Lagos on 29 October 1943. He joined the Nigeria Police Force in 1970 and served for about 32 years, retiring in 2002 as an assistant inspector-general. The Lagos kingmakers chose him on 23 May 2003, the state confirmed him as the 21st Oba, and he was crowned on 9 August 2003. His reign has drawn controversy: remarks threatening Igbo residents ahead of the 2015 governorship election were widely condemned, and during the #EndSARS unrest of October 2020 protesters invaded his palace and briefly carried off his staff of office. The Akinsemoyin royal family has long challenged his accession in court. He turned 80 in 2023.
rulers.dispute: Usually called the 21st Oba of Lagos (counting Ashipa and the restored reigns differently from this list).

thrones.title: Soun of Ogbomoso
thrones.established: Mid-17th century (Ogunlola, said to have reigned 1659–1714)
thrones.about: The Soun is the paramount ruler of Ogbomoso, a large Oyo-Yoruba city founded in the 17th century by the hunter Ogunlola. Early rulers were styled Baale and their dates are traditional; the published list has gaps and overlaps. The present Soun's selection was challenged in court and upheld on appeal in 2025.

authority.text: The Soun is a traditional ruler whose office is civil and cultural, without a formal priestly title in Yoruba traditional religion; he performs customary rites at installation and presides over town festivals. The office has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Ogbomoso grew from the settlement of Ogunlola, a hunter probably of Bariba origin, in the mid-17th century. Its name recalls his killing of the raider Elemoso, who had harassed the Oyo kingdom; the Alaafin is said to have honoured Ogunlola, who preferred to stay at his settlement and became the first Soun.

Ogbomoso lay on the northern frontier of the Oyo Empire. When Oyo collapsed and the Fulani-led Ilorin emirate expanded in the 19th century, about 147 towns and villages were deserted and many of their people sought refuge in Ogbomoso, which grew into one of the largest Yoruba towns.

Under British rule the Soun (then styled Baale) headed the local native authority, and from the 1950s holders were styled Oba. Jimoh Oyewumi (1973–2021) reigned for 48 years, built a modern palace and was the first Soun to wear a beaded crown. After his death the selection of Ghandi Olaoye was contested in the courts.
sections.selection: The Soun is chosen from the royal houses of Ogbomoso by the kingmakers (Afobaje); in 1973, 92 of 94 kingmakers voted for Oyewumi. The Oyo State government approves the choice and presents the staff of office. Disputes over nomination procedure can be taken to court, as in 2023–2025.
sections.council: The Soun rules with a traditional council (the Ilus) of seven principal titleholders led by the Areago, who acts as the Soun's deputy and guarantor of political continuity, and with other chiefs and quarter heads. He is a member of the Oyo State Council of Obas.
sections.palace: The Soun's palace stands on the site of Ogunlola's compound by the Ajagbon tree, a rallying point for the people of Ogbomoso; a modern palace was built under Oyewumi. Royal occasions include coronation anniversaries and town festivals.
sections.today: The Soun has no executive power but is the senior traditional ruler of Ogbomoso and an important figure in Oyo State. The court fight over Olaoye's selection, upheld by the Court of Appeal in February 2025 with a Supreme Court appeal threatened, is the main recent controversy.

rulers.name: Olabanjo Ogunlola Ogundiran
rulers.note: Founder and first Soun: a hunter, probably of Ibariba (Bariba) origin, whose settlement became Ogbomoso after he killed the raider Elemoso.
rulers.bio: Ogunlola is remembered as a hunter, probably of Bariba origin, who settled near the Ajagbon tree in the mid-17th century. When a raider named Elemoso harassed the Oyo country, Ogunlola killed him, and his settlement became known as the place of the one who took Elemoso's head (Ogbori Elemoso), later shortened to Ogbomoso. Tradition says the Alaafin, impressed, invited him to Oyo-Ile, but he chose to remain at his settlement. He became the first Soun and set up the town's political and defensive organisation; his compound by the Ajagbon tree became the site of the palace.
rulers.dispute: The early rulers after Ogunlola are listed with the title Baale; the dates are traditional.

rulers.name: Toyeje Akanni

rulers.name: Olaoye Atanda Orumogege
rulers.note: Long reign; ancestor of the present Soun.

rulers.name: Bello Afolabi Oyewumi Ajagungbade II
rulers.note: Father of Jimoh Oyewumi.

rulers.name: Jimoh Oladunni Oyewumi (Ajagungbade III)
rulers.parent: Son of Bello Afolabi Oyewumi Ajagungbade II
rulers.note: Businessman; reigned 48 years, the longest of any Soun, and was the first Soun to wear a beaded crown.
rulers.bio: Jimoh Oladunni Oyewumi was born in Ogbomoso on 27 May 1926, a son of Soun Bello Afolabi Oyewumi. After his father's death in 1940 he left school and from 1944 traded in Jos, later founding a hotel business. In 1973 the kingmakers chose him by 92 votes out of 94; he succeeded Salami Itabiyi on 24 October and was crowned on 14 December 1973 as Ajagungbade III. He built a modern palace, promoted industry in Ogbomoso and became the first Soun to wear a beaded crown, which caused controversy among Yoruba obas. He died on 12 December 2021, aged 95, after a 48-year reign.

rulers.name: Ghandi Afolabi Olaoye (Orumogege III)
rulers.note: Descendant of Soun Olaoye Orumogege; crowned by Governor Seyi Makinde in 2023. A high court nullified his selection in October 2023, but the Court of Appeal upheld it in February 2025. The reigning Soun.
rulers.bio: Ghandi Afolabi Olaoye is a descendant of the 9th Soun, Olaoye Orumogege, and was chosen to succeed Oyewumi after a long vacancy. Governor Seyi Makinde presented his staff of office and he was crowned in 2023 as Orumogege III. On 25 October 2023 an Oyo State High Court sitting in Ogbomoso declared his nomination irregular and void, but in February 2025 the Court of Appeal in Ibadan set that ruling aside, holding that the lower court lacked jurisdiction; his rivals said they would go to the Supreme Court.

rulers.dispute: Wikipedia gives his coronation as 21 December 2023 but lists his reign from 2024; he is called the 28th Soun, although the published list has fewer names.

thrones.title: Ataoja of Osogbo
thrones.established: Founded by Larooye Gbadewolu, who moved his people from Ipole (traditionally 17th–18th century)
thrones.about: The Ataoja is the paramount ruler of Osogbo, capital of Osun State. The title is explained as 'one who stretches out his hand and takes the fish', recalling the founding covenant between the first king, Larooye, and the river goddess Osun. The Ataoja leads the Osun-Osogbo festival in the UNESCO-listed sacred grove. Early dates are traditional and regnal numbering differs between sources.

authority.text: The Ataoja is a sacred king in Yoruba traditional religion as well as a traditional ruler. His office rests on the founding covenant with the river goddess Osun, and each year he leads the Osun-Osogbo festival, in which he performs rites in the sacred grove with the Arugba (the votive maiden who carries the offerings), the Osun priestesses and other priests. He is regarded as the custodian of the Osun shrine and grove. The office has no formal role in Christianity or Islam.

sections.history:
Osogbo tradition says that Oba Larooye of Ipole, suffering from repeated droughts, sent his hunter Timehin to find a better home. The hunters reached the Osun river, and Larooye moved his people there, building his first palace at Idi-Osun while Timehin built the Ogun shrine at Idi-Ogun. In the founding story the river goddess Osun accepted the settlers on condition that they honour her, and the king's title commemorates the fish that came to his hand as a sign of the pact.

Osogbo grew in the 19th century as refugees arrived after the fall of Oyo. Around 1840 an Ibadan army defeated the forces of Ilorin near Osogbo, halting the southward advance of the Ilorin emirate, after which Osogbo was in Ibadan's sphere.

Under British rule the railway reached Osogbo in the early 20th century and it became a busy trading town. From the 1950s the Austrian-born artist Susanne Wenger and local artists restored the sacred grove with new sculptures, and Osogbo became famous for its modern art movement. In 1991 it became the capital of the new Osun State, and in 2005 the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
sections.selection: The Ataoja is chosen in turn from the recognised ruling houses descended from earlier Ataojas (such as the Lahanmi/Matanmi line). The ruling house nominates candidates, the Osogbo kingmakers choose, Ifa is consulted, and the Osun State government approves the choice and presents the staff of office.
sections.council: The Ataoja rules with his council of high chiefs and quarter heads, and with the priests and priestesses of Osun and other orisa who serve the grove and festival. He is a permanent member of the Osun State Council of Obas, where the ranking of the Ataoja relative to other obas such as the Oluwo of Iwo has been disputed.
sections.palace: The present palace stands in the centre of Osogbo; the old palace building is now part of the Oja Oba market. The Osun-Osogbo festival, held each August, culminates in a procession to the sacred grove led by the Ataoja and the Arugba, drawing large crowds of devotees and tourists. The Ataoja has also promoted local adire (tie-dye) cloth at the festival.
sections.today: The Ataoja has no executive powers but, as ruler of the state capital and custodian of the Osun festival, is one of the most visible obas in Osun State. Recent controversies include disputes over the ranking of obas on the state council and criticism of his public political statements in 2026.

rulers.name: Larooye Gbadewolu
rulers.note: Founder: moved his people from Ipole to the banks of the Osun river and, in tradition, made a pact with the river goddess Osun.
rulers.bio: Larooye ruled at Ipole, where repeated droughts destroyed farms and livestock. He sent his chief hunter Timehin and other hunters to look for a better site, and they found the Osun river. Larooye moved his people and their market to the new place; his first palace stood at Idi-Osun, by the river, while Timehin built the Ogun shrine at Idi-Ogun. Tradition says the river goddess Osun promised to protect and multiply the settlers if they honoured her, a covenant renewed every year in the Osun-Osogbo festival. He is said to have died in 1760.
rulers.dispute: Dates for the earliest Ataojas are traditional; the founding of Osogbo is often placed in the 17th century.

sections.title: What a traditional ruler is
sections.text:
A traditional ruler in Nigeria is the recognised head of a community, clan, kingdom or emirate whose office comes from custom and history rather than from election. The titles differ from people to people: Emir and Sultan in much of the North, Oba among the Yoruba and Edo, Obi, Igwe and Eze among the Igbo, Obong among the Efik and Ibibio, Amanyanabo in the Ijaw city-states, Olu among the Itsekiri, Ovie and Orodje among the Urhobo and Okpe, Attah among the Igala, Tor Tiv among the Tiv and Aku Uka among the Jukun.

Today these rulers are non-sovereign monarchs. They hold no formal executive, legislative or judicial power under the Nigerian constitution, yet they keep wide respect and influence. In practice they act as custodians of culture and custom, as a bridge between communities and government, as mediators in local disputes, and as conferrers of chieftaincy titles.

Many thrones are centuries old and descend from independent precolonial states; others were created or upgraded during the colonial era or by state governments after independence. A few, such as the office of Tor Tiv (created in 1947 for the Tiv, who had no centralised king), were invented to give a decentralised people a single recognised head.

sections.title: History: from sovereign states to state-recognised rulers
sections.text:
Before colonial rule, the territory that became Nigeria held many kinds of government. There were large states and empires such as Kanem-Borno, the Oyo Empire, the Benin Kingdom and, from the early nineteenth century, the Sokoto Caliphate, whose emirs owed allegiance to the Sultan of Sokoto. There were coastal trading city-states such as Bonny, Calabar, Brass and Lagos, and there were many societies, notably among the Igbo and Tiv, where authority was spread among elders, title societies and age grades rather than held by one king.

British rule changed these rulers from sovereigns into subordinate 'native authorities'. Through treaties of 'protection' and conquest between the 1880s and early 1900s, and then under Frederick Lugard's system of indirect rule, the colonial state governed through existing rulers, using them to collect tax, keep order and run native courts. Indirect rule worked most smoothly in the emirates of the North. Where no single ruler existed, as in much of Igboland, the British appointed 'warrant chiefs', an imposition that was widely resented and helped spark the 1929 Women's War in the South-East.

At independence in 1960 each region had a House of Chiefs, and rulers sat in legislatures and even held executive posts: the Ooni of Ife, Oba Adesoji Aderemi, served as Governor of the Western Region from 1960 to 1962. Military rule from 1966 and the 1976 Local Government Reform, which created a uniform system of elected local councils, removed traditional rulers from formal administration and left them in advisory traditional councils. Some politicians have since blamed that change for weakening grassroots intelligence and security.

The 1999 Constitution, like the current framework generally, is silent on traditional rulers and gives them no defined role, although the 1979 Constitution had made room for traditional rulers on the National Council of State. Rulers' bodies have repeatedly asked for constitutional recognition, and in October 2025 President Bola Tinubu publicly backed the idea, but no amendment had been adopted at the time of writing.

sections.title: Legal status: chieftaincy laws, grading and deposition
sections.text:
Because the federal constitution says nothing about them, traditional rulers are regulated by each of the 36 states through their own Chiefs, Chieftaincy or Traditional Rulers Laws. These laws set out which stools are recognised, which ruling houses may produce candidates, how kingmakers select a candidate, and how the government approves the choice. A ruler only becomes the legal holder of a stool once the state governor approves the selection and presents a staff of office (in many northern states, a letter and staff of appointment).

Most states grade their rulers, a practice inherited from the colonial era. Rulers are typically ranked as first-, second- or third-class, with first-class rulers heading the oldest or largest domains and sitting at the top of state councils. Grading affects precedence, stipends and status, and upgrades are politically sensitive: in 2010, for example, Kwara State recognised the Emir of Kaiama as first-class while two new stools were graded third-class. In the South-East, Cross River and Akwa Ibom, the laws often recognise 'paramount rulers' of local government areas or clans and the heads of autonomous communities, rather than old kingdoms alone.

The same laws give governors strong powers over rulers. Governors can suspend or depose a ruler, withdraw recognition and the staff of office, split a domain, or create new stools, usually 'in the interest of peace, order and good government'. Recent examples include Bayelsa's removal of the paramount ruler of Swali community in mid-2026 over insecurity, under section 6 of the state's Chieftaincy Law; Edo's removal of the Okuokpellagbe of Okpella in April 2025, which a state High Court declared null and void in March 2026; and court cases such as the 2023 Ondo judgment that annulled the appointment of a first-class oba because he was not from the ruling house whose turn it was. Disputes over who is the rightful heir frequently end in court.

sections.title: Councils of traditional rulers
sections.text:
Every state has a council of traditional rulers (named variously as a Council of Chiefs, Council of Obas and Chiefs, Traditional Rulers Council or Council of Ndi Eze), set up by state law to advise the government on custom, chieftaincy and community matters. Some councils have a permanent chair held by the most senior ruler; in others, especially in the South-East and South-South, the governor appoints or the members elect a chairman for a term. Enugu State's 8th council, inaugurated in 2024 and chaired by Igwe Samuel Asadu, was asked by the governor to serve as the government's 'eyes and ears' on community security.

At the national level, the National Council of Traditional Rulers of Nigeria (NCTRN) brings together senior rulers from all states. It is co-chaired by the Sultan of Sokoto, Muhammad Sa'ad Abubakar, and the Ooni of Ife, Adeyeye Enitan Ogunwusi. A Senate bill sponsored by Senator Simon Lalong, which passed second reading in March 2025, would make these two thrones permanent co-chairs. It drew strong objections from Ohanaeze Ndigbo, the Middle Belt Forum and others, who argued that it sidelined other traditional institutions and, in the Forum's view, tilted the council towards one religion; they proposed rotation or election instead.

Regional bodies also exist. In the North, emirs and chiefs meet in state councils and in a regional council of northern traditional rulers in which the Sultan is the senior figure. In the South, the Southern Nigeria Traditional Rulers Council was inaugurated at Owerri, Imo State, around 1 August 2024, with the Ooni of Ife as chairman and rulers from 17 southern states attending; its stated aim is unity and mutual respect among the South's cultures, although some South-East monarchs publicly questioned its membership and mandate. Diaspora and community groups, such as the council of Akwa Ibom traditional rulers and religious leaders in the FCT, also organise rulers away from their home states.

sections.title: What traditional rulers do today
sections.text:
Peace and security are the most cited roles. Rulers know their communities, can identify strangers and are often the first to hear of trouble, so governments regularly ask them to support policing, community vigilance and early warning; Rivers State, for instance, has tasked its rulers with preventing gender-based violence. Many rulers also say they are seldom consulted before security decisions in their domains, and they continue to press for a defined constitutional role.

Rulers have been decisive in public-health campaigns. In northern Nigeria, partnerships with traditional institutions from 2009 onward, including the Sultan's foundation and the Engagement of Traditional Institutions project, saw emirs and district heads run vaccination drives from their palaces, accompany vaccinators and persuade hesitant parents. These efforts are credited with helping Nigeria end wild poliovirus, certified in 2020, and they continue against circulating variant poliovirus.

Education and social reform are another field. UNICEF has documented village heads in Kebbi State who wrote to education officials, bought uniforms for poor children and persuaded parents to move children from Quranic-only schooling into primary school. In the South-East, rulers such as the Obi of Onitsha and the Igwe of Nnewi have led moves to abolish the Osu caste system, a matter that state courts and governments have largely left to traditional institutions.

Rulers also mediate land and boundary disputes, chieftaincy quarrels and inter-communal conflicts, as in peace efforts around the Ife–Modakeke and Tiv–Jukun conflicts, and they remain custodians of festivals, language and heritage such as the Ofala of Onitsha, the durbars of the northern emirates and the Igue festival in Benin. Their palaces are routine stops for politicians seeking endorsement, which brings both influence and accusations of partisanship.

sections.title: Traditional authority and religious authority
sections.text:
In much of northern Nigeria there is often no clear line between a traditional ruler and a religious leader. The emirates descend from the Sokoto Caliphate, an Islamic state founded in a jihad in the early 1800s. The Sultan of Sokoto carries the title Sarkin Musulmi (Commander of the Faithful), is the President-General of the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs and is the senior Muslim leader in the country, while emirs such as those of Kano, Zazzau and Gwandu, and the Shehu of Borno, lead their people both as monarchs and as Islamic leaders, for example in announcing the sighting of the new moon, leading Eid prayers and overseeing the appointment of imams.

In many southern and Middle Belt kingdoms, by contrast, kingship is sacred within indigenous religion. The Oba of Benin, the Ooni of Ife, the Eze Nri, the Attah of Igala and the Aku Uka of the Jukun are seen as ritual figures who link their people with ancestors and deities; their installation includes seclusion and rites, and they preside over shrines and festivals. Many Yoruba stools are bound up with Ifa, orisa cults and societies such as Osugbo/Ogboni. Elsewhere, especially among the Igbo autonomous communities and many paramount rulers created in the twentieth century, the office is mainly civil, with only ceremonial religious elements, and holders are commonly Christians or Muslims.

This mix matters in public life. It shapes how rulers are appointed (emirs are expected to be Muslims of the ruling dynasty, and religious credentials count); it feeds into debates over Sharia, which was extended to criminal law in twelve northern states from 1999; and it fuels interfaith tension where a Muslim emirate system covers Christian or traditional-religion communities. In Southern Kaduna, for example, separate chiefdoms were created in 2000–2001 after disputes, and a later move to restyle four chiefdom rulers as emirs drew protests. In the South-West, Christian or Muslim obas sometimes resist traditional rites: Ogun State's 2020 bill to let rulers be installed and buried according to their own faith was opposed by traditional worshippers, and the Islamic burial of the Awujale of Ijebuland in July 2025 led Ifa adherents to threaten legal action.

A related debate is whether senior rulers who are also religious leaders should hold national positions. The opposition to making the Sultan a permanent co-chair of the national council partly rested on the argument that a religious office should not lead a body representing a secular, multi-faith country, while supporters point to the Sultan's long role as a voice for peace and coexistence.

sections.title: Controversies: depositions, splits and succession
sections.text:
The most prominent recent dispute concerns Kano. Muhammadu Sanusi II became Emir of Kano in June 2014. In 2019 Governor Abdullahi Ganduje's government created four new emirates (Bichi, Rano, Karaye and Gaya) from the Kano domain, and on 9 March 2020 it deposed Sanusi and installed Aminu Ado Bayero. In May 2024 a new administration under Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf repealed the law, dissolved the four emirates, removed Bayero and reinstated Sanusi. Conflicting judgments followed, and in April 2026 the Supreme Court adjourned the appeal to April 2027. Meanwhile Sanusi occupies the main Gidan Rumfa palace and Bayero the smaller Nassarawa palace, each claiming the throne.

Kano is not unique. Governors have repeatedly split large emirates and kingdoms or created new stools, often in ways that reward allies or weaken rivals: Yobe expanded from four emirates to thirteen in 2000, and several states have multiplied first-class stools. Politicisation runs in both directions, since rulers frequently endorse governors and presidents, and governors use recognition, stipends, vehicles and staff of office as levers. Nigeria's history also has older examples, such as the deposition of the Olu of Warri in 1964 and his reinstatement in 1966, and the 1984 travel restrictions placed on the Ooni of Ife and the Emir of Kano.

Succession disputes are common because many thrones rotate among several ruling houses and rely on kingmakers whose own legitimacy can be contested. Recent examples include the long contest over the Obong of Calabar, the extended selection process for a new Awujale of Ijebuland after Oba Sikiru Adetona's death in July 2025, and contested regencies in several Niger Delta kingdoms. Such disputes can last years, involve rival coronations and end only in the Supreme Court.

sections.title: Women and traditional rule
sections.text:
Traditional rule in Nigeria has been male-dominated, but women have long held power. Legend and chronicle place women at the foundations of several states: Ebulejonu is remembered as the first Attah of Igala, succeeded by her brother; Amina of Zazzau, whose exact dates are disputed but are often given as the late sixteenth century, is remembered as a warrior ruler credited with city walls; and Moremi of Ile-Ife is honoured in Yoruba tradition as the heroine who saved Ife. Daura's founding traditions also feature a line of queens.

Many kingdoms have powerful women's offices alongside the king. In Benin, Oba Esigie created the title of Iyoba (Queen Mother) for his mother Idia in the early sixteenth century; the Iyoba had her own palace at Uselu and ranked with senior chiefs. Among the western Igbo of Delta State, the Omu is a female ruler responsible for women and markets; Obi Martha Dunkwu, the Omu of Anioma, was widely described as the only woman king in Delta State until her death. Yoruba towns have women chiefs such as the Iyalode, and northern palaces have titled women such as the Magajiya and Iya.

Women still occasionally hold thrones in their own right. In Kumbwada, a small Muslim community in Niger State, the throne has passed through six generations of women, and the current ruler is known for promoting girls' education. In colonial Enugu-Ezike, Ahebi Ugbabe served as a warrant chief from about 1918 and then as eze (king) in the 1920s and 1930s, the only recognised female king in colonial Nigeria. Women regents have also governed Yoruba kingdoms during interregna. In the 1950s, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti and Margaret Ekpo sat in the regional Houses of Chiefs, reflecting the political role of women leaders.
